lessons.title: The Territory
lessons.blurb: Six regions between a cache line and two capsules on a screen. Start anywhere.

chapters.title: This is a map, not a menu
chapters.text: What you are looking at is the whole territory on one screen. Six regions, roughly ordered from the silicon at the left to a running game at the right. The arrows are roads, not prerequisites. Nothing here demands that you read it in order, and the fastest way to ruin this is to treat it as a list to get through. Pick the region that annoys you most and go there.

chapters.title: Start on the ground if you think in cache lines
chapters.text: The far left is memory, and it is the shortest path in for anyone who has ever cared about a stride. Entities are not objects scattered across the heap. They are rows in fixed size blocks of sixteen kilobytes, one contiguous array per component type, and every design decision above this one falls out of that arrangement. If you understand the chunk you can derive most of the rest by reasoning.

chapters.title: The middle is where it stops being local
chapters.text: Then the wire, and the moment the story stops being about one process. The rule is small enough to hold in one sentence. The client sends intent. The server sends truth. Nothing else crosses, ever. Two floats saying which direction somebody wants to move, going one way, and delta compressed snapshots coming back the other way. Every complication in this whole handbook is a consequence of those two sentences and the fact that they take time.

chapters.title: Where it gets genuinely hard
chapters.text: Just past the wire is the part that catches everyone, and it is the reason this map exists at all. The client is running two clocks. Some entities are played back from the past, some are guessed forward into the future, and which is which depends on who owns them. Then the rollback loop next to it is what fixes the guesses. Then under load, with real latency and a player who is willing to modify the client, everything you assumed gets tested.

chapters.title: The blank regions are real
chapters.text: Two regions on this map have no maps behind them yet. The engine's update loop, and the stack of libraries we build on. Both have written chapters, neither has been drawn. I have left them on the map rather than hiding them, because a map that only shows the surveyed parts is a brochure. The atlas plans forty of these. Twelve exist. That gap is the honest state of the work, and it is also where the interesting problems are.

chunk.short: Sixteen kilobytes, one allocation, one stride. The ground floor.
chunk.deep: This is where the entity component system stops being a design pattern and becomes an actual memory layout you can measure. A header, then one contiguous array per component type, and an entity that is nothing but a shared subscript into all of them. If you have ever hand tuned a loop for the prefetcher, this will feel familiar in a way that surprises you.

machine.short: Worlds, systems, jobs — one process, several isolated universes.
machine.deep: A world is a complete isolated instance: its own entities, its own systems, its own memory. A client world and a server world can sit in the same process, tick one after the other in the same frame, and share absolutely nothing. That isolation is what makes the security model possible and what makes debugging confusing.

loop.short: Bootstrap, system groups, baking. Chapters written, no map yet.
loop.deep: This region covers where your world actually comes from: the custom bootstrap that creates it, the tree of system groups that decides what runs when, and the baking step that turns editor objects into entities. That last one is a compile step that nobody tells you is a compile step, which is why the errors from it are so surprising the first time.

stack.short: Core, Grove, Canopy, Nerve. Commercial packages, no map yet.
stack.deep: The layer between the engine and our game. The interesting one is Grove, which is a visual graph on the surface and a bytecode virtual machine underneath: nodes bake into a blob image, and generated dispatch walks it. The chapters describe the behaviour; the source is not ours to paste, so everything here is written from the outside in.

wire.short: Intent goes out, snapshots come back, and that is the whole protocol.
wire.deep: One direction carries a bounded statement of what the player wants. The other carries delta compressed state, prioritised, cut off at whatever fits in a packet. A snapshot is not the world; it is as much of the world as fits, sorted by importance. Once you accept that, most of the rest of the network layer stops looking arbitrary.

clocks.short: Two timelines on one client, and ownership decides which you are on.
clocks.deep: This is the single thing most worth understanding before you touch the Inspector. Some entities are played back out of a buffer from the server's past. Others are simulated ahead into the client's future and corrected. The two cannot interact correctly, which turns one innocent dropdown into an architectural commitment.

rollback.short: Restore, replay, carry on. The correction machine.
rollback.deep: Every frame the client rewinds its predicted entities to the last tick the server confirmed and resimulates forward to the present. What surprises people is that there is no comparison step. The server's state is written over the prediction whether or not the prediction was right, and when it was right the write simply changes nothing.

adversary.short: Physics under rollback, lag compensation, and a client that lies.
adversary.deep: This region is where the comfortable assumptions get tested. Physics inside a loop that runs the same tick repeatedly. A server rewinding its collision world to the moment a shooter actually saw. And the standing assumption that the machine on the other end is modified, which is not paranoia, it is the default.

capsules.short: The destination: two capsules, one server, and nothing else.
capsules.deep: The whole handbook is built around the smallest project that is genuinely a networked game rather than a demo. Two players, two capsules, a real client and server split, and a real connection lifecycle. Small enough to hold entirely in your head, complete enough that nothing important has been faked.

lessons.title: The Machine
lessons.blurb: Six worlds in one process, and the one thin channel between them.

chapters.title: One process, many machines
chapters.text: Everything you are looking at runs inside a single Unity process, in a single frame, one world after another. A world is an entity manager plus a list of systems. Two worlds share nothing. Same silicon, same frame, zero shared memory. Think separate address spaces, not threads.

chapters.title: The only thing that crosses
chapters.text: Between the client world and the server world there is exactly one channel, and only two kinds of traffic on it. Going right: commands, which are intent. Going left: snapshots, which are truth. The client never sends a position. If it could, it could teleport, and no amount of server code downstream would save you.

chapters.title: Where truth lives
chapters.text: The server world is inside its own boundary on this map for a reason. It is the only world allowed to write authoritative state. Every other world either asks for something, or observes the result. When you are deciding where a new rule belongs, ask who owns the outcome. If the answer is the server, the rule lives in a system that runs on both sides but is only believed on one.

chapters.title: Who builds the worlds
chapters.text: Nothing here is automatic. The service world never dies, and it owns the application state graph. When that graph reaches the game state, it calls a node that asks the bootstrap to create the client and server worlds. The menu world is destroyed at the same moment. World creation is a decision the graph makes, not a side effect of pressing play.

chapters.title: How content reaches a world
chapters.text: This is the path people lose entities in. A settings asset sits on a settings authoring prefab. That prefab is instantiated in a scene. That scene is listed in a sub scene set carrying a world flag. Only then does baking put the entity in the world you expected. Four hops, and every one of them fails silently.

input.short: The Input System, holding managed keyboard state.
input.deep: Managed memory means Burst cannot touch it. That is why the system reading it is deliberately not Burst compiled — and that is a correct decision, not a compromise. Read devices on the managed side, write a plain struct, and let every downstream system be fast.

client.short: The client world. It predicts your capsule, renders everything, and owns nothing.
client.deep: It runs ahead of the server by roughly half the round trip, so its commands land just in time. It draws your capsule at that predicted tick and everyone else's at an interpolated tick in the past. Two different clocks, on one screen, deliberately.

server.short: The server world. It holds the truth and decides what each client may know.
server.deep: It is inside its own boundary on this map because it is the only world allowed to write authoritative state. It also decides relevancy, which is a security boundary as much as a bandwidth one: information you never send cannot be extracted by a modified client.

service.short: The service world outlives everything and owns the application state graph.
service.deep: It is created at startup and never destroyed. Because it survives world transitions, it is the right home for anything that must outlive a match: authentication, analytics, and the state machine that decides whether you are in the menu or in a game.

bootstrap.short: The bootstrap decides which worlds exist and what they are called.
bootstrap.deep: It implements Unity's custom bootstrap hook. The important consequence is that world creation is an explicit decision made by a graph node, not a side effect of entering play mode. That is also why a virtual player with the wrong play type will build a second server world and fail to bind the port.

gpu.short: Entities Graphics uploads matrices to the GPU and issues batched draws.
gpu.deep: The rule worth carrying: presentation reads simulation and never the reverse. If you ever feed a smoothed or interpolated visual value back into simulation, you have built a feedback loop between what is true and what is drawn, and it will diverge.

settings.short: A settings asset is a scriptable object that bakes into an entity.
settings.deep: It is the bridge between a designer's number in the inspector and blittable data in a chunk. The world it lands in is decided by an attribute on the class, which a utility reads to insert the asset into the right authoring prefab. Never hand edit that array.

subscenes.short: A sub scene set maps scenes to worlds using load flags.
subscenes.deep: This is the routing table. A scene listed with the client flag loads into client worlds; the server flag, server worlds. When an entity you expected is missing from a world, walk this path backwards — asset, prefab, scene, set, flag — and you will find the broken link.

lessons.title: Keypress to Pixel
lessons.blurb: One float two of intent, and every consequence it causes.

chapters.title: Eight bytes cross the wire
chapters.text: Follow one key press. The only thing that will actually leave this machine is a direction: two floats, saying which way the player wants to go. Everything else on this map is a local consequence of those eight bytes. Hold on to that, because it is the whole security model in one sentence.

chapters.title: Intent, never results
chapters.text: The gather system reads the keyboard and writes a move direction onto your capsule, and only yours. It filters on ghost owner is local, so it cannot accidentally drive another player. Notice what it does not write. It does not write a position, a velocity, or a final answer. A direction is bounded; the server applies its own speed and its own delta to it, so a modified client gains nothing.

chapters.title: The ring buffer
chapters.text: The input does not go straight onto the wire. It goes into a ring buffer, and every slot is stamped with the tick it belongs to. This is a circular buffer with a timestamp per slot, and the consumer reads by timestamp rather than by position. That single design choice is what makes rollback possible later.

chapters.title: The instant local answer
chapters.text: In the same frame, before the server has seen anything, the client reads that tick's input back out of the ring and runs the movement rule. Your capsule has already moved. Perceived input latency is zero. The price is that you may be wrong, and the map's snapshot arrow is where being wrong gets fixed.

chapters.title: The same code, twice
chapters.text: On the server, the very same movement system runs. Not a server version. The same system, with one world filter naming both sides. Two implementations would mean two behaviours, and two behaviours mean permanent disagreement. One rule, executed twice, is what server authoritative with client prediction actually means in code.

chapters.title: Snapshots, and three different nows
chapters.text: The server delta compresses its truth against what each client last acknowledged, fills a packet up to the maximum size, and sends it unreliably. When it arrives, either it agrees with your prediction and nothing happens, or it disagrees and the client restores and replays. Meanwhile the other player sees your capsule interpolated, about a hundred milliseconds in the past. Nobody on either screen is seeing now.

gather.short: Reads the keyboard and writes a direction onto the capsule you own.
gather.deep: It filters on ghost owner is local, a tag NetCode adds to ghosts whose owner id matches yours. Without that filter you would write your input into every player's capsule in your world. It is also not Burst compiled, because the keyboard is managed.

ring.short: A ring of about sixty four ticks, each slot stamped with its tick.
ring.deep: History, not a single value. The server needs several ticks to tolerate loss, and rollback needs to replay the exact input of each replayed tick. A circular buffer with a timestamp per slot, where the consumer reads by timestamp rather than position.

send.short: Sends the last several ticks in one unreliable packet.
send.deep: The redundancy lives in the payload rather than the protocol, which is why input feels solid on a lossy link while positions still visibly hitch. A retransmit would arrive too late to matter, so nothing is retransmitted.

predict.short: The client's copy of the movement rule, running inside prediction.
predict.deep: It only touches entities whose simulate bit is enabled for the tick being simulated. Simulate is a clock enable line: the clock is running, and that bit decides who latches this edge. Omit it and a ten tick replay moves your capsule ten times too far.

srvmove.short: The server's copy of that same system. Same code, same constants.
srvmove.deep: One world filter names both client and server simulation, so there is literally one implementation. Two would mean two behaviours, and two behaviours mean permanent disagreement. This is what server authoritative with client prediction means in practice.

ghostsend.short: Delta compresses truth against each connection's acknowledged baseline.
ghostsend.deep: Every client has acknowledged a different tick, so the server remembers what each one knows and encodes against that. It then sorts by importance and fills a packet until the maximum size. A snapshot is not the world; it is as much of the world as fits, prioritised.

gpu.short: Your capsule is drawn ahead of the server; everyone else's, behind it.
gpu.deep: That is not a bug, it is the entire trade made explicit. You need your own capsule to answer instantly, and you need theirs to be smooth. Prediction buys the first, interpolation buys the second, and nobody renders the server's actual present.

lessons.title: Connection Lifecycle
lessons.blurb: Socket to spawned capsule, and the two places it silently stops.

chapters.title: The connection is an entity
chapters.text: There is no connection class anywhere in this system. A connection is an entity, and the set of components on it is its state machine. Each step of joining adds one more component. If you learn that chain, you can diagnose any join failure by asking a single question: which component is missing?

chapters.title: Getting a network id
chapters.text: First the socket opens and a network stream connection component appears. Then the handshake runs, and this is where a protocol version mismatch will reject you, because the ghost schemas on both sides must agree exactly. If the handshake passes, the server assigns a network id. Only now do you have an identity that anything else can reason about.

chapters.title: Admission
chapters.text: Next the connection must be approved. Approval adds two components: connection approved, and an account identity. The spawn path requires both. Here is the first silent gap. Approval is off by default, and when it is off both approval systems disable themselves in their own on create. So nothing ever adds those components, no player ever spawns, and absolutely nothing is logged.

chapters.title: Arming the snapshot system
chapters.text: Now the client graph acts. It adds network stream in game to the connection and sends a go in game request. That one flag is what arms the entire snapshot system. Without it the server sends zero ghosts, not fewer. This is the second silent gap: the node that does this ships with the framework, but it only runs inside a client graph, and the sample never authored one.

chapters.title: Spawn and replicate
chapters.text: With the connection approved and in game, the session system spawns two entities per player: a controller, which is the persistent identity, and a controlled pawn, which is the current body. Snapshots begin, and the ghosts materialise on the client without the client ever calling instantiate. Two players should therefore show four ghosts. If you see three, two connections adopted the same controller.

client.short: The connection entity. Watch its component set grow.
client.deep: Connection, then network id, then approved and account identity, then in game, then command target. There is no connection class anywhere. The component set is the state machine, and a missing component is always the answer to why a join stopped.

graph.short: The client state graph. It tracks the connection and holds a gate until we are in game.
graph.deep: It reads this tick's connection facts, latches them into durable graph state, and sends the go in game request exactly once per connection identity. Keying on identity rather than a boolean means a reconnect resends correctly while a retry does not spam.

wire.short: Inter process communication in one process, UDP otherwise.
wire.deep: Snapshots and commands ride unreliable channels because a retransmit would arrive after the data was already stale. Remote procedure calls ride a reliable ordered channel, because a lost go in game request would strand the player forever.

server.short: Admits the connection, approves it, and spawns for it.
server.deep: Its approval path only skips real token validation when the world is not a netcode server world. A separate server world in one process is still a server world, so turning approval on here really does mean a network call to Unity Authentication.

session.short: Its query is the specification for who is allowed to spawn.
session.deep: Approved, account identity, network id, and command target must all be present. That is why the connection ladder is really just asking which of those four is missing. It then spawns two entities per player and links them.

lessons.title: The Client Graph
lessons.blurb: A state machine whose only job is to arm replication, and to notice when it stops.

chapters.title: States that contain states
chapters.text: This is a hierarchical state machine. The key idea is that a state can contain other states, and at any moment the machine has an active path from the root down to a leaf, not a single active state. Both root and the current child are running. That sounds academic until you see what it buys, which is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Why the tracker lives on root
chapters.text: The connection tracker is attached to root, and blocks on root run every tick in every child state. Attach it to connecting instead and you would stop detecting disconnects the moment you successfully entered the game, which is the worst possible time to find that bug. Put shared watchdogs at the top of the hierarchy, always.

chapters.title: The gate that cannot be skipped
chapters.text: Connecting holds an initialize block, which drives a startup gate, which holds the go in game node. That chain looks like ceremony, but the types force it. The go in game node operates on an initialize state, only a startup gate supplies one, and only the initialize block can drive a gate from a state. It is pin compatibility, enforced at author time. You cannot wire it wrong.

chapters.title: The gate is the retry loop
chapters.text: Every block inside the gate reports whether it is completed, and the gate advances only when all of them say yes. So while the connection has no network id, the gate simply holds. When the request has been sent but the server has not confirmed, it holds. No timers, no coroutines, no retry counters. The barrier is the retry loop, and reaching gameplay is proof the whole chain worked.

chapters.title: Losing the connection
chapters.text: Connection events live for exactly one tick. If you poll them from something that does not run every tick, you will miss disconnects intermittently, which is a miserable bug. So the tracker latches them immediately into durable graph state, along with the reason, and jumps to disconnected. Because disconnected has a real path back to connecting, it is a recoverable failure and not a dead end.

root.short: Always on the active path. Anything here runs in every child state.
root.deep: That is the whole reason the connection tracker lives here. Attach a watchdog to a child state and it stops watching the moment you leave that state, which for a disconnect detector is exactly the wrong time. Shared watchdogs go at the top of the hierarchy.

connecting.short: The default child. It holds the block that drives the startup gate.
connecting.deep: Every composite state must declare exactly one default child, and the validator proves that at author time rather than letting you find it at runtime. It also proves your state ids do not collide after hashing, which is a lovely thing to catch offline.

gameplay.short: The destination, and only reachable through the gate.
gameplay.deep: That is what makes it a falsifiable check. Delete the old workaround, run, and read the state id. If it says gameplay, the graph sent the request, because no other code path can set it. An outcome can have many causes; a mechanism has one.

disconnected.short: A recoverable failure. The reason is latched into graph state.
disconnected.deep: Connection events survive exactly one tick, so the tracker copies them immediately into durable state along with the disconnect reason. It also distinguishes voluntary from involuntary: quitting looks different from being kicked at the door, and the interface should say different things.

lessons.title: Inside One Chunk
lessons.blurb: Sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty four bytes, and the stride is the entire point.

chapters.title: One allocation, and you can read it
chapters.text: Everything on this map is one allocation. Sixteen kilobytes, taken from a pool, reused. Sixty four bytes of header at the front, deliberately a whole cache line, and then nothing but arrays until the end. There is no object graph here, no vtable, no pointer to follow. If you have ever drawn a memory map on a whiteboard to explain a driver, this is that drawing, and it is the honest layout rather than a metaphor for one.

chapters.title: One array per component type
chapters.text: After the header comes the entity array, always first, then one contiguous array per component type in this chunk's archetype. Each has a fixed stride: a transform is thirty two bytes, a ghost identity is twelve, a movement input is eight. Within an array, element three sits exactly three strides past the base. No indirection, no holes, no per element metadata. Just a run of identical records, which is the only shape a hardware prefetcher can actually predict.

chapters.title: An entity is a subscript, not a struct
chapters.text: Here is the part that takes a while to sit right. Entity number three does not exist anywhere as a contiguous object. Its transform is in one array, its ghost identity is in another, its input is in a third, and those three pieces may be thousands of bytes apart. What ties them together is nothing but the shared index. That is structure of arrays, chosen for exactly the reason you would choose it in C, and it is why a system that only wants transforms never pulls a single byte of anything else into cache.

chapters.title: What a job actually sees
chapters.text: A job is handed one chunk at a time. Inside that chunk, every entity has identical structure by definition, so there is no branch on type and no virtual call anywhere in the loop. It walks one array forward at a fixed stride and ignores every other array in the block. This is why the unit of parallel work is a chunk rather than an entity: a chunk is exactly one cache friendly range with a known length.

chapters.title: The consequence nobody warns you about
chapters.text: Capacity is the usable buffer divided by the sum of the strides. So adding one component to an entity does two things at once. It changes the archetype, which means the entity has to move to a different chunk, which is a memory copy of every one of its components. And it changes capacity, so a block that held one hundred and twenty eight entities might now hold one hundred and thirteen. That is what a structural change actually costs, and that is why you batch them.

archetype.short: The exact set of component types, shared by every chunk that matches it.
archetype.deep: An archetype is a set, not an object. It owns the layout: which arrays exist, in what order, at what offsets, and how many entities fit. Every chunk with the same archetype has a byte identical layout, which is what lets a query iterate many chunks with one set of type offsets computed once.

slot.short: One entity, expressed as the same index into several unrelated arrays.
slot.deep: There is no object here to hold. The address of entity three's transform is the transform array base plus three times thirty two. The address of its input is a completely different base plus three times eight. Those two addresses have nothing to do with each other except that the same number three produced both of them.

header.short: Sixty four bytes at the front, sized to a cache line on purpose.
header.deep: It carries a globally unique sequence number, some flags, and the identity of the meta entity that holds this chunk's chunk level components. Only twenty four of those bytes are actually serialized when a chunk is written to disk; the rest is runtime bookkeeping. The buffer offset is sixty four so that the first real array starts on a cache line boundary.

entities.short: The entity array, always first, eight bytes per slot.
entities.deep: An entity handle is an index plus a version number. The version is the trick that makes a stale reference detectable instead of catastrophic: reuse the index, bump the version, and any handle carrying the old version now fails a cheap comparison instead of silently addressing somebody else's data.

transform.short: Thirty two bytes per entity, contiguous, no gaps.
transform.deep: Position, rotation and a uniform scale, packed. It is the array almost every system touches, which is why its stride matters more than most. A run of these is the best case the memory system ever sees: sequential, aligned, predictable, and completely free of anything the loop does not need.

ghost.short: Twelve bytes: a network identity, a prefab type, and a spawn tick.
ghost.deep: The identifier alone is not unique over time, because identifiers get recycled when ghosts are destroyed. It is the pair of identifier and spawn tick that is guaranteed unique, which is a detail you only care about at exactly the moment it bites you during despawn and respawn in the same window.

input.short: Eight bytes of intent, and the only thing that leaves this machine.
input.deep: Two floats saying which direction the player wants to go. It sits in this chunk exactly like everything else, with the same stride discipline, and the fact that it is the one component destined for the wire is invisible from the memory layout. That is the point: replication is a property of the schema, not of how the data is stored.

sweep.short: One job, one chunk, one linear pass with no pointer ever dereferenced.
sweep.deep: The loop gets a base address and a count. Inside it there is no polymorphism, no null check on a reference, and no cache miss that was not implied by the data you asked for. Arrays this chunk holds but the job did not request are never read, so they never displace anything you do need.

lessons.title: The Archetype Is a Set
lessons.blurb: Adding a component never edits an entity. It hashes a different set, finds a different chunk, and copies the entity there.

chapters.title: A set, not an object
chapters.text: The word archetype sounds like a class, and that is the wrong instinct. An archetype is a sorted array of component type numbers. That array is not a description of the archetype, it is the archetype. Two archetypes are the same thing exactly when their arrays are byte for byte identical, and there is code that literally does that memory comparison to decide.

chapters.title: The edge you cannot find
chapters.text: Here is the part I did not expect. There is no graph. Nothing stores an edge saying from this archetype, adding a transform gets you to that one. What happens instead is that the runtime copies the sorted array onto the stack, inserts one element in its sorted position, hashes the whole thing, and probes an open addressed table. Hit means an archetype with that exact set already exists. Miss means one gets created on the spot. The set is the key, and that is the entire data structure.

chapters.title: Why that is the right call
chapters.text: Think about how many edges you would have to store. An archetype with twenty component types has twenty ways to remove one, and thousands of plausible ways to add one, and every one of those would need a slot. So they do not cache the edges. They recompute the key every time, because the key is one hash over a few hundred bytes and one probe. It is cheaper to redo the lookup than to remember the answer. That trade shows up all over this codebase once you start looking for it.

chapters.title: What the entity actually pays
chapters.text: Now the entity has to move, because its data lives in a chunk and a chunk belongs to exactly one archetype. The copy is nicer than you would guess. Both type arrays are sorted, so the copy walks them together like a merge, from the back. A type present in both gets one memory copy of count times stride. A type present only in the destination gets zeroed, and if it is one of the switchable ones its bit is set to enabled. A type present only in the source is simply dropped. So it is not one big block copy, it is one small copy per surviving component.

chapters.title: Two bills you did not ask for
chapters.text: Then two things happen that nobody warns you about. The new archetype recomputes its own chunk capacity from the sum of the strides, so a chunk that held a hundred and twenty eight entities might now hold ninety, and the ceiling is a hundred and twenty eight no matter how small your components are. And every archetype keeps a list of back pointers to the queries that match it, so touching its chunk list drops the cached chunk list of every one of those queries. That second bill is not paid here. It is paid by whichever system iterates next.

srcset.short: The exact set of component types the entity has right now.
srcset.deep: Not a name, not an object, not a class. A sorted array of type numbers, plus the layout that follows from it: which arrays exist, at what offsets, with what strides, and how many entities fit. Every chunk carrying that archetype has a byte identical layout, which is the whole reason one set of offsets can drive iteration over thousands of chunks.
srcset.gotoLabel: What one chunk of it looks like

insert.short: Copy the sorted array, slide one element in, keep it sorted.
insert.deep: This happens on the stack, so there is no allocation and no garbage. The insertion point is found by walking the array until the existing type is no longer smaller than the new one. If the type is already there the function returns nothing at all, which is how adding a component you already have becomes free rather than an error.

lookup.short: Hash the whole array, probe an open addressed table, confirm with a memory compare.
lookup.deep: The hash covers every byte of the type array, so it is a hash of the set itself rather than of any one type. Collisions are handled by walking forward one slot at a time, and a candidate is only accepted after its type count matches and a memory comparison of the whole array comes back equal. Two sentinel hash values are reserved so that empty and deleted slots can be told apart from real ones.

dst.short: The archetype the entity is about to belong to, found or freshly built.
dst.deep: Creating one is more work than it sounds. It computes memory ordering for the types, offsets, strides, a stable hash for serialisation, a bloom filter mask for query matching, and two derived archetypes: one for instantiating, which strips prefab and cleanup components, and one for copying, which strips only cleanup. All of that is done once, at creation, and never again.

capacity.short: How many entities fit, recomputed for the new set of strides.
capacity.deep: Capacity is the usable part of the block divided by the sum of every component's stride, then reduced until the per array alignment padding also fits. On top of that there is a hard ceiling of a hundred and twenty eight entities per chunk, which exists because the position inside a chunk is stored in a single byte in the entity slot table.

convert.short: Two sorted type arrays walked in step, one memory copy per shared type.
convert.deep: Because both arrays are sorted by type number, the copy is a two pointer merge walked backwards. Types in both get copied. Types only in the destination get cleared to zero, and if they are switchable their enabled bit is set true, because a component you just added should be on. Types only in the source are noted for deallocation, which matters when one of them owned a buffer.

dstchunk.short: A different allocation, a different slot number, and every old pointer now lies.
dstchunk.deep: This is why a structural change is not something you can do while jobs are running. Anything holding a raw pointer into the old chunk is now pointing at memory that has been reused or moved. The handle you hold is still valid, because a handle is an index plus a version rather than an address, but every array pointer derived from it is stale.

queries.short: Every query that matches this archetype loses its cached chunk list.
queries.deep: An archetype carries back pointers to the query data of every query that ever matched it. When its chunk list changes, the runtime walks a linked list of archetypes touched during this batch and clears a valid flag on each of their queries. Nothing is rebuilt right then. The rebuild happens lazily, the next time somebody iterates, which is why the cost shows up in a system that did nothing wrong.
queries.gotoLabel: What a query does with that list

lessons.title: One Word, and the Bit That Says Alive
lessons.blurb: An entity handle is sixty four bits with no pointer in it, and the version field is what turns a dangling reference into a null instead of a disaster.

chapters.title: Eight bytes, no address
chapters.text: An entity is not an object and it is not a pointer. It is one sixty four bit word, and if you look at the source you find something better than the two integers everyone quotes. It is a single raw field with three bit fields packed into it: twenty eight bits of index, twelve bits of type identifier, and twenty four bits of version. Index and version are properties that mask and shift, not fields you can take the address of. Which means comparing two entities is one compare of one word, and nothing else.

chapters.title: Why a version at all
chapters.text: Twenty eight bits gives you about two hundred and sixty eight million indices, and in a game that spawns and destroys constantly you will chew through those and start reusing them. Without a generation counter, a handle you kept from three seconds ago would silently address whatever now occupies that index. With one, the handle fails a comparison you were already paying for, because the lookup has to read that slot anyway. You get detection for free out of work you could not avoid.

chapters.title: The slot table, and one clever bit
chapters.text: The index selects a slot, and the slot is itself one packed word holding the version, the chunk, and the position inside that chunk. Then comes the detail I enjoyed most. A slot whose version has its low bit clear holds no live entity. Live means odd. That is the same trick as an even and odd sequence counter in lock free code, and it means the null entity, whose version is zero, falls out of the rule for free rather than needing a special case.

chapters.title: Two outcomes, no third
chapters.text: So the lookup is: mask the index, read the slot, compare the version. Equal, and you get a chunk and a slot number unpacked from the same word you already loaded. Not equal, and you get nothing. There is no third branch where it half works. A stale handle in this system is a null, not a corrupted read, and that difference is the whole reason you can hand entity handles around inside components without fear.

chapters.title: Three consequences worth carrying
chapters.text: First, the hash code of an entity is its index alone, with the version thrown away, so a recycled handle collides with the one it replaced in a hash map. Second, sorting entities sorts on index, again ignoring the version. Third, the position inside a chunk is stored in a single byte, which is exactly why a chunk can never hold more than a hundred and twenty eight entities however small your components are. The identity design and the chunk capacity limit are the same decision seen from two ends.

handle.short: One sixty four bit word, and there is no address anywhere in it.
handle.deep: The struct is declared with an explicit size of eight bytes and holds exactly one raw field. Everything you think of as a field is a property that masks and shifts. That is what lets the equality operator compare the two words directly, and it is why passing entities around by value costs the same as passing a long integer.

bits.short: Twenty four bits of version, twelve of type identifier, twenty eight of index.
bits.deep: The comment in the source says the layout deliberately matches the engine's own identifier type, so a reinterpret cast between them is byte identical. That is the seam where the entity system meets the rest of the engine, and it is the reason this layout is packed rather than the two plain integers older documentation describes.

slot.short: One word per index, holding version, chunk, and position inside the chunk together.
slot.deep: It lives on the engine side now rather than inside the entity package, and the package reads it through a static that both compiled and interpreted code agree on. Reads use a volatile load, because entity ids can be allocated from worker threads without a lock, which is what makes recording a create inside a job possible at all.

check.short: Compare the version in the slot against the version in your hand.
check.deep: One integer comparison, on a word the lookup had to load anyway to find the chunk. That is the entire safety mechanism. It costs a compare and a predictable branch, and in exchange every stale handle in the program becomes a detected null instead of a silent read of somebody else's data.

resolve.short: A chunk and a position inside it, unpacked from the word you already read.
resolve.deep: No second load, no pointer chase. The chunk index and the position are bit fields of the same slot word as the version, so a successful lookup and a failed one cost nearly the same. From there the actual component address is the chunk buffer, plus the type's offset, plus the position times the stride.

stale.short: Versions differ, so the lookup hands back nothing at all.
stale.deep: Not an exception in a shipping build, not a crash, not a garbage pointer. A null chunk, which every caller already has to handle. In development builds there is an extra check that throws with a message naming the destroyed entity, but the shipping behaviour is the quiet one, and it is quiet on purpose.

recycle.short: Destroy an entity and its index goes back to be handed out again.
recycle.deep: The index is the scarce resource, so it gets reused aggressively, and the version is what keeps that reuse honest. Every reuse bumps the version, so no handle from a previous life ever compares equal. The low bit of the version doubles as the liveness flag, which means the counter effectively advances by one on death and one on rebirth.
recycle.gotoLabel: Who mints ids from inside a job

lessons.title: Where a Query Actually Filters
lessons.blurb: Five rejections at five granularities, and only the last one costs anything per entity.

chapters.title: The filtering is not where you think
chapters.text: The word query makes you picture a scan. It is not a scan. By the time your update runs, the answer is a flat array of chunk indices that was computed earlier and cached. Everything on the left of this map happens when the query is created, or when a new archetype is born, and neither of those is per frame. What is left inside your loop is two bit tricks.

chapters.title: A bloom filter, in an entity system
chapters.text: This one surprised me. Every component type hashes to five bits of a sixty four bit word. An archetype's mask is the bitwise or of all its types' masks. A query's mask is the or of everything it requires. Then the first test is one and operation: if the required bits are not all present, this archetype cannot possibly match, and it is rejected without reading a single type number. The source even explains the choice of five bits: fewer and different types collide, more and or-ing enough masks together hides a missing type. It is a probabilistic reject in front of an exact one, exactly like a cache tag in front of a tag comparison.

chapters.title: Then the honest comparison
chapters.text: Survivors go through the cheap categorical rejects first. Disabled, prefab, system instance, meta chunk. All four are excluded unless you asked for them, which is why your first query mysteriously misses your prefabs. Only after that does it walk the two sorted arrays, the archetype's types and the query's required types, and check the required set, the excluded set, the any set. That walk is linear and it is the expensive part, which is precisely why the bloom filter sits in front of it.

chapters.title: The chunk list is a flat array
chapters.text: A match records two things: the archetype in the query's list, and a back pointer to the query on the archetype. Then all the matching archetypes' chunk lists get flattened into one array of chunk indices, with a parallel array saying which archetype each chunk came from. Archetypes holding zero entities are skipped during that flatten. And the whole thing is guarded by a valid flag, which somebody else drops for you whenever a structural change touches a matching archetype.

chapters.title: Two bit tricks, and that is all
chapters.text: Inside the loop there are exactly two filters left. The version filter compares a stored version number and can skip a whole chunk without touching it, and it has a hard ceiling of two shared values and two changed types, which is a real limit you can hit. Then the switchable component state is two sixty four bit words, one bit per slot. Finding the next entity is count trailing zeros. Advancing past it is clearing the lowest set bit with a single and. If nothing in the chunk is switchable the mask is all ones and the loop is a plain range. That is the entire per entity cost of a query.

desc.short: The required, optional, excluded and present sets, written once.
desc.deep: You build this in create, not in update, and the system caches it. The four sets are not symmetric: required and present affect matching in different ways, and the excluded set is the one that quietly makes an archetype invisible to you forever. Options on top of it decide whether disabled entities, prefabs, system instances and meta chunks are even considered.
desc.gotoLabel: Where queries sit in the whole machine

bloom.short: One and operation against a sixty four bit mask rejects most archetypes.
bloom.deep: Each component type hashes deterministically to five set bits. An archetype ors together the masks of every type it holds; a query ors together the masks of what it requires. If the query's bits are not a subset of the archetype's, no match is possible. False positives cost you an exact check you would have done anyway. False negatives cannot happen, which is what makes it safe.

types.short: The categorical rejects, then a walk of two sorted arrays.
types.deep: Disabled, prefab, system instance and meta chunk archetypes are excluded unless the query explicitly asked for them, and each is a single flag test. Then the required, present and excluded sets are checked by walking the archetype's sorted type array. There is also an early exit when the archetype simply has fewer types than the query requires.

matched.short: Recorded in both directions, once, when the archetype first matches.
matched.deep: The query gets a record naming the archetype and the position of each requested type inside it, so iteration never has to search for a type again. The archetype gets a back pointer to the query. That back pointer is what lets a structural change find every query it just invalidated without searching, and it is the quiet reason invalidation is cheap.

chunks.short: Every matching chunk from every matching archetype, flattened into one array.
chunks.deep: Alongside the chunk indices there are two parallel arrays: which matching archetype each chunk belongs to, and its position within that archetype's own list. A valid flag guards the whole thing, and the rebuild simply clears and refills, skipping archetypes with no entities. The rebuild itself is compiled to native code, because it runs often enough to matter.

filter.short: A version compare that can skip a whole chunk without reading it.
filter.deep: Two flavours: filter by a shared component value, or filter by whether a component type has been written since a given version. Both have a capacity of exactly two, which is a real ceiling rather than a soft guideline. And both operate per chunk, so change filtering is coarse: one write anywhere in a chunk makes the whole chunk look changed.

mask.short: Two sixty four bit words per chunk, walked with count trailing zeros.
mask.deep: Switchable components let you turn an entity off without moving it to a different chunk, and the state lives as a bit mask in the chunk. The enumerator finds the next set bit with count trailing zeros and then clears the lowest set bit with a single and. It is the same loop you would write to service a pending interrupt register, and it is the only genuinely per entity work a query does.
mask.gotoLabel: The one bit that eats projects

lessons.title: The Graph You Never Wrote
lessons.blurb: One write fence and seventeen read fences per component type. Every edge in your job graph falls out of that array.

chapters.title: It is a scoreboard
chapters.text: You have seen this structure before, in a processor. For every component type there is one slot holding the fence of the last job that wrote it, and a small array of slots holding the fences of jobs that are currently reading it. That is a reader writer scoreboard, and every dependency edge you never wrote comes out of it by the same rules you would use for register hazards.

chapters.title: The rule, in one sentence
chapters.text: When you ask for your dependency, for every type you read it takes that type's write fence, and for every type you write it takes the write fence and every read fence. Then it combines them into one handle. Read the consequence off that: a reader waits for writers, a writer waits for writers and for all readers, and two readers of the same type are never ordered against each other. Read after write, write after read, write after write. Read after read is not a hazard, so it never becomes an edge.

chapters.title: Lazy on the way in, automatic on the way out
chapters.text: Before your update runs, the system just sets a flag saying it will need the fences. It does not fetch them. The first time you actually touch the dependency, the fetch happens and the flag clears. If you never touch it, nothing is combined at all. On the way out, if you scheduled anything, the runtime submits the batched jobs and writes your returned handle into the fence slots of every type you declared. That is the step that makes the next system's dependency correct without either system knowing the other exists.

chapters.title: Seventeen readers, and then a spill
chapters.text: The read slots are a fixed size array. One write fence, seventeen read fences, per type, for every type the type manager knows. When the eighteenth reader arrives there is nowhere to put it, so the seventeen are combined into a single handle, that handle goes back into slot zero, and the count drops to one. It is a spill, and it is the moment the graph quietly gets coarser. Those seventeen jobs are now indistinguishable from each other to anything that comes later.

chapters.title: What never becomes an edge
chapters.text: Three things get dropped before the graph is ever built. A zero sized type that is not switchable is removed from both lists entirely, because a tag has no data to race on. Declaring a write on a type you also read removes it from the reading list, so write wins. And a job that declares no types at all is registered as a reader of the entity type itself, purely so that the next full barrier still catches it. That last one is not about correctness of ordering, it is about not leaking a job that nobody will ever wait on.

types.short: Which component types you read, and which you write.
types.deep: This comes straight out of the queries you built, plus anything you asked for by hand. You never write the graph, you write the access pattern, and the graph is derived from it. That is the whole trade: you give up the ability to hand tune the ordering, and in exchange you cannot get it wrong.

get.short: Combine the fences that could actually collide with you.
get.deep: For each type you read it takes only the write fence. For each type you write it takes the write fence and every registered read fence. Everything gathered goes into one combined handle. The asymmetry is the point: it is why two systems reading the same transforms run at the same time, and why a third writing them waits for both.

run.short: You schedule, and the handle you get back is now the chain.
run.deep: The handle in and the handle out are both yours to manage. Schedule several jobs and you can chain them by hand or fan them out and combine. Assign the dependency yourself and the automatic fetch is skipped entirely, which is both the escape hatch and the way to break your own ordering if you are careless.
run.gotoLabel: What the job is compiled into

put.short: After your update, your handle goes into the slots of every type you touched.
put.deep: It only happens if you actually scheduled something and did not already complete it, which is a real optimisation for systems that only run work on the main thread. Just before the registration the runtime submits the batched jobs, so scheduling many small jobs in one update costs one submission rather than many.

slots.short: One write fence and seventeen read fences, for every component type.
slots.deep: Two flat arrays allocated once at world creation, indexed by a compact type number. Types are only given a slot the first time somebody actually declares access to them, so most of the array stays untouched. The whole structure is cleared wholesale at every full barrier rather than being maintained incrementally.

spill.short: The eighteenth reader forces the previous seventeen into one handle.
spill.deep: The combine writes the result back into the first read slot and resets the count to one, which frees sixteen slots immediately. Nothing breaks, but the graph loses resolution: anything that later waits on that type now waits on all seventeen as a unit. If you ever wonder why a system seems to wait longer than its declared conflicts justify, this is a candidate.

stall.short: Or you can wait right here, on purpose.
stall.deep: Completing the dependency instead of chaining it turns your system into a barrier for every type it declared. Sometimes that is exactly right, because you are about to do something on the main thread that cannot be expressed as a job. It is a sync point either way, and the honest version is the one you chose deliberately.

lessons.title: Two Compilers, One Assembly
lessons.blurb: Burst does not speed your code up. It compiles a different language that happens to be spelled the same, and the way back is a function pointer.

chapters.title: A cross compiler, not an optimiser
chapters.text: The useful way to hold this is that Burst is a cross compiler for a restricted dialect. Same source file, same intermediate language, two different back ends. One produces managed code with a garbage collector, write barriers and safe points underneath it. The other produces machine code with none of those, because the dialect it accepts has no managed objects in it. That is why it can vectorise: it is compiling a language where aliasing is declarable and every value has a known size.

chapters.title: The package is a shim now
chapters.text: If you go looking for Burst in the project's packages you will be disappointed, and it is worth knowing why. The package is version two point zero and its entire runtime folder is a single file of type forwarders. The attribute, the compiler, the intrinsics, the shared static, all of it now lives inside the editor and the engine. So there is no Burst source in the project to read. What you can read is everything that calls it, and that turns out to be more instructive anyway.

chapters.title: The attribute has to be on both
chapters.text: The classic mistake is putting the attribute on the method and not on the containing type, which silently does nothing. There is an analyzer for that now, warning number E A zero zero one zero, and its message names the fix. But read the analyzer and you find it deliberately returns without warning for anything implementing the system interface. So the one case a handbook warns you about, a system struct with the attribute on update but not on the struct, is precisely the case that still stays quiet.

chapters.title: The doorway is a discarded body
chapters.text: Native code cannot call a managed method. So how does compiled code inside the command buffer reach the managed part of playback? The generated bridge is lovely. There is a small method marked so that Burst deletes its body from the native build. In managed code it sets a flag to true. In native code the call vanishes and the flag stays false. Calling a method and observing that nothing happened is how the code works out which world it is running in.

chapters.title: And then an address in a shared static
chapters.text: Once it knows, it needs somewhere both worlds can see. That is the shared static: a global that compiled and interpreted code agree points at the same bytes. The managed side marshals a delegate into a raw function pointer and parks it there. The native side loads it and calls it. In the other direction a managed delegate is compiled to native and invoked. Every crossing is an indirect call over a marshalling boundary, and everything on the far side runs at managed speed. That is the real reason a stray managed call in a hot loop costs what it costs.

attrs.short: The attribute belongs on the method and on the containing type.
attrs.deep: Missing it on the type raises a warning that names the type, names the method, and tells you exactly what to add. But the analyzer skips anything implementing the system interface on purpose, so the most common instance of this mistake is the one it will never tell you about. That is worth remembering the next time a system is mysteriously slow.

src.short: The code you wrote, before either compiler has looked at it.
src.deep: There is only one source file and only one set of semantics you can reason about, which is the strength of the whole design. The restriction is not on what you write but on what the second compiler will accept, and the gap between those two is where every confusing Burst error comes from.

il.short: What the C sharp compiler emits, and the only input either back end sees.
il.deep: This matters more than it sounds. Burst does not parse your source, it consumes the intermediate language, which is why source generators and the compiler's own transformations are already applied by the time it looks. It is also why an attribute is the only signal available: there is no other way to mark a method at that level.

burst.short: Intermediate form to machine code, ahead of time rather than just in time.
burst.deep: The whole package in the project is now a file of type forwarders, because the compiler moved into the editor and the engine. Two things follow. There is no Burst source to read alongside your project, and the version you are compiling against is the editor's version rather than the package's.

native.short: Machine code with no collector, no virtual dispatch, no unwind tables.
native.deep: The absences are the point. No collector means no write barriers and no safe point polling in your loop. No managed objects means every value has a known size and can live in a register. Declared aliasing means the vectoriser is allowed to be aggressive. You are not getting faster C sharp, you are getting a different language that costs less to execute.

bridge.short: One address, parked in a static that both worlds agree on.
bridge.deep: A shared static is the only sanctioned way to have a global that compiled and interpreted code both see. The managed side marshals a delegate into a raw pointer and stores it there once, at initialisation, keeping a reference alive so the collector does not eat the delegate. After that, calling across is a load and an indirect call.

managed.short: Where the deleted bodies live, reached only by an indirect call.
managed.deep: Everything the command buffer does with managed components ends up here, because none of it can exist in a native build. The playback walker keeps a flag per chain and picks the native or the managed path from it. Crossing is never automatic and never silent in the source, even though it is completely invisible in the profiler unless you know the marker to look for.

lessons.title: The Barrier You Paid For
lessons.blurb: A structural change cannot start until every tracked job everywhere in the world has finished, and the bill arrives twice.

chapters.title: Why it has to stop
chapters.text: A structural change moves an entity from one chunk to another, and a chunk is a raw allocation that jobs are holding raw pointers into. If a job is still running when the move happens, it is reading memory that has been overwritten or freed. There is no clever way around that. Either you stop everything, or you defer the change until a moment when nothing is running. This map is what stopping everything actually looks like.

chapters.title: It is not selective
chapters.text: Here is the thing worth internalising. It does not complete the jobs that touch this archetype. It does not complete the jobs that touch these component types. It walks every type that has a fence registered, gathers the write fence and every read fence of each one, combines them all into a single handle, and waits on that. Then it forgets every fence it was tracking, so the whole dependency graph restarts from empty. One entity gaining one tag drains the entire world.

chapters.title: How to actually see one
chapters.text: The wait is wrapped in a profiler marker named, helpfully, Complete All Jobs. If you have never gone looking for it, go and look. And notice the early exit: if no fences are registered at all, the whole thing is skipped. So a frame where you scheduled nothing pays nothing for its structural changes, and a frame with a deep job graph pays for the longest chain in it. The cost of a barrier is not a property of the barrier. It is a property of what was running when you hit it.

chapters.title: The second bill
chapters.text: After the change lands, two more things run. Any newly created archetypes are offered to every existing query so they can be matched. Then every archetype whose chunk list changed walks its back pointers and clears the valid flag on each matching query's cached chunk list. Nothing is rebuilt right then. The rebuild happens the next time somebody iterates, which means the cost of your structural change is billed to a system that had nothing to do with it. That is the part that makes profiles confusing.

chapters.title: Three honest levers
chapters.text: First, record the change into a command buffer instead, so many small barriers collapse into one barrier at a known system where you can see it. Second, use switchable components, so turning a thing off flips a bit in a mask rather than moving an entity between chunks. Third, operate on a whole query at once rather than one entity at a time, because the barrier is per operation, not per entity. And if you genuinely need a barrier every single update, there is an attribute for that, which is at least honest about what it is doing.

running.short: Jobs in flight, fences accumulating, nobody waiting on anything.
running.deep: This is where you want to be, and it is the default. Systems schedule work, hand each other handles through the scoreboard, and the main thread stays ahead of the workers. Nothing on this map happens at all until somebody asks to change the shape of an entity.
running.gotoLabel: The graph that is about to be drained

ask.short: Add, remove, create, or destroy. Any of the four is structural.
ask.deep: Setting a component's value is not structural, because the bytes already have a home. Changing which components an entity has is, because it changes which archetype the entity belongs to, and therefore which chunk. Creating and destroying are structural for the same reason: a slot in a chunk has to appear or disappear.

wait.short: Every fence of every registered type, combined and waited on.
wait.deep: One guard function sits in front of every structural change and calls the same completion. It gathers the write fence and all read fences of every type currently in the table, combines them into one handle, completes it, and then clears the table. In development builds it also invalidates every outstanding array handle, so anything still holding one fails loudly rather than quietly.

change.short: Single threaded, by definition, one memory copy per moved entity.
change.deep: Nothing else is running, so the change itself is a plain serial walk. Entities are moved chunk by chunk where possible rather than one at a time, and a chunk whose every entity is moving can be relabelled wholesale instead of copied. That batching is the single biggest reason operating on a query beats operating on entities in a loop.

resume.short: The fence table is empty, so the dependency graph starts again from nothing.
resume.deep: That emptiness has a consequence people miss. The first system to schedule after a barrier has no fences to wait on, so it starts immediately, but it also cannot inherit any ordering from before the barrier. Everything that mattered was already completed, so the graph really can restart clean.

ecb.short: Record the change and let a known system apply it later.
ecb.deep: This does not make the barrier free, it makes it countable. Instead of a barrier wherever the change was requested, you get one barrier in one system whose position in the update order you chose. That is the difference between a stall you can find in a profile and a hundred you cannot.

idle.short: Workers finish what they have and nothing is queued behind it.
idle.deep: This is the visible cost and it is the one people mean when they say sync point. But the shape matters: it is not a fixed price, it is however long the longest outstanding job chain still had to run. A barrier right after you scheduled a deep graph is expensive. The same barrier in a frame where nothing was scheduled is free.

caches.short: Every query matching a changed archetype loses its chunk list.
caches.deep: The runtime keeps a linked list of archetypes touched during this batch, walks it, and clears a flag on each of their queries. That is all it does. The actual rebuild is lazy, so the work lands on whichever system next iterates one of those queries, which is why the profile blames the wrong system.
caches.gotoLabel: The cache that just got dropped

lessons.title: Record Now, Merge Later
lessons.blurb: Every worker writes its own lock free chain, and playback merges them with a heap keyed on a number you chose.

chapters.title: Why there is no lock
chapters.text: The trick is embarrassingly simple and it is the right kind of simple. There is one chain per worker thread, plus one for the main thread. A parallel writer picks its chain from the thread index and nothing else. Two threads therefore never touch the same bytes while recording, so there is no lock, no atomic, no contention. Each chain is a linked list of four kilobyte blocks, and appending a command is bumping an offset inside the current block.

chapters.title: Playback is a k-way merge
chapters.text: At playback, every non-empty chain becomes one entry in a min heap keyed on the sort key of its next command. Pop the smallest, run that chain until it would pass the next smallest key, push it back with its new head key, repeat. That is a k-way merge of already-sorted sequences, exactly the algorithm you would use to merge sorted files. Which means the order commands are applied in depends only on the keys, and not at all on which thread recorded them or in what order the threads ran.

chapters.title: The key is the whole contract
chapters.text: So the sort key is not a hint, it is the total order. The documentation names the value to pass: the chunk index within the query. That index is stable for a given world state, which is what makes playback repeatable across runs and across machines. Pass a constant and every command ties, and the tie is not defined. Pass the entity index and you have coupled your ordering to an allocation pattern. This is the one parameter in the whole API where getting it wrong shows up as a bug you cannot reproduce.

chapters.title: The main thread always goes last
chapters.text: Here is a detail with real consequences. Commands recorded on the main thread are stamped with the largest possible integer. Since the merge always takes the smallest key next, that means everything you record outside a job is applied after everything recorded inside one, no matter what order you wrote the code in. If you have ever had a main thread destroy apparently happen after a job's add, that is why, and it is deliberate rather than accidental.

chapters.title: The handles were never placeholders
chapters.text: This is the one that overturned something I thought I knew. Folklore says a command buffer create hands you a fake entity with a negative index that gets patched during playback. Read the code and that is not what happens any more. Recording a create allocates real entity identifiers on the spot, from the same global table everything else uses, from inside the job. The documentation says it plainly: the entity is valid immediately, it simply has no chunk until playback puts it in one. There is even a source comment worrying about the atomic contention that costs on some processors.

key.short: A number you choose, and it is the entire ordering contract.
key.deep: The documentation names the chunk index within the query as the value to pass, and there is a reason. It is stable for a given world state, it is unique per chunk, and it is available for free inside the loop. Anything else you pass is either not stable, in which case playback is not repeatable, or not unique, in which case the ties are undefined.

chain.short: One chain per worker thread, four kilobyte blocks, no synchronisation at all.
chain.deep: A parallel writer resolves its chain purely from the thread index, so two threads recording at the same instant are writing into different allocations. Each block records the smallest key it contains, which is what lets playback seed the heap without scanning. When a block fills, another is linked on.

flush.short: The system completes its producers, then plays everything back.
flush.deep: This is the moment the deferred work becomes a real barrier, and it is the point of the whole exercise: one barrier at a system whose position in the update order you picked, rather than one wherever the change was requested. Playback failures are caught per buffer and reported with the name of the system that recorded them, which is unusually kind.

heap.short: A min heap over the chains, always taking the smallest key next.
heap.deep: Each chain contributes one heap entry holding its next key. The loop pops the smallest, runs that chain forward until it would overtake the current second smallest, then pushes the chain back with its updated key. Chains that run out are simply popped. The whole thing is the classic merge of sorted runs, and it is why the number of threads never affects the result.

apply.short: One command at a time, on the main thread, with the world stopped.
apply.deep: Every structural change here is a real structural change with everything the barrier implies, they are just all happening in one place. Chains that recorded nothing managed are walked by compiled code; chains that touched a managed component fall back to the interpreted walker, chosen from a flag stored on the chain itself.

last.short: Main thread commands carry the largest possible key, so they play last.
last.deep: Not a convention, a constant in the source. Since the merge takes the smallest key next, the largest key sorts to the end of everything. So a create you record on the main thread lands after every create recorded in a job, regardless of when either line of code ran. Worth knowing before you debug the ordering for an hour.

real.short: Recording a create mints a real entity identifier, right then, inside the job.
real.deep: The identifier comes from the same global slot table every other entity uses, allocated with atomics so a worker thread can do it without a lock. What playback adds is not the identity but the storage: the entity gets a chunk and a slot. This is also why the source carries a comment worrying about atomic contention on processors where that is expensive.

lessons.title: Where Your World Comes From
lessons.blurb: Nobody calls new world. A reflection scan picks one owner, and everything after that is a census.

chapters.title: Nobody calls new world
chapters.text: Here is the first strange thing about this engine. You never write the line that creates your world. Before the first scene has loaded, before a single script has woken up, the engine reflects over every type you have compiled, looking for one that says I will take over world creation. If it finds one, it hands the whole job over. If it does not, it builds one plain world and gets on with it. Either way, the thing your entities live in was constructed by a function you did not call, from a list you did not write.

chapters.title: The scan, and what it does with ties
chapters.text: The scan collects every type implementing the bootstrap interface, skips the abstract ones, and then does something worth knowing about. If one candidate is assignable from another, the more derived one wins silently. That is the whole inheritance trick: a package ships a bootstrap, you subclass it, and yours quietly replaces it with no registration step anywhere. But if two candidates are unrelated, the engine logs an error and picks arbitrarily. So the mechanism that makes layering effortless is also the one that makes a second unrelated bootstrap a genuinely confusing bug.

chapters.title: A world is a census result
chapters.text: Once someone owns creation, populating a world is one question asked repeatedly: give me every system carrying this filter flag. The server world asks for server simulation. The client world asks for client simulation plus presentation. The service world asks for a bit BovineLabs invented at position twenty one. Same question, different arguments, different worlds. There is no registry, no manifest, no ordering file. The list of systems in a world is a query result over the type system, computed at startup.

chapters.title: The word default means two different things
chapters.text: This is the part that costs people days. The default filter flag has two expansions and which one you get depends on who is asking. When a world is being populated, default expands to local simulation plus presentation, and that is a literal line of code. When a system is being classified, default expands to whatever its enclosing group declares as its child default, walking up the ordering chain. If that walk reaches a group with no parent, the fallback is local plus server plus client. That second one is what you meet in practice, because the root simulation group carries no filter attribute at all. Think of the flags as a decoder's address map. Default is not an address. It is an instruction that says: decode from the enclosing region.

chapters.title: Placement, and the silent default
chapters.text: Every system in the census is then handed to a group. The group attribute says which one. If a system has no such attribute at all, it is not dropped, and it does not error. It is added to the simulation group. Then each of the three roots is sorted once, topologically, from the ordering attributes. That sort happens exactly once at startup, which is why enabling and disabling systems later is free, and why adding one at runtime is not.

chapters.title: The splice that makes it a frame
chapters.text: None of this ticks yet. A world with a perfectly sorted system tree does nothing at all until its groups are inserted into Unity's own player loop. Initialization goes into the engine's initialization phase, simulation into update, presentation into the phase just before late update. That is it. That is the entire connection between the entity world and the game running. Three insertions into a data structure the engine already walks every frame, which is also why a second world is not a thread, not a process, and not free. It is three more entries in the same sequential list.

scan.short: Reflection over every compiled type, looking for one that claims world creation.
scan.deep: It runs before the first scene loads, so there is no ordering question about whether your scripts got a chance first. They did not. Types marked as opting out are filtered away, and among what remains the most derived candidate wins. That single rule is why a package can ship a bootstrap and you can extend it without registering anything anywhere.

custom.short: Return true and the engine builds nothing of its own.
custom.deep: The contract is blunt: your initialize method returns a boolean, and true means you have already created a world and set the default injection pointer. The engine asserts that you did, then returns your world untouched. Netcode's implementation branches on one setting, the requested play type, and from that decides whether a server world, a client world, or both come into existence.

fallback.short: No bootstrap, or one that declined: the engine builds a single plain world.
fallback.deep: It is named, flagged as a game world, made the default injection target, and populated with the default filter expansion, which is local simulation plus presentation. That is the single player configuration. Every tutorial you have read assumes this world exists, and in a netcode project it usually does not.

nerve.short: A lifecycle on top: one world that never dies, and others built on demand.
nerve.deep: Nerve is a bootstrap in its own right and separately extends the netcode one, which is exactly the inheritance trick the scan enables. It constructs a persistent service world from a filter bit of its own, then hand picks the Unity scene and entity systems it wants alongside. Client and server worlds are created and destroyed later, on a state graph transition. Netcode decides whether those worlds exist. Nerve decides when.

census.short: Ask the type manager for every system carrying a given filter flag.
census.deep: This is the only mechanism by which a system ends up in a world. There is no registration call and no configuration file. Which is also why a missing filter attribute is such a quiet failure: the system is not absent, it is present in three worlds at once, running your rule three times on three different sets of entities.
census.gotoLabel: Every flag, and what it selects

place.short: Each system is handed to the group its attribute names, then everything is sorted once.
place.deep: The three root groups are created first, unconditionally, whether or not anything will go in them. Then every system in the census is placed. A system with no group attribute is not an error and is not dropped; it lands in the simulation group. The sort is topological over the ordering attributes and it happens exactly once, at startup.
place.gotoLabel: The tree it sorts them into

loop.short: Three groups spliced into three phases of the engine's own frame.
loop.deep: Initialization goes into the engine's initialization phase, simulation into update, presentation into the phase before late update. That is the whole connection between an entity world and a running game. It also means every world in the process is walked sequentially inside one frame, on the main thread, one after another. Six worlds is six walks, not six threads.
loop.gotoLabel: What one system does inside that tick

lessons.title: The Update Tree
lessons.blurb: Three roots, three player loop phases, and the netcode groups at the positions their attributes actually give them.

chapters.title: Nothing here is a convention
