chapters.text: Every box on this map is at the position an attribute put it, and every one of those attributes was read out of the packages rather than remembered. That matters more than it sounds, because most of what people believe about this tree is folklore. The one fact worth carrying away before anything else: prediction runs before the ordinary fixed step, not after it. If your mental model has physics first and rollback second, it is backwards, and the attribute that proves it is four lines from the top of the netcode prediction file.

chapters.title: Three roots, and only three
chapters.text: Initialization, simulation and presentation are created in every world before any of your systems exist. They are not registered, they are hardcoded as the three things that count as roots. Each is spliced into a different phase of the engine's frame. And they are not symmetrical. The presentation group carries an attribute saying its children default to presentation only, which is why an unfiltered system placed in it never reaches a server. The simulation group carries no attribute at all, which is why an unfiltered system placed in it reaches every game world including the server.

chapters.title: The bucket at the front
chapters.text: Inside simulation there are three buckets, not one. A group can pin itself to the front, pin itself to the back, or say nothing and land in the middle. Four groups on this map pin themselves to the front, and then order among themselves with before and after edges. Network receive comes first because packets have to be in memory before anything reads them. Ghost simulation comes next because snapshots have to be applied before prediction restores from them. Then prediction. Then the ordinary fixed step. Read those four attributes in order and the frame stops being mysterious.

chapters.title: There are two fixed steps
chapters.text: Here is the thing nobody tells you. Netcode does not reuse the engine's fixed step group for prediction. It declares a second one, pinned to the front of the prediction group, and that is the one that replays. The outer fixed step is still there, still running, and it runs after the whole prediction loop has finished. So if you put a physics step in the outer group expecting it to be rolled back, it will not be. It will run once per frame, downstream of a replay that never saw it. The two groups have almost the same name and completely different lives.

chapters.title: Where your system actually lands
chapters.text: Write a system, add no attributes at all, and it goes into the middle bucket of the simulation group, in every game world. Not into initialization. Not into prediction. Not nowhere. It runs once per frame, after every group that pinned itself first, on client and server and local worlds simultaneously. Half of all why did that run twice questions end right there. The other half end at the trap in the ordering attributes: before and after only work between systems in the same group. Point one across a group boundary and the engine logs a warning and ignores it.

chapters.title: What this map leaves out, and why
chapters.text: There is more in the real tree. Command buffer systems bracket every group, pinned first and last. There is a variable rate group and a late simulation group. Command send and command receive sit inside ghost simulation and network receive. BovineLabs adds several of its own around scene loading and transforms. None of them are drawn here, and that is deliberate, because the mechanism for finding any of them is identical: open the file, read four attributes, and you know exactly where it runs.

init.short: The first root group. Scene resolution and subscene streaming live here.
init.deep: It is spliced into the engine's initialization phase, which is before the ordinary update. That placement is why a subscene section can become resident before any simulation system runs that frame, and why entities from a scene appear at the top of a frame rather than in the middle of one.

sim.short: The second root, and the one with no world filter at all.
sim.deep: Because it declares nothing, a chain of group attributes that ends here falls through to the fallback expansion: local, server and client simulation. That single absence is the mechanism behind the most common ECS bug there is, an unfiltered gameplay system quietly running in three worlds. It is also the default destination for any system that names no group.
sim.gotoLabel: Why an unfiltered system lands everywhere

pres.short: The one root group that overrides what its children default to.
pres.deep: Its attribute passes a second argument naming presentation, so an unfiltered system placed inside it is presentation only and will never exist on a server. Every other root leaves that argument at its default and therefore delegates the question upward. If you want a rule that only runs where there is a screen, this group is the enforcement mechanism, not a naming convention.
pres.gotoLabel: Where presentation sits in the whole stack

netrecv.short: Pinned to the front of simulation, and ordered before ghost simulation.
netrecv.deep: Its attributes say three things: order first, after the begin command buffer system, and before ghost simulation. So packets are pulled off the socket and into memory before any system that wants to read them has run. This is also where connection handling and command receive live on the server.

ghost.short: Applies snapshots and gathers input, before prediction and before fixed step.
ghost.deep: It declares itself before both the fixed step group and the prediction group, which is the ordering that makes the whole rollback scheme work: the authoritative state has to be written over the predicted state before the replay decides where to rewind to. The input gathering group and the command send group both live inside it.

predict.short: Pinned to the front of simulation and ordered before the ordinary fixed step.
predict.deep: On a client it runs many times in one frame, once per replayed tick. On a server it runs once. It is the same group with the same children either side, which is what lets one implementation of a movement rule be the authority and the prediction at the same time. Its own attribute uses the default filter, so it exists on the server too, which surprises people who read the word predicted as client only.

pfixed.short: A second fixed step group, pinned first inside prediction. This is the one that replays.
pfixed.deep: It exists because the ordinary fixed step group is outside prediction and therefore cannot be rolled back. Anything you want resimulated on a correction goes here. The two groups have nearly identical names and completely different behaviour, and putting your step in the wrong one produces a bug that looks like bad physics rather than bad ordering.

fixed.short: The ordinary fixed step, pinned to the front but ordered after prediction.
fixed.deep: It runs on a fixed delta with a catch up loop, and it runs once the whole prediction loop has already finished for this frame. Nothing in it is rolled back, replayed or corrected. For deterministic non networked work that is exactly what you want, and for anything a snapshot might disagree with it is exactly what you do not.
fixed.gotoLabel: The two clocks these steps serve

yours.short: A system with no attributes at all. It lands here, in every game world.
yours.deep: Not in initialization, not in prediction, and not nowhere. The placement code adds it to the simulation group when no group attribute is present, and the classification code resolves its filter through the fallback, which names local, server and client. So the laziest possible system is also the most widely distributed one you can write.
yours.gotoLabel: What happens to it every frame

lessons.title: One System, One Frame
lessons.blurb: Two switches ANDed in a single if, and a one-bit latch that turns the result into edges.

chapters.title: The whole thing is one if statement
chapters.text: There is a temptation to imagine a scheduler here, something that decides which systems are eligible this frame and builds a list. There is nothing of the kind. The group walks its sorted array, and for every entry it evaluates one condition: the enabled bit, ANDed with a requirement test. True runs your update. False does not. That is the entire gating mechanism, and it is written the same way for both the managed and the unmanaged flavour of system.

chapters.title: Creation is not part of the frame
chapters.text: Your create callback runs once, when the world is built, before any group has ticked. It runs whether or not the system will ever update again. This is where queries are built and where you declare what your update requires, and both of those are structural decisions that then hold for the life of the world. If you are used to lazy initialisation on first use, unlearn it here: by the time the first frame happens, every system in the world has already had its create callback run.

chapters.title: Two switches, and they are not the same switch
chapters.text: The first switch is a bit you own. Set it false and the system stops updating, immediately, with no other side effects. The second switch is the requirement test, and it belongs to the data. If you declared that your update requires a component, the test asks whether any chunk anywhere holds one. If you declared nothing, it returns true immediately. Think of the first as a chip select you drive by hand and the second as a data ready line the world raises for you. They are ANDed, so either one low means no update.

chapters.title: A skipped system is still there
chapters.text: Turning a system off does not remove it from anything. It stays in its group's sorted array, it is visited every frame, the sort is not recomputed, and turning it back on costs nothing but the next evaluation of that if. This is worth internalising because it sets the price of the feature. Toggling systems is a branch not taken, so it is cheap enough to do per frame and per world. Adding or removing a system at runtime is not that; that is a structural change to the tree and a resort.

chapters.title: The latch that makes edges
chapters.text: There is a single stored bit remembering whether the system ran last frame, and it is what turns a level into edges. The first frame the gate is true, that bit is set and the start callback fires once. The first frame the gate goes false after having been true, the engine completes any jobs the system still owns, fires the stop callback once, and clears the bit. It is an edge detector, in the plain hardware sense. Which is why the stop callback is the correct place to release anything the system was holding, and the update callback never is.

chapters.title: The requirement test ignores your filters
chapters.text: Here is the sharp edge. The requirement test checks each required query with an emptiness test that deliberately ignores filters. That means enableable components do not count, and shared component filters do not count. Require a component that exists on a thousand entities and is disabled on all thousand of them, and the gate opens anyway. Your update runs, your query matches nothing, and you spend an afternoon convinced the gate is broken. It is not. It was answering a coarser question than you asked.

create.short: Runs once, at world construction, before any group has ticked.
create.deep: Queries are built here, and so is the declaration of what the update requires. Both are structural, and both hold for the life of the world. It also runs on systems that will never update even once, because creation is driven by the world's system list rather than by whether anything will match.
create.gotoLabel: Where the world that created it came from

gate.short: The enabled bit ANDed with the requirement test, evaluated every single frame.
gate.deep: One condition, in one place, for both managed and unmanaged systems. The enabled half is a single bit inside the system's flag word, so reading and writing it is free. The requirement half walks the required queries and asks each whether it is empty, short circuiting on the first empty one. Declare no requirements and it returns true without looking at anything.
gate.gotoLabel: What that emptiness test is really asking

run.short: The only place your work happens, and the level the two edge callbacks bracket.
run.deep: By the time it is called, the system's dependency handle already carries whatever the safety system worked out from your reads and writes. Most updates schedule rather than execute, so the interesting cost is usually not in here at all; it is in what this method hands to the job system before returning.

skip.short: The gate closed. The system is still sorted, still visited, and costs one branch.
skip.deep: Nothing is removed and nothing is recomputed. This is the mechanism that makes disabling a system a per frame decision you can afford: the only cost of an off system is evaluating the condition that keeps it off. Contrast that with adding or removing a system, which changes the tree and forces a resort.
skip.gotoLabel: The group that keeps visiting it

stop.short: Fires once, on the falling edge, after pending jobs have been completed.
stop.deep: A single stored bit remembers last frame's answer, so this callback cannot fire twice in a row and cannot fire on a system that never ran. Before it is called the engine completes the system's outstanding dependency, which means it is the one safe place to release native containers the system was still handing to jobs.

destroy.short: Runs when the world goes away, even for a system that never updated once.
destroy.deep: It is guaranteed in a way the running callbacks are not: those depend on edges that may never happen, this one depends only on the world being disposed. Anything allocated in the create callback belongs here. In a project where worlds are built and torn down on state transitions rather than once at startup, this stops being a shutdown detail and becomes a per session one.
destroy.gotoLabel: The worlds that get destroyed on purpose

lessons.title: Baking Is a Compile Step
lessons.blurb: A source language, a dependency-tracked front end, whole-program passes, a strip, and an object file you ship.

chapters.title: Nobody tells you it is a compiler
chapters.text: Read the documentation and baking sounds like a conversion utility. It is not. It is a compiler, and once you see it that way every confusing thing about it becomes ordinary. There is a source language, which is game objects and their components. There is a front end with dependency tracking, which is bakers. There are whole program passes that run after the front end, which are baking systems. There is a dead code pass, which is the strip. And there is an object file, which is the entity section file that actually ships. The player contains no compiler at all.

chapters.title: A baker cannot look around
chapters.text: Each baker gets exactly one authoring component and is expected to write components onto an entity. It cannot query the scene. It cannot see what the baker next to it did. That looks like a limitation until you notice what it buys: because a baker can only reach what it explicitly asks for, and every ask is recorded, the system knows precisely which bakers to re-run when you drag a slider. Change one field and one baker runs. The restriction is the entire incremental story.

chapters.title: The dependency record is the key
chapters.text: Every read a baker makes is registered as a dependency. That record is the cache key. And the failure mode that follows is the single most common baking bug there is: read something without declaring it, and the value is baked correctly the first time, then never updated again. You edit the asset, nothing happens, you assume the runtime is broken, and you spend an hour in the wrong file. The bake was never re-run because as far as the record is concerned nothing you touched was an input.

chapters.title: The passes, in order
chapters.text: Bakers are not the whole compile. First a pre-baking group runs, for cleanup before anything is read. Then every baker. Then transform baking, which resolves hierarchies into world matrices. Then the ordinary baking systems, which unlike bakers can query the entire scene at once and are therefore where anything cross cutting belongs. Then linked entity groups, then companion objects, then a post-baking group, and finally the strip. Eight ordered phases, all inside a world that is created and thrown away in one call.

chapters.title: The strip is the dead code pass
chapters.text: Every type marked as temporary is queried and removed before serialization. That is what makes the scaffolding pattern safe: you can invent a component whose whole purpose is to carry information from a baker to a later baking system, and be certain it never reaches the player. It also explains something people find eerie, which is that you cannot inspect any of this at runtime. There is nothing to inspect. It was compiled out.

chapters.title: Sections are the output units
chapters.text: The last thing the compile decides is how the output is split. A shared component partitions the baked entities into numbered sections, each section is moved into its own private world, and each is serialized into its own file. Section zero is the one that always comes with the scene. Everything else is separately requestable. Which means your streaming granularity is not a runtime setting at all. It was fixed at bake time, and changing it means recompiling the scene.

go.short: The source language: components you can see, click and drag.
go.deep: Game objects are what a designer edits and what version control diffs. Nothing about them survives into the runtime data; they are input to a compile, in the same sense that a header file is input to one. Their only job is to be readable by a human and by a baker.

dep.short: Every value a baker touched, recorded as the key that decides whether it re-runs.
dep.deep: This is the mechanism behind incremental baking, and behind its most confusing failure. Read a value through a declared dependency and edits to it trigger a re-bake of exactly that baker. Read it some other way and the record does not know it was an input, so your edit changes nothing and no error is ever printed.

baker.short: One per authoring component, and structurally unable to see its neighbours.
baker.deep: It is handed a component and writes to an entity. It cannot run a query, and every value it reaches for outside its own component is registered as a dependency. That restriction is what makes the whole pass cacheable at the granularity of a single component, which is what makes editing a scene with thousands of objects feel instant.
baker.gotoLabel: What a baker builds when the data is big

bsys.short: Ordinary systems that run after every baker, with full query access to the scene.
bsys.deep: This is where anything cross cutting belongs: building a lookup table from every object of a kind, resolving references between separately baked objects, computing something that needs a total. They run in the baking world with a filter flag of their own, and they are marked to never be auto created anywhere else.
bsys.gotoLabel: What adding a component costs, even here

strip.short: Queries every temporary type and removes it, always last.
strip.deep: It is a dead code pass. Types marked as temporary baking types exist during the compile so that one phase can hand information to the next, and they are deleted before serialization so none of it reaches the player. Which is why a component you invented purely as scaffolding is invisible to every runtime inspector, correctly.
strip.gotoLabel: The other strip, the per-world one

file.short: A serialized chunk image, one file per section. This is the object file.
file.deep: It is not a scene format in any recognisable sense. It is the memory layout of the chunks themselves, written out, with entity references converted to indices and blob handles converted to offsets. Which is why loading it is closer to mapping a binary than to parsing a document.
file.gotoLabel: What a chunk image looks like inside

load.short: At runtime the bytes are read, the references are patched, and the entities are moved in.
load.deep: There is no baker in the player. Not disabled, not stripped down: absent, because bakers live in editor only assemblies. So if a value is wrong at runtime, no runtime code made it wrong, and no runtime code can fix it. The only correct place to look is upstream of the build.

lessons.title: What Is Resident, and When
lessons.blurb: One component is the whole switch. A section loads in a private world nobody can see, then arrives all at once.

chapters.title: One component is the entire interface
chapters.text: There is no load function you call and no handle you keep. There is a component. Add it to a scene entity and the section streams in. Remove it and the section streams out. That is the whole public interface, and it means loading is a piece of data rather than a piece of control flow, which in turn means the load state of your world is something a system can query, save and replicate like anything else.

chapters.title: Two entities you never authored
chapters.text: Before anything loads, a resolve step reads the section header and creates one meta entity per section, hanging them off the scene entity in a buffer. At that moment the world knows how many sections exist and where they are, and holds none of their contents. The request then propagates from the scene entity down to the section entities unless you asked it not to. So the granularity you are really controlling is not scenes; it is sections, and there is an entity per section sitting there waiting to be switched on individually.

chapters.title: It is deserialized somewhere else on purpose
chapters.text: This is the part that surprises people. A section is not deserialized into your world. It is deserialized into a separate world flagged as streaming, one per section in flight, four in flight by default. That world is populated only with systems carrying a process after load filter, so almost nothing you wrote exists there. Your world never sees a half constructed section, and a system running in your world genuinely cannot observe the intermediate state, because the intermediate state is in a different address space.

chapters.title: Arrival is a move, not a copy
chapters.text: When the streaming world is finished, the entire section is moved across in one bulk operation, and by default only one world is moved per update. Two consequences follow and both are visible in a profile. The section appears all at once, in a single frame, rather than trickling in over several. And the frame it arrives on is the expensive one, because that is where the chunks are relocated and the references are remapped. If your loading hitch has a sharp single frame spike rather than a broad hump, this is where to look.

chapters.title: Unloading is a query, not a list
chapters.text: Every entity that came from a section carries a shared component naming its section entity. Unloading sets that as a filter and destroys the matching query. Nothing walks a list of loaded entities, because nothing keeps one. The archetype structure does the walking, and the cost scales with matching chunks rather than with entity count. Which is why unloading a big section can be cheaper than you expect, and why an entity that lost its tag becomes a leak nothing will ever collect.

ask.short: Adding one component to the scene entity is the entire load request.
ask.deep: It carries a small set of flags: block until imported, block until streamed, do not auto load the sections, load a fresh instance. Everything else about the load is decided by the file. Removing this component is the unload request, so the load state of the world is data, which means it can be inspected, saved and replicated like any other component.

resolve.short: Reads the header, then creates one meta entity per section.
resolve.deep: The header is a small blob listing the sections and their bounding volumes. Resolving it costs a file read and produces a buffer of section entities on the scene entity, with no section contents in memory. From that point the sections are individually switchable, which is the granularity people usually mean when they say streaming.

stream.short: A separate world, flagged as streaming, that your systems do not live in.
stream.deep: Four sections can be in flight at once by default, each in its own world. That world is populated only with systems carrying the process after load filter, and the code explicitly refuses to let system entities exist inside it. So your world never observes a partially built section, not because anyone is careful, but because it is not in your address space yet.
stream.gotoLabel: The other worlds in this process

after.short: Systems that exist only in the streaming world, given their own filter flag.
after.deep: This is the hook for anything that must happen to a section's data before the rest of the game can see it: fixing up references, building runtime caches, converting a baked representation into a live one. Write one and it will never appear in your game world, because the flag it carries is only ever asked for when a streaming world is being populated.
after.gotoLabel: How a world gets its system list

live.short: The whole section moved across in one operation, tagged and queryable.
live.deep: One bulk move, and by default one world moved per update, which serialises arrivals rather than interleaving them. That is why a section appears in a single frame and why that frame costs more than its neighbours. Everything that arrives carries a shared tag naming the section it came from, which is what makes the reverse operation cheap.

gone.short: Remove the request, and a filtered destroy takes the section out.
gone.deep: The shared tag is set as a query filter and the matching entities are destroyed. There is no list, no reference count on individual entities, and no traversal of anything you spawned. The consequence worth remembering is the other direction: an entity you created at runtime and gave no scene tag will never be removed by an unload, which is usually right and occasionally the leak you are hunting.
gone.gotoLabel: How the filtered destroy finds them

lessons.title: Position-Independent Data
lessons.blurb: Every pointer inside a blob is an offset from its own address, so the block is valid wherever it lands.

chapters.title: The whole idea is one line of code
chapters.text: A blob pointer does not store an address. It stores a signed thirty two bit offset, and dereferencing it takes the address of the offset field itself and adds the offset to that. Read that twice, because everything else follows from it. The pointer is relative to its own location, so nothing inside the block knows or cares where the block lives. You can memory copy it, write it to disk, read it back at a different address, map it into a different process, and every internal reference is still correct. It is position independent code, applied to data.

chapters.title: Built in scratch, then flattened
chapters.text: You do not build a blob in place. The builder hands out allocations from scratch chunks as you ask for them, wherever they happen to fit, and remembers what points at what. Only at the end does it compute the total size, allocate one contiguous region, copy everything in, and rewrite every internal pointer as an offset. That two phase shape is why you construct a root first and then allocate arrays inside it, and why you can build a tree without knowing its size up front.

chapters.title: The thirty-two bytes in front
chapters.text: Immediately before the data sits a fixed thirty two byte header carrying a validation pointer, the length, the allocator handle and a hash. The validation pointer is the interesting one: it is set to point just past itself, and checking it is how a use after dispose becomes an assert instead of a page of garbage. When a blob is serialized that field is written as null and filled in on load, which tells you something about the intent. The header is a runtime concern. The data is the artifact.

chapters.title: One word of fixup, and only one
chapters.text: Here is what the relative pointers actually buy. When a section file loads, the loader walks the components that hold blob handles, and for each one replaces a stored byte offset with the batch base address plus that offset. One word written, per reference, per entity. It never goes inside the block. It never touches an array, never follows a chain, never walks a graph. So the fixup cost is proportional to how many things point at your blob, and completely independent of how big the blob is. A hundred megabyte navigation mesh costs the same to load as an eight byte one.

chapters.title: What that buys, and the one way to break it
chapters.text: A million entities can share one block with no duplication and no synchronisation, because the block is immutable by contract and every job can read it at once. The engine defends that contract with an attribute saying certain types may only live in blob storage, and a compiler analyser that refuses to let you copy one out by value. That defence is not pedantry. Copy a blob array field into a local and you have copied the offset without its context, so it now points at whatever happens to be that far from your stack frame.

builder.short: Allocates from scratch chunks as you ask, then flattens everything at the end.
builder.deep: The two phase shape is what lets you build a variable sized structure without knowing its total size first. You construct a root, allocate arrays and pointers inside it, fill them, and only when you ask for the finished reference does the builder compute the total, take one allocation, and copy everything in with the offsets rewritten.

block.short: One contiguous allocation: a fixed thirty-two byte header, then all the data.
block.deep: The header carries a validation pointer, the length, the allocator handle and a hash, and it is sized to keep the data aligned. The validation pointer is set to point just past itself, so a dangling reference fails an equality check rather than reading nonsense. On serialization it is written as null and reconstructed on load.

rel.short: Every internal pointer is a signed offset from the address of the offset field itself.
rel.deep: Dereferencing pins the field, takes its address, and adds the stored offset to it. Nothing in the block ever refers to an absolute address, which is why copying the bytes is a complete and correct clone, and why the same bytes are valid at a different base in a different process. Zero means null, which is why an offset of zero is reserved rather than legal.

ref.short: The handle on the component. The only genuinely absolute pointer in the scheme.
ref.deep: It is the boundary between the two worlds: outside it, ordinary pointers and ordinary lifetimes; inside it, nothing but offsets. That is also why it is the only thing that needs fixing up on load, and why it is the only field the serializer has to know about in a component that carries a blob.
ref.gotoLabel: The component array it sits in

batch.short: The blocks written end to end inside the section file.
batch.deep: Because no pointer inside a block is absolute, writing one out is a copy and reading it back is a copy. The file stores each handle as a byte offset into this batch, so the entire relocation problem collapses into arithmetic on one integer per reference.
batch.gotoLabel: The pass that wrote this file

patch.short: The batch base plus the stored offset. One word per handle, and nothing else.
patch.deep: The loader walks components whose type carries blob reference offsets and rewrites each handle in place. Minus one is the null sentinel and stays null. The block itself is never entered, so the cost of loading a blob is set by how many things reference it, not by how large it is. That is the property that makes mapping a blob straight off disk a reasonable thing to imagine.

read.short: Shared by every entity that references it, immutable, and never copied.
read.deep: Immutability is the contract that lets every job read it concurrently with no synchronisation at all. The engine defends that contract with an attribute marking types that may only live in blob storage, and an analyser that refuses to compile a copy out by value. That is not style enforcement: a copied blob field is an offset separated from the address it was measured against.
read.gotoLabel: Why every job can read it at once

lessons.title: Worlds on the Wire
lessons.blurb: Two worlds in one process are still two machines. And the host flag is false for both of them here.

chapters.title: One process, two machines
chapters.text: Press play in the editor and you get two worlds. A server world and a client world, in one operating system process, sharing one address space. It is tempting to read that as one program wearing two hats. It is not. They have separate entity managers, separate singletons, separate copies of every system, and they talk to each other over a socket. Nothing crosses between them except bytes on a connection. If you keep that one fact, most of the confusing behaviour in this package stops being confusing.

chapters.title: A world is a flag word
chapters.text: There is no world class hierarchy here. A world carries a flags field, and netcode reads bits out of it. One bit means game server. Another means game client. A third means thin client. Every question the package asks about a world is a bit test on that word. Is this the server? Test one bit. Is this a client? Test one bit, or the thin bit. That is the entire type system, and it is the reason a world can be interrogated from Burst compiled code with no branches worth mentioning.

chapters.title: The AND that is false here
chapters.text: Now the interesting one. The host test is defined as: is a client, and is a server. Both, on the same world. Read that again with the flag word in mind. It is asking whether one world carries both bits at once. In this project it never does. The bootstrap built two worlds, and each got exactly one bit. So the host test returns false on the server world, and false on the client world, and there is nowhere in this topology where it could return true. Our own client state system says so in a comment, right where it fills the field in.

chapters.title: Where it would be true
chapters.text: There is a shape where it is true, and it is worth knowing so you can recognise it when you read package code. A single world host builds one world with both flags set at once, so the client half and the server half share an entity manager and never touch a socket. It is guarded behind an experimental define and a configuration setting, and it is off here. But netcode is full of branches that check for it, and those branches are the reason a comment saying our topology is not a host world is a load bearing comment, not a note.

chapters.title: The thin client is an amputation
chapters.text: The thin client world is not a client with rendering turned off. It is built from a different filter entirely, so the systems that were never marked for thin client simulation do not exist in it at all. No presentation, no rendering, no interpolated ghost application. It holds a connection open and generates command traffic, which is exactly what you want for testing fifty players. The surprise arrives when something you assumed was universal turns out to have been marked client only, and simply is not there. That includes, in this project, the subscene loading that brings up the client graph.

chapters.title: They still talk over a socket
chapters.text: Even in one process, the two worlds do not read each other's memory. The server binds a port and listens. The client connects. Netcode registers two transports for this: a shared memory transport for the pair inside one process, and a real socket for everyone else, including a second editor instance on the same machine. That is why the server row in the tools window shows two endpoints. The in-process pair takes the fast path, and it is still a connection, with an identifier, a state machine, and a disconnect reason.

playtype.short: One enum, read once at startup, deciding which worlds exist at all.
playtype.deep: It has three values: client and server, client only, server only. The bootstrap reads it once and builds accordingly. Everything downstream, including whether your player can even spawn, is a consequence of this one read. In the editor it comes from a preference, and that preference is shared between editor instances, which is its own chapter.
playtype.gotoLabel: Why a second editor reads the same value

server.short: The only world with authority, and the only one that never renders.
server.deep: It carries the game server flag and nothing else. Systems land in it because they declared the server simulation filter. It owns the truth, it owns the port, and it is the only place where a decision is final. Everything you see on any screen is some client's approximation of what happened here, at a tick that has already passed.
server.gotoLabel: Which world does my system land in?

client.short: Carries the game client flag, renders, and runs two clocks of its own.
client.deep: It never has authority over anything. What it does have is two derived timelines, one behind the server and one ahead of it, and every replicated entity in it is assigned to one of them. That assignment is the single largest performance decision in the project, and it is made per prefab at bake time.
client.gotoLabel: The two clocks inside this world

thin.short: Built from a different system filter, so most of the client is simply absent.
thin.deep: It is not a client with features disabled. Systems are gathered by the thin client simulation filter, and anything that did not opt in was never added. It exists to hold a connection and fabricate input, which makes it perfect for load testing and misleading for anything else. In this project it also does not load the client subscenes, so it has no state graph.
thin.gotoLabel: Every topology these worlds can form

wire.short: One listening port, two transports: shared memory in-process, a real socket outside.
wire.deep: The driver store registers more than one driver type. A client and server in the same process get a shared memory transport with no kernel involved. Anything else, including a second editor instance on this same machine, takes a real socket to the same port. Both look identical to your code, because a connection is an entity either way.

ishost.short: Defined as: is a client, and is a server, on the same world. False here, twice.
ishost.deep: This is a bit test conjunction, not a configuration option. Two separate worlds cannot satisfy it, because each carries only one of the two flags. Package code branches on it in a couple of dozen places, and every one of those branches takes the two-world path in this project. Reading it as meaning our client and server are in the same process is the mistake that costs an afternoon.

single.short: One world carrying both flags, which is the only shape the host test accepts.
single.deep: Behind an experimental define, the bootstrap can build a single world holding the server simulation, the client simulation and presentation together. There is no socket between the halves. That is the topology the host branches were written for, and it changes command timing, prediction and spawn handling in ways the two-world path never sees. It is off here, and knowing it exists is what makes the false host test make sense.

lessons.title: Four Timelines
lessons.blurb: The package counts four, not three. The fourth hides behind the third whenever forced input latency is zero.

chapters.title: Count them again
chapters.text: Everybody teaches this as three clocks. Interpolated behind, server in the middle, predicted ahead. That is the picture in most articles and it is the picture in this handbook's earlier chapters. The package disagrees, in a comment, in one line, and it is worth reading literally. It says the four timelines are, in order: interpolation tick, oldest. Then snapshot arrival tick, from the server. Then server tick, which is client prediction. Then input target tick, which is inputs being raised and sent. Four. So where did the fourth one go?

chapters.title: The second timeline nobody draws
chapters.text: Start with the one that gets left out of every diagram, including this book's. The snapshot arrival tick. The newest server state the client actually has in hand. It is not the server's present, because that state left the server half a round trip ago. It is not the predicted tick, because the client has run ahead of it. And it is not the interpolation tick, because the client is deliberately reading behind it. It is a fourth number, it moves in jumps as packets land, and both of the client's smooth clocks are built out of it.

chapters.title: The client never reads the server clock
chapters.text: Here is the part that should feel familiar from hardware. The client has no wire carrying the server's tick counter. What it has is an estimate of the tick it expects to receive next, maintained as an exponential average of how wrong it has been. Every frame the estimate is advanced by elapsed ticks and then corrected against what actually arrived. Both of the client's clocks are derived from that estimate, in opposite directions. So this is not clock recovery from an edge. It is a phase estimator with a feedback term, and everything downstream inherits its error.

chapters.title: One estimate, two directions
chapters.text: From the estimate, subtract the interpolation depth and you have the tick you render other players at. From the same estimate, add round trip time in ticks plus a command slack margin, and you have the tick you are predicting. Each of those has its own rate multiplier, nudged by a fraction of the current error every frame, and each multiplier is clamped: prediction between nine tenths and one and a tenth, interpolation between eighty five hundredths and one and a tenth. They are servo loops. They slew, they do not step, unless the error gets large enough to give up and snap.

chapters.title: The fourth, and what hides it
chapters.text: Now the fourth. The tick you stamp your input with is not the tick you are predicting. It is the predicted tick plus the effective input latency. By default that latency is zero, the two numbers are identical, and the fourth timeline sits exactly on top of the third. That is why everyone counts three. Set forced input latency above zero and they separate: the client keeps predicting the near tick while your keypress is filed for a later one. Your capsule stops answering instantly, and in exchange the rollback depth drops sharply. That is the trade, stated as an offset.

chapters.title: It is not always your choice
chapters.text: And here is the sting. The effective latency is not simply the value you set. It is the larger of your setting and whatever the ping forces. If round trip plus slack exceeds the maximum predict ahead time, five hundred milliseconds by default, netcode raises the latency itself to keep the prediction window bounded. A high ping player therefore gets forced input latency whether or not anyone configured it. In a single world host there is a third contributor: an off frame adds one more tick. So the fourth timeline can appear on somebody else's machine and never on yours.

chapters.title: When the order inverts
chapters.text: One last mechanism, and it is the sort of detail that only exists because somebody hit it. Push forced latency high enough and the predicted tick falls behind the interpolation tick. The four timelines would be out of order. Netcode refuses. It drags the interpolation target forward to meet the predicted tick, which quietly lengthens the interpolation window. So the two knobs are coupled at the extreme. Tune one far enough and you have moved the other, and nothing in the inspector tells you that happened.

servertick.short: The one authoritative timeline, and no screen anywhere is showing it.
servertick.deep: It advances at the simulation rate and it is the only tick that is not an estimate of something else. Every other number on this map is a client's attempt to be somewhere useful relative to it. One side lags it deliberately, one side runs ahead of it deliberately, and neither is ever equal to it.
servertick.gotoLabel: Which world this clock lives in

arrive.short: The newest server tick the client actually holds. It moves in jumps.
arrive.deep: This is the timeline the standard three clock picture omits. It is not the server's present, because that packet took half a round trip to get here. It is not either of the client's own clocks. It is the raw arrival edge, and both smooth clocks are phase estimates built from it.
arrive.gotoLabel: What is inside one of those packets

estimate.short: The client's running guess at the tick it is about to receive next.
estimate.deep: Maintained as an exponential average of how wrong the last guess was, advanced by elapsed ticks each frame and corrected when a packet lands. It also tracks the average and deviation of the gap between snapshots, which is what lets the interpolation depth react to a worsening link without anyone touching a setting.

predict.short: Estimate plus round trip plus command slack. The tick the client simulates.
predict.deep: It is far enough ahead that a command stamped now arrives before the server simulates that tick. Its rate is scaled by a tenth of the current command age error, clamped between nine tenths and one and a tenth of normal, so it drifts into alignment rather than jumping. A jump of more than ten ticks logs an error, because that usually means a stall rather than a network event.
predict.gotoLabel: What runs at this tick, every frame

interp.short: Estimate minus the interpolation depth. The tick you see everyone else at.
interp.deep: Its rate multiplier is clamped between eighty five hundredths and one and a tenth, and it corrects a tenth of the remaining error per frame. Only an error above ten ticks makes it snap. The depth it trails by is not a constant: it is the larger of your configured window and a jitter derived estimate, so a lossy link deepens it for you.
interp.gotoLabel: Inside the buffer this reads from

input.short: Predicted tick plus effective input latency. Zero by default, so it hides.
input.deep: This is the fourth timeline, and it is the tick your command data is stamped with. Because the default latency is zero it normally equals the predicted tick exactly, which is why almost every diagram shows three clocks. It separates when forced latency is configured, when ping exceeds the maximum predict ahead time, or on an off frame in single world host mode.
input.gotoLabel: Follow one keypress from this tick

clamp.short: The guard that refuses to let prediction fall behind interpolation.
clamp.deep: With enough forced latency the predicted tick can drop below the interpolation tick, which would put the four timelines out of order. Netcode detects that and pulls the interpolation target forward to meet the predicted tick instead. The visible consequence is that the interpolation window lengthens on its own, so the two settings are coupled at the extreme.
clamp.gotoLabel: Why these clocks must stay ordered

lessons.title: As Much World As Fits
lessons.blurb: A snapshot is not the world. It is a prioritised prefix of the world, cut off wherever the packet ends.

chapters.title: The sentence that reframes everything
chapters.text: A snapshot is not a picture of the world. It is as much of the world as fits in one packet, chosen in priority order, encoded as differences against what this one client already acknowledged. Every word there is doing work. As much as fits: there is a hard byte ceiling. Chosen in priority order: the list is sorted before a single bit is written. This one client: the encoding is different for every connection. And differences: almost nothing on the wire is an absolute value.

chapters.title: Order first, then write
chapters.text: The first thing that happens is not encoding. It is sorting. The server walks the ghost chunks for this connection, computes a priority for each one, and sorts the whole list descending before writing anything. That order is what makes the cut meaningful. If it wrote in arbitrary order and stopped when full, the packet would carry a random sample. Because it sorts first, the packet carries the most important prefix, and whatever fell off the end keeps ageing so its priority climbs for next time.

chapters.title: Every client has a different past
chapters.text: Now the encoding, and this is the part that surprises people who expect a broadcast. The server does not encode one snapshot and send it to everybody. It keeps a per connection history of what it sent and which slots each client acknowledged, and it delta encodes against that client's own acknowledged state. Two clients on the same tick receive genuinely different bytes for the same entity, because they last confirmed different ticks. This is why send cost scales with connections times ghosts and not with ghosts alone.

chapters.title: Three baselines, one prediction
chapters.text: It goes further than a simple difference. For each entity the serializer finds up to three acknowledged baselines and uses them to extrapolate a prediction of the current value, then encodes only the residual against that prediction. Constant velocity therefore costs almost nothing: the extrapolation is right and the residual is near zero, and a near zero residual costs a handful of bits after entropy coding. That is a linear predictor plus an entropy coder, which is a familiar shape if you have looked at any lossless codec.

chapters.title: Where the world gets cut
chapters.text: Writing continues until the bit budget runs out, and then it stops mid list. Nothing is dropped, nothing is queued, nothing errors. The chunks below the line simply were not sent this tick, and their age term keeps climbing, so they rise in the sort and go out on a later one. Starvation is prevented by ageing rather than by a queue. This is bus arbitration with a priority that increments while you wait, and if you have built one of those in hardware you already know its failure modes.

chapters.title: What lands, and where it goes
chapters.text: On the client the packet is decoded against the same baselines, and the result is written into a ring buffer attached to each ghost. Thirty two slots by default, each stamped with its tick, sized for about half a second of round trip. Note what did not happen: nothing was applied to any entity yet. The receive path only fills slots. The decision about which slot to read is somebody else's job, one system later, and it depends on which timeline that particular ghost lives on.

chapters.title: The same buffer, two different reads
chapters.text: The update system is where the split happens. For an interpolated ghost it reads at the interpolation tick, finds the two slots that bracket it, and blends. For a predicted ghost it reads at the tick being predicted, pins the blend factor to zero, and uses the result as a rollback point rather than a display value. One buffer, one arrival path, two entirely different meanings depending on a flag on the entity. That is the cleanest place in the whole package to see that prediction and interpolation are two readers of one queue.

sort.short: The chunk list is sorted by priority before a single bit is written.
sort.deep: Priority is a base importance multiplied by how many ticks it has been since this connection last saw that chunk, then adjusted by whatever scaling function you supplied. Sorting first is what makes the packet a meaningful prefix rather than a random sample, and the age term is what stops a low priority chunk from starving forever.

baselines.short: Per connection history of what was sent and what came back acknowledged.
baselines.deep: Thirty two slots per chunk, each holding a previously serialised snapshot. Only slots this client acknowledged can be used as baselines, and a baseline older than the maximum age is discarded. Because every connection acknowledges a different tick, every connection gets a different encoding of the same world.

encode.short: Change mask, then a residual against a prediction, then an entropy coder.
encode.deep: Up to three baselines are found per entity and used to extrapolate what the value probably is now. Only the difference from that extrapolation is written. Fields are quantised to integers first, so a float that jitters in its last decimal place compares equal and costs zero bits. Constant motion is therefore nearly free on the wire.

packet.short: One unreliable packet per connection per network tick, with a hard ceiling.
packet.deep: The budget is the transport payload capacity minus the pipeline header, unless you override it per connection. If not even one ghost fits, the size is doubled and the entire serialisation is thrown away and redone, up to eight times. That retry is expensive and it warns, and it usually means a configured packet size that is too small rather than a ghost that is too large.

cut.short: The chunks below the line. Not lost, not queued, just not this tick.
cut.deep: Their age term keeps climbing, so their priority climbs, so they rise in the next sort. This is what makes the system degrade gracefully instead of falling over: a crowded world does not fail, it just refreshes distant things less often. The visible symptom of a badly tuned priority is something important updating at the rate of scenery.

recv.short: Decode against our copy of the baseline, then write into a ring slot.
recv.deep: The client keeps the same thirty two slot history the server assumes it has, which is why the two stay in step. Nothing is applied to an entity here. This stage only fills a slot and stamps it with its tick. It also builds the acknowledgement that rides back on the command stream and tells the server which baselines it may use next.
recv.gotoLabel: When the ghost arriving is one you already made

apply.short: Reads the ring at whichever tick this ghost's timeline names.
apply.deep: For an interpolated ghost the target is the interpolation tick and the two bracketing slots are blended. For a predicted ghost the target is the tick being predicted, the blend factor is pinned to zero, and the value becomes a rollback point rather than something to display. Same buffer, same arrival path, two completely different meanings.

lessons.title: The Rollback Loop
lessons.blurb: Restore, replay, carry on. The same machine every frame, whether or not anything went wrong.

chapters.title: It is a loop, not an incident
chapters.text: Most explanations of rollback tell it as a story. Something goes wrong, the client notices, drama happens, the client repairs itself. That framing is wrong and it makes the code impossible to reason about. This is a loop that runs every frame at the same cost whether the prediction was perfect or hopeless. Read it as a machine with a program counter and it becomes simple.

chapters.title: The restore is unconditional
chapters.text: First move: the server's fields are copied over the predicted entity. Not compared, copied. There is no branch anywhere that asks whether the prediction was right. If it was right, the copy writes identical bytes and costs exactly the same as if it were wrong. That is a genuinely surprising piece of engineering, and once you see it, half the confusion about when rollback happens evaporates. It always happens.

chapters.title: One loop head for the whole set
chapters.text: Second move: work out which tick to start from. Every predicted entity carries the tick it should start predicting from, and the loop takes the oldest one across the entire predicted set. One entity that has not heard from the server in a while drags the whole loop back with it, because there is one loop, not one per entity. Then on every iteration this same loop head chooses the next tick and enables the simulate bit on exactly the entities that should run for it.

chapters.title: One tick, your systems, again
chapters.text: Third move: run one tick of your own gameplay systems. The same code the server ran, with the input that was recorded for that exact tick pulled back out of the command ring. Then the loop head increments and does it again. This is where anything that is not idempotent per tick betrays you. Integrating a transform is fine. Playing a sound is not, because you are about to play it eight more times.

chapters.title: When nothing arrives
chapters.text: Most frames no snapshot arrives at all, because you render far more often than the server sends. In that case there is nothing authoritative to restore from, so the loop restores from its own backup of the last full tick it simulated and carries on. The machine does not stall waiting for the network. It runs on its own history and accepts the correction whenever it eventually shows up.

chapters.title: The cost, and the one honest lever
chapters.text: Cost is replayed ticks, times predicted entities, times whatever your predicted systems do. The first term is round trip time and you do not control it. The third you can optimise but only so far. The second is the one you actually chose, and it is the one that quietly grows, because prediction spreads to everything a predicted thing touches. Keeping the predicted set small is not a micro optimisation. It is the design.

snap.short: The server's state for a tick that already happened.
snap.deep: It is delta compressed against whatever this connection last acknowledged, sent unreliably, and by the time it lands the client has already simulated well past it. Nothing is retransmitted, because a retransmit would arrive too late to be worth anything. The next snapshot simply re-bases.
snap.gotoLabel: Which domain is this ghost in?

nosnap.short: The usual case: no new server data this frame at all.
nosnap.deep: At sixty frames a second against a twenty hertz send rate, two frames out of three have nothing new to apply. The loop still runs. It restores from the client's own backup of its last fully simulated tick and keeps going, which is why prediction feels continuous rather than stepping every time a packet lands.

restore.short: Server fields written over the predicted state, every time, no comparison.
restore.deep: Only fields that are actually part of the replicated schema get written. Everything else keeps whatever the last replay left in it, which is a sharp edge: mutate an unreplicated field inside the prediction loop and that mutation is applied once per replayed tick and never undone. It looks correct until the first dropped packet.

start.short: The loop head: picks the next tick and enables the simulate bit.
start.deep: It runs once per iteration, not once per frame. Each time round it advances the tick being predicted, asks every predicted entity whether it should run for that tick, and sets the enable bit accordingly. Think of it as the clock generator plus the enable decoder for the whole predicted set.

step.short: One tick of your own systems, with that tick's recorded input.
step.deep: The same systems the server runs, under one world filter naming both sides, so there is literally one implementation. Anything with an external side effect must be gated on the flag that marks the first time a tick is fully predicted, or it happens once per replay. That flag is the difference between a sound effect and a machine gun.

now.short: The client's present, roughly half a round trip ahead of the server.
now.deep: This is what gets rendered for anything you own, and it is deliberately ahead of the truth so that your input has zero perceived latency. Everything else on screen is behind the truth instead. Nobody, on any machine, is looking at the server's actual present.

backup.short: A memory copy of the predicted state after the last full tick.
backup.deep: It has two jobs. It is the floor the loop restarts from when no snapshot arrives, and it is the reference the smoothing and error reporting compare against. The copy takes the whole component but the restore touches only the replicated part, which preserves any local state you keep alongside it.

lessons.title: The Delay Line
lessons.blurb: An irregular write pointer, a servo-driven read pointer, and the guess it makes when the waypoints run out.

chapters.title: Only the buffer, this time
chapters.text: The decision about which entities are interpolated at all belongs elsewhere. This map assumes that decision is made and opens the box. Inside is a queue with two pointers moving at different rhythms, a depth that is not the depth you configured, a clock that slews rather than steps, and an extrapolation path that most people are told does not exist. If you have ever tuned an elastic buffer between two clock domains, you will recognise every single part of this, including which knob you will reach for first and why it will be the wrong one.

chapters.title: The write side is irregular
chapters.text: Packets land whenever the network delivers them, which is not a rhythm. Each one is decoded and dropped into a slot in a ring, and the slot is stamped with the tick it describes. Thirty two slots per ghost by default, and an index recording which slot is newest. That is the whole write side. It is a circular buffer with a timestamp per entry, and the consumer reads by timestamp rather than by position, which is the design choice that makes everything else possible.

chapters.title: The depth is not what you set
chapters.text: Here is the first surprise. You configure a window of two network ticks. That is a floor, not a value. Alongside it netcode measures the actual gap between arriving snapshots, keeps a mean and an approximate deviation, and computes a competing depth as mean plus one and a quarter deviations. The larger of the two wins, clamped at six network intervals. So a jittery link deepens your buffer on its own, without telling you, and the latency you measured on a clean connection is not the latency your players get.

chapters.title: The read pointer is a servo
chapters.text: The read pointer does not jump to where it should be. It corrects a tenth of the remaining error per frame, with its rate clamped between eighty five hundredths and one and a tenth of normal speed. Only an error above ten ticks makes it give up and snap outright. So the read pointer is a phase locked loop with a bounded slew rate and a fallback to a hard resync. Every visible smoothness property of interpolated motion comes from those three numbers, and all three are on the same settings struct.

chapters.title: Finding the two waypoints
chapters.text: To produce a value, the lookup walks the ring from newest backwards. Anything newer than the target becomes the after waypoint, overwritten each time it finds something closer. The first slot at or older than the target becomes the before waypoint. Then the factor is the distance from before to target divided by the distance from before to after, plus the fractional part of the tick if we are mid tick. Two known good points and a position between them. Late, but never invented.

chapters.title: Except when it is invented
chapters.text: And here is where the usual teaching is wrong, including this book's own interpolation chapter. If there is no slot newer than the target, and the ghost is dynamic rather than static, the lookup does not hold the last value. It takes the before waypoint and the one behind it, runs that pair forward, and inverts the factor. That is extrapolation, and it is on by default. It is clamped at twenty simulation ticks, after which it holds. A static ghost never takes that path, and a ghost with exactly one slot has its factor pinned to zero and does not move at all.

chapters.title: What each failure looks like
chapters.text: Now you can read the symptoms directly off the mechanism. Visible teleporting means the read pointer outran the write pointer and extrapolation ran past its clamp. Smooth but noticeably late means the measured depth won over your configured one, which means the link is worse than you think. A brief freeze followed by a jump means a ghost fell out of the relevant set and came back with a gap in its ring. And motion that is smooth on a clean link and jerky under loss usually means the depth is oscillating, which is the correction fraction being too aggressive.

arrive.short: A packet lands. Irregular by nature, and that irregularity is the whole problem.
arrive.deep: The gap between arrivals is measured every time, in both wall clock milliseconds and in simulation ticks. Those two measurements feed different things: the tick delta feeds the depth calculation, the wall clock delta feeds the perceived send rate. Neither is the number the server thinks it is sending at.

ring.short: Thirty two tick-stamped slots per ghost, with an index naming the newest.
ring.deep: It is a circular buffer where the consumer reads by timestamp rather than by position. The default of thirty two is sized for about half a second of round trip at sixty hertz. Two smaller sizes exist behind compile symbols, and shrinking it trades memory against the server's ability to delta compress, because unacknowledged slots stop being usable as baselines.
ring.gotoLabel: Where this buffer actually lives in memory

jitter.short: The measured gap between arrivals: a mean and an approximate deviation.
jitter.deep: Both are exponential moving averages, and the deviation reacts faster than the mean deliberately, so that a burst of loss widens the buffer quickly and a return to normal narrows it slowly. The deviation is multiplied by a jitter scale of one and a quarter before it is used, which is a safety margin you can tune.

delay.short: The larger of your configured window and the jitter derived estimate.
delay.deep: Your setting is a floor expressed in network ticks, converted into simulation ticks by the ratio between the two rates. The competing estimate is the measured arrival gap plus jitter, clamped at six network intervals. Whichever is larger wins, and it moves toward its target no faster than a tenth of the frame's ticks, so the depth itself is rate limited.
delay.gotoLabel: How this depth positions the whole timeline

read.short: The interpolation tick: the arrival estimate minus the depth, slewed not stepped.
read.deep: It corrects a tenth of its remaining error per frame with its rate clamped between eighty five hundredths and one and a tenth. Only an error above ten ticks causes an outright snap. That is a phase locked loop with a bounded slew and a hard resync fallback, and those three numbers are the entire smoothness budget.
read.gotoLabel: This pointer as one of four timelines

bracket.short: The two slots straddling the read pointer, and a factor between zero and one.
bracket.deep: The lookup walks the ring from newest backwards, keeping the closest slot newer than the target and taking the first slot at or older than it. The factor is how far the target sits between them, plus the fractional part of the tick. With only one usable slot the factor is pinned to zero, which is why a ghost that has just appeared sits still for a moment.
bracket.gotoLabel: Why this entity is on this timeline at all

extrap.short: No slot newer than the target, so the last known pair is run forward.
extrap.deep: It takes the before waypoint and the one behind it, extends that segment past the target, and inverts the interpolation factor. The clamp is twenty simulation ticks by default, after which it holds. Static ghosts never take this path. This is the part most explanations of interpolation leave out, including the interpolation chapter in this book.
extrap.gotoLabel: Reading this failing, in the counters

lessons.title: The Other Channel
lessons.blurb: A remote call is an entity that becomes bits on the reliable pipeline, and an entity again on the far side.

chapters.title: There is no call
chapters.text: The name is a lie, and getting past it is most of the work. Nothing here calls anything. You create an entity. That entity carries your data component and a marker saying it wants to be sent. A generated system finds it, serialises it, and destroys it. On the other machine an entity appears carrying your data component and a marker saying where it came from. Two entities, one on each side, that never meet. If you try to think of this as a function invocation you will keep looking for a return value that does not exist.

chapters.title: Raising one is a spawn
chapters.text: Sending is a structural change. You add your component and a send request to a fresh entity. The send request holds one field that matters: which connection to send it to, or nothing at all, which means broadcast. That is why sending a hundred of them in one frame is a hundred entity creations, and why doing it in a hot loop shows up in the profiler as a structural change storm rather than as network cost. The wire is not usually your problem here. The entity manager is.

chapters.title: Into a byte buffer, not a socket
chapters.text: A source generator has already written a system for each of your command types. It queries for entities holding that type plus a send request, writes an index, a bit length and your serialised payload into a byte buffer hanging off the connection entity, and destroys the request entity. Nothing has been sent yet. The buffer is drained at the end of the frame. This matters because the order things are sent in is the order they were serialised, which is not necessarily the order in which you created the entities.

chapters.title: Many messages, one packet
chapters.text: When the buffer is drained, the sender opens a packet on the reliable pipeline, writes a five byte header, and then fills the rest with as many whole messages as will fit. Never a partial one. If a single message will not fit in one packet at all, that is a hard error and it throws, because there is no fragmentation on this path. So a large remote call is not slow, it is impossible, and the failure is loud rather than silent. That is the right choice, and it is the opposite of how the snapshot path handles the same problem.

chapters.title: Two pipelines on one socket
chapters.text: Now the contrast that gives this map its name. Both channels are the same connection and the same socket. They differ only in which pipeline stages the transport composed. The reliable one acknowledges, retransmits, and delivers in order. The unreliable one carries snapshots and commands, keeps the newest, and never makes up a loss. Snapshots are unreliable on purpose: a lost one is not worth resending, because a newer one with better truth is already twenty milliseconds behind it. Retransmission would deliver stale data late.

chapters.title: The guarantee, stated exactly
chapters.text: Here is a sentence worth memorising, because it is where people get burned. Remote calls arrive in the order they were sent, relative to each other. Nothing whatsoever is guaranteed about a remote call relative to a snapshot. Send one announcing a state change and then send the snapshot carrying that change and you must assume either order. That is why go in game is a remote call and the ghost stream is not, and why a remote call announcing something the snapshot also carries is a race you will lose intermittently.

chapters.title: It becomes an entity again
chapters.text: On the receiving side, the system reads an index, looks up a function pointer, and invokes it. The default generated implementation creates an entity carrying your component and a receive request naming the connection it came from. That connection is your only sender identity, and it is the right one, because it cannot be forged by the payload. Then it checks that the number of bits read matches the number declared. If they disagree the connection is disconnected on the spot, because a desynchronised bit stream cannot be recovered from.

app.short: You create an entity. That is the entire send side of the API.
app.deep: Your data component plus a send request on one entity. The request names a target connection, or leaves it null to broadcast. There is no call, no handle, no completion. It is a structural change, so a burst of them costs entity manager work long before it costs bandwidth.
app.gotoLabel: The one this project actually sends

gen.short: A generated system per command type, serialising into a per-connection buffer.
gen.deep: The source generator emits a serializer and a request system for each type you declare. It writes an index, a payload bit length and the packed payload into an outgoing byte buffer on the connection entity, then destroys the request entity. Nothing has touched the network yet; the buffer is drained at the end of the frame.
gen.gotoLabel: The generator that wrote this system

rel.short: Acknowledged, retransmitted, delivered in the order it was serialised.
rel.deep: The packet carries a five byte common header and then whole messages until it is full. Nothing is ever split. If a single message cannot fit, that throws, because there is no fragmentation here. When the reliable window is full the send simply does not happen and is retried on a later tick, which is expected rather than exceptional.
rel.gotoLabel: The pipeline stack this sits on

unrel.short: The same socket, different stages: snapshots and commands, newest wins.
unrel.deep: Losses are never made up, and that is deliberate. A retransmitted snapshot would arrive after a newer one carrying better truth, so resending it would deliver stale data late. Commands solve the same problem differently, by putting redundancy in the payload rather than in the protocol.

rpc.short: Reads an index, invokes a function pointer, and checks the bits afterwards.
rpc.deep: There is no reflection and no dispatch table lookup by name. The index selects a Burst function pointer registered at startup. After invoking it, the system compares bits read against bits declared; a mismatch disconnects the sender immediately, because a desynchronised bit stream cannot be recovered. An unknown index disconnects too.
rpc.gotoLabel: Why this is a trust boundary

dest.short: An entity appears carrying your component and the connection it came from.
dest.deep: That connection entity is your only sender identity, and it is the trustworthy one, because it is attached by the receiver and cannot be forged in the payload. Consume it and destroy the entity when you have handled it. If you never do, it just sits there, and an age warning is the only thing that will tell you.
dest.gotoLabel: The state graph that consumes ours

lessons.title: Grove Is a Bytecode VM
lessons.blurb: A graph you drew, compiled into an instruction image, and decoded by a switch that a compiler wrote for you.

chapters.title: Not a visual scripting tool
chapters.text: Call it visual scripting and you will misjudge it completely. What is actually here is a small virtual machine. There is an ahead of time linker, a flat instruction image, and an interpreter built from a switch statement that a source generator emits at compile time. If you have ever written a bootloader, or a microcode table, you have already built one of these. The only unusual part is that the assembler has a mouse.

chapters.title: One node, four different shapes
chapters.text: The single most common confusion is that a node is one thing. It is four. In the editor it is a box you can drag, and that is the source code. After the importer runs it is a small settings object, and that is the object file. After baking it is a run of bytes inside a blob, and that is the image. And at runtime it is a static method, which is the instruction set. Four artefacts, four assemblies, one idea. Every mystery about grove dissolves once you can say which of the four you are looking at.

chapters.title: The image, and why it holds no pointers
chapters.text: The whole graph flattens into one blob asset. Every internal reference is a relative offset rather than an address, which means the image can be copied anywhere and still work. That is position independent code, arrived at for exactly the same reason it was invented for: nobody knows where it is going to be loaded. It also means the image can be shared, read only, by every entity running that graph, and that has a consequence we will chase in the next map.

chapters.title: Opcode assignment, from both directions
chapters.text: Here is the part I find genuinely delightful. The authoring object exposes a node type number, and that number gets written into the header when the image is built. Separately, an attribute on a static method claims the same number for that method. Two entirely different assemblies agreeing on an integer. That is exactly what an instruction set architecture is, and each package takes its own range, counting downward from a negative offset, so that grove, canopy and nerve can extend the same machine without ever colliding.

chapters.title: The decode step has to be code
chapters.text: A blob cannot hold a function pointer, because a function pointer is an address and the whole point of the image is that it contains no addresses. So the instruction can only store a number, and the decoding has to live in real compiled code. That is what the generator emits: a switch on that integer, with one case per claimed opcode. It emits a separate copy for each context type, so everything is specialised and nothing is generic at runtime. Burst turns a dense integer switch into a jump table and will happily inline straight through it. No virtual call anywhere.

chapters.title: What the instruction can see
chapters.text: The methods are static and hold no fields, which sounds crippling until you see the context. Every node receives a context struct by reference, and the fields on it are yours: the buffers for this chunk, the component lookups, a command buffer to write into. A partial declaration and the generator fills in the plumbing by reading your field types. So a node is a pure function of its own data and that context, and the context is the only window it has onto the world. Register file on one side, memory mapped input and output on the other.

graph.short: The graph asset you actually edit, stored as text on disk.
graph.deep: It carries node positions, wires and authored values, and nothing else in the pipeline ever reads it again after import. The file extension is what decides which graph type it is, and therefore which nodes the editor will even offer you. That is the first place a graph can quietly be wrong.

auth.short: One small settings object per node, each carrying its own opcode.
auth.deep: The importer walks the graph and creates one of these for every node, as sub assets of the file. Each one knows its node type number and knows how to write itself into a blob builder. This is the object file stage, and it is the last point at which anything is still editable.

blob.short: One blob for the whole graph, addressed by offsets rather than pointers.
