blob.deep: It holds a root pointer, a table of every node keyed by node id, and the declared inputs and outputs of the graph. Because it contains no absolute addresses it can be memory mapped, shared read only, and handed to thousands of entities at once. Nothing per entity can possibly live here.
blob.gotoLabel: Why an image with no pointers in it

header.short: The instruction: a type number, an authored node id, and the payload right behind it.
header.deep: Every execution node in the image starts with this header, and its own data struct sits immediately after it in memory. Reading a node's data is pointer arithmetic on a known offset, not a lookup. The node id is kept so that state, debugging and history can all key off the authored identity rather than a position.

attr.short: An attribute on a static method, claiming one opcode for that method.
attr.deep: It takes the number, and optionally the input type for nodes that receive a value. The generator finds these purely by attribute name, collects every claim across every assembly it can see, and builds the dispatch from that set. Nothing registers at runtime and nothing is discovered by reflection while the game is running.

ctx.short: The struct that carries everything a node is allowed to touch.
ctx.deep: You declare the fields; the generator writes the code that creates them, refreshes them each update, and re-points them at each chunk. Because the executor copies the context by value when it builds an execution, anything you assign after that copy is what the run actually sees. That ordering detail is subtle and it has bitten people.
ctx.gotoLabel: Where a node keeps what it remembers

swi.short: The dispatch switch, written by a generator, once per context type.
swi.deep: It switches on the header's integer and calls the matching static method. Generating one copy per context means every call is fully specialised, with no generic dispatch left at runtime. This is the reason grove is cheap enough to run per entity, per tick, inside a job.
swi.gotoLabel: Another generator, reading another set of attributes

exec.short: The static method that is the node's actual behaviour.
exec.deep: It takes its own data by reference, the entity context, and your context, and it holds no state of its own between calls. That is not a stylistic choice. There is exactly one copy of the method and one copy of the node data in the image, shared by every entity, so a field on it would be a field shared by everybody.
exec.gotoLabel: Four of these instructions, wired into a real machine

lessons.title: Grove State Is the RAM
lessons.blurb: The image is read only and shared, so everything a node remembers lives in a hash map inside a buffer on the entity.

chapters.title: A constraint, and its consequence
chapters.text: Start from a single fact and the rest of this map is forced. The graph image is one blob, shared read only by every entity running that graph. There is exactly one copy of a node's data. So if a node wants to remember something about this entity, there is nowhere in the image it could possibly put it. Read only program store on one side, writable per instance memory on the other. That is a Harvard architecture, and grove state is the memory half.

chapters.title: The memory is a buffer on the entity
chapters.text: It is a dynamic buffer, which means it is entity data like any other. It travels in the chunk, it gets copied when the entity is instantiated, it saves and loads, and it is deleted when the entity is. Nothing had to be written to make any of that work. Choosing entity storage instead of a side table is the whole reason this design has no lifetime problems.

chapters.title: Untyped, and what that really means
chapters.text: The buffer is declared as an untyped hash map, and that word is doing real work. Inside one buffer there is a header, a bucket array, a key array, a per entry size array, and a data region. Values are bump allocated into that data region and the size of each one is stored beside it as a small integer. So a boolean can sit next to a connection snapshot next to a node identifier, in the same map, and everything is still one allocation. It is a tiny arena allocator living inside a component.

chapters.title: Why the key is four words wide
chapters.text: The key starts with the graph identifier, then an owner scope, then the local key itself. Graph first, because one entity can be running more than one graph and their memory must not alias. Scope next, because the same node can appear in several places and each copy deserves its own memory. And because the graph identifier leads, tearing one graph down is a scan for entries whose first word matches, and a remove. Deallocation by prefix.

chapters.title: The state machine is just another tenant
chapters.text: This is the part that surprised me. The hierarchical state machine on top of grove does not get its own storage. It keeps its active leaf, its per parent history, and its transition version in the same map, under keys taken from the very top of the number space and counting down. Which means the executor's entire query is: entities that have this buffer. There is no state machine component to look for. The machine is a handful of entries in the memory of the machine it runs on.

blob.short: The graph image: structure, constants and wiring, identical for everyone.
blob.deep: It is a blob, so it is relocatable bytes with no addresses inside. That is exactly what makes it shareable, and exactly what makes it useless as storage. Anything in here is the same for the ten thousandth entity as it was for the first.
blob.gotoLabel: How that image gets built in the first place

node.short: A node's method: static, and holding nothing at all between calls.
node.deep: Because there is one copy of the method and one copy of its data, a field on either would be a field shared by every entity in the world. So nodes read and write the map instead. Once you see that, the slightly ceremonial look of node code stops being ceremony and starts being the only option.

ctx.short: The context's handle on the buffers for the chunk being processed.
ctx.deep: It is refreshed once per chunk rather than once per entity, and then indexed by the entity's slot inside that chunk. So getting at an entity's memory is an array index, not a lookup. This is the same trick every other system in this codebase uses, applied to a container that happens to be a hash map.

key.short: Graph, then owner scope, then the local key. Built fresh on every access.
key.deep: It is never stored, only computed, which is why it can be four words wide without costing anything in the buffer. The ordering matters more than the width: graph first means an entire graph's memory can be found and removed by matching one field.

buffer.short: A dynamic buffer on the entity, which is where all of it actually lives.
buffer.deep: Entity data, so it moves with the entity through chunks, survives instantiate, and serialises for free. Its declared element is a single byte, because the element type is a formality: the real layout is a hash map header and everything that follows it.

map.short: Buckets, keys and a next array, all addressed as offsets from the header.
map.deep: Because every internal reference is an offset rather than a pointer, the whole structure survives being moved when the buffer grows or when the entity changes chunk. It is the same discipline the blob uses, applied to writable memory instead of read only memory.
map.gotoLabel: The container library this comes from

arena.short: Values are bump allocated into a data region, with each size stored beside it.
arena.deep: That is what lets one map hold values of different types and different sizes. The price is that nothing checks your type on the way back out: read an entry as the wrong struct and you get bytes, not an exception. In practice a node always uses its own key with its own type, so the risk is theoretical until someone gets clever.

canopy.short: The state machine's cursor and history, kept as ordinary entries in the same map.
canopy.deep: The active leaf, one history entry per remembering parent, and a transition version counter. Their keys are carved out of the top of the number space, counting downward, so they cannot collide with anything a node would ever choose. The machine has no storage of its own at all.
canopy.gotoLabel: What that one number is actually doing

lessons.title: The Active Path
lessons.blurb: One stored number, a path rebuilt from it every tick, and a jump by name that only touches the part that changed.

chapters.title: Not one active state. A path.
chapters.text: The first thing to unlearn is that a hierarchical state machine has an active state. It has an active path, running from the root down to a leaf, and every state on that path is active at once. Blocks attached to the root run in every child state, every tick. That single sentence explains why a connection watcher belongs on the root and stops working the moment somebody moves it onto a child, and it explains why the bug only ever appears after a successful connection.

chapters.title: One number, and the rest is recomputed
chapters.text: Here is what genuinely surprised me. The machine stores the leaf, and only the leaf. A single number in graph state. Every tick it takes that number, walks up the parent pointers in the image, and reverses the list. That is the path. Nothing else is persisted, so there is no path to get out of sync, no invariant to maintain, and no repair code. A cursor, and a chain you can always chase back to the root.

chapters.title: A named jump, and the common ancestor
chapters.text: There are no transition edges in the graph at all. A node simply names a state. The machine resolves the name, builds the path that name implies, and then walks both paths together until they diverge. Everything above that divergence is shared, so it is never exited and never re-entered. Which means a jump between two siblings deep in the tree leaves every parent untouched, and a jump to your own current state is a no operation for free. The arithmetic is the mechanism.

chapters.title: Up, then down
chapters.text: Everything below the divergence exits, deepest first. Then everything on the new branch enters, shallowest first. On the way up, any parent that remembers history records the child it just lost, which is what makes a pause menu return you where you were. On the way down, the stored leaf number advances state by state, so if something throws halfway the machine is left pointing at somewhere real rather than at nothing.

chapters.title: The version counter
chapters.text: A block can jump while the machine is in the middle of walking. So every transition bumps a version number, and the enter and update loops recheck it after each state and abandon the walk if it moved. A jump fired from inside enter therefore wins, and the older walk stops quietly rather than fighting it. A jump fired from inside exit is a different matter: that one throws, because unwinding while unwinding has no sensible answer.

chapters.title: The check that runs at author time
chapters.text: The validator refuses more than one parentless state, a composite with no default child or with two, and a cycle in the parent chain. And then the good one. State names are hashed down to a single thirty-two bit integer, and two different names can land on the same integer. So the validator brute forces the comparison at author time and refuses the graph. That is a content addressable memory with collision checking done at programming time, for the same reason you do it there: because the lookup has to be fast and correct, and a one in four billion failure found in production is not a bug you can debug.

leaf.short: One number, held in graph state. That is the entire persisted machine.
leaf.deep: It identifies the deepest active state. Nothing above it is stored, because everything above it can be recovered by following parent pointers. A machine whose whole persisted form is one integer is also a machine you can inspect from a debugger in one read.
leaf.gotoLabel: The map that number lives in

path.short: Root down to leaf, rebuilt from that number on every single tick.
path.deep: The rebuild walks up the parent chain into a small pooled list and then reverses it, so the root runs first and the leaf runs last. Every state on the path gets its blocks executed, which is the definition of a state being active. It is cheap enough to redo every tick because the depth of a real graph is three or four.

goto.short: A node names a state. There are no transition edges anywhere in the graph.
goto.deep: This is a deliberate trade. Edges in a visual graph become unreadable spaghetti at about fifteen nodes, so canopy makes the jump a named one and is honest that it is a goto. The target name is hashed to an integer at author time and resolved back to a node by scanning the graph at runtime, which is why the uniqueness check matters so much.

split.short: Walk the old path and the new one together until they differ.
split.deep: Everything before the divergence is common to both, so those states stay active and never see an exit or an enter. This is what makes deep jumps cheap and what makes a jump to the state you are already in cost nothing. The comparison is a simple loop over two small lists.

exit.short: Everything below the split exits, deepest first, and history is written here.
exit.deep: Each state's blocks are called with the exit signal, and every block is expected to check for it and bail out of its normal work. Forget that check and your block runs while its own state is being torn down, usually just after the data it depends on has gone. Jumping again from inside exit throws, deliberately.

enter.short: Then down the new branch, shallowest first, with the stored leaf moving along.
enter.deep: A composite that has been entered chooses its next child either from history, if it remembers, or from its single default child. That is the ordinary shallow history of a classic state chart, and it costs one extra entry in graph state per remembering parent.
enter.gotoLabel: One of these machines, doing a real job

reject.short: Two roots, a missing default child, a cycle, or two names that hash alike.
reject.deep: The last one is the interesting one. State names collapse to a single integer, so two different names can collide, and the validator checks every pair at author time rather than shipping a one in four billion mystery. It is the same instinct as validating a perfect hash offline: if the lookup must be constant time and correct, prove the key set is clean before you build it.

lessons.title: How a Session Gets Built
lessons.blurb: Worlds created by a state graph, scenes routed by a bit mask, and a player that is two entities rather than one.

chapters.title: The bootstrap barely does anything
chapters.text: You would expect the bootstrap to build the worlds. It does not. It creates one service world and stops. Every other world is created by a node inside a state graph, and destroyed when that state exits. So world lifetime equals state lifetime, which is a strong and unusual claim: leaving the game state is what tears the game world down, and there is no separate shutdown path to forget to call.

chapters.title: Which scene ends up in which world
chapters.text: A settings asset holds a list of scene sets. Each set carries a mask naming the kinds of world it belongs to: game, service, menu, client, server, thin client. At bake time that mask is converted into world flags and stamped onto a controller entity, one per set. At runtime the loader is doing exactly one interesting thing. It takes the mask off the entity, ands it with the flags of the world it happens to be running in, and skips the entity if the result is zero. That is the whole routing system. A bitwise and.

chapters.title: Where our own client settings ride
chapters.text: Our project puts a world attribute on a settings class naming the client world. The editor reads that attribute and writes the asset onto the settings prefab registered for the client. That prefab lives in the client scene. The client scene is in a set whose mask includes client. So the baked state machine entity appears in the client world, and the system that drives it filters on client simulation. Five hops, none of them a runtime lookup, and if you ever wonder where a missing entity went, you walk that chain backwards.

chapters.title: The gate that is switched off
chapters.text: Connection approval is controlled by one flag, and it defaults to off. With it off, both approval systems disable themselves on create. Nothing ever grants the approved marker, and nothing ever attaches an account identity. And the spawner only acts on connections that carry both. So on a fresh project, every connection succeeds, every handshake completes, and no player ever appears. No error, no warning. That failure mode is worth memorising because everything about it looks healthy.

chapters.title: Two entities, and only one of them is you
chapters.text: A player is a controller and a controlled entity. The controller carries the account identity and is the durable half; the controlled entity is the body. When a connection drops, the controller is not destroyed, it is disabled, and it waits. When someone reconnects with the same account, the spawner finds that controller, re-points ownership and the command target at it, and switches it back on. Persistence without a save file, because the identity is a string rather than a network number. It is also why two players in our test show up as four ghosts, and why three would mean two clients had adopted the same controller.

boot.short: Creates exactly one world at startup, and then gets out of the way.
boot.deep: It is the ordinary custom bootstrap hook, and when netcode is present the same class instead extends the netcode bootstrap so the world model swaps cleanly onto Unity's. What it deliberately does not do is create a game world, because deciding when a game exists is a gameplay question, not a startup question.

graph.short: A node in the service graph opens the client world and the server world, and closes them again.
graph.deep: Entering the state calls back into the bootstrap to create; exiting it destroys. Which play type you asked for decides whether you get a client, a server, or both. This is the seam where a hierarchical state machine ends up owning process level lifetime, and it is the reason there is no separate teardown to forget.
graph.gotoLabel: Which world am I actually in?

sets.short: Scene sets, each carrying a mask of the world kinds it belongs to.
sets.deep: One baked controller entity is created per set, and only for sets whose mask could ever match, so a set that is irrelevant to a world does not even produce an entity there. The flag with the required marker also forces the wait for load behaviour on, regardless of what you asked for.

loader.short: Ands the set's mask against this world's flags, and skips it if nothing matches.
loader.deep: That single test is the entire routing mechanism. There is no registry, no lookup, no per state switching. If a set is marked to wait for load, the loader pauses the whole world until streaming finishes, which is how you get a deterministic first frame instead of a race.

approve.short: A token, sent before a network identifier has been granted at all.
approve.deep: Netcode reserves a special class of remote call that is allowed to travel before approval, and this rides it. The server validates the token asynchronously, and on success attaches the approved marker plus an account identity. Every rejection path ends the same way: a request to disconnect with an approval failure reason, which is classified as not worth retrying.

spawn.short: Turns an approved connection into a controller, or finds the one it left behind.
spawn.deep: Three passes each tick: mark controllers inactive for connections that dropped, reattach an approved connection to an existing controller with the same account, or instantiate a fresh controller and body. It also guards against two connections claiming the same account in the same frame, and kicks the duplicate.

ctrl.short: The durable half of a player: the account, kept across a disconnect.
ctrl.deep: It is disabled rather than destroyed when the connection goes, along with everything linked to it, and re-enabled when the same account returns. Ownership is re-pointed while everything is still disabled, and the enabling happens last, after every other system has had its chance to repair state.

pawn.short: The body: the entity that this player's input is actually pointed at.
pawn.deep: It carries only a back pointer to its controller. The connection's command target is what routes input to it, and the ghost owner field is what tells every client which one of these is theirs. Two entities per player is what lets identity outlive a respawn without any special casing.
pawn.gotoLabel: Why ownership decides which clock you run on

lessons.title: UI Without a Round Trip
lessons.blurb: There is no per-frame sync pass. One comparison inside a generated setter decides whether the managed world hears about the write at all.

chapters.title: The thing that is not here
chapters.text: I went looking for the system that scans the bindings every frame and pushes changes into the interface. It does not exist. There is no diff pass, no flush queue, no dirty list. Which means the answer to how the interface stays cheap is not a clever batching scheme. It is that the expensive path is never taken unless a value actually changed, and the test for that lives at the write itself.

chapters.title: What a system actually writes
chapters.text: A system holds a raw pointer to a plain unmanaged struct and assigns a field on it. That is the whole author facing surface. No component, no singleton, no callback registration. It has to happen on the main thread, and writing from a scheduled job is explicitly unsupported, because the change path can end in a managed dictionary lookup and that is not something a worker thread may do.

chapters.title: The comparison is the mechanism
chapters.text: The property you assign is generated, and its setter is hard wired to a helper that compares the old value with the new one and returns immediately if they match. So an idle screen with fifty bound fields, written every frame, costs fifty comparisons and nothing else. No allocation, no delegate, no boundary crossing. And because the setter is generated, there is no way to write the field and skip the check, which is exactly the property you want from a mechanism like this.

chapters.title: One call out of the fast side
chapters.text: When the values genuinely differ, the write has to reach managed code, and that is a real problem: compiled fast code cannot call a normal delegate. The solution is a function pointer trampoline, installed once at code load, that packs any argument struct into a pointer and a length. So one callback signature serves every kind of notification. On the other side the arguments are unpacked, the change is applied, and the ordinary property changed events are raised synchronously, right there at the write.

chapters.title: The address is the identity
chapters.text: How does the fast side say which object it means, when it cannot hold a managed reference? By pointer. The view model keeps its unmanaged data on a small box, that box is pinned so the garbage collector cannot move it, and the resulting address is registered as a key in a dictionary that maps back to the managed object. So the identity crossing the boundary is a raw address. Pinning is not an optimisation here, it is the correctness requirement: move the object and the key stops meaning anything.

chapters.title: And then it is just an interface
chapters.text: From the view model onward there is nothing special left. It raises the standard change notification, the standard binding machinery hears it, and the element redraws. The element knows nothing about entities, worlds, or jobs. That separation is the actual product: everything upstream of the view model is data oriented, everything downstream is ordinary user interface code, and the seam between them is one comparison and one function pointer.

sys.short: A system assigns a field on an unmanaged struct it holds a pointer to.
sys.deep: The helper resolves the view model from a service container, pins it, and caches the address. It can also build a query so the system only updates while the relevant screen is the active destination, which is how a view model stops costing anything the moment its screen is gone.
sys.gotoLabel: Where a system sits in the whole stack

attr.short: One attribute on a private field. That is the entire declaration.
attr.deep: It has to sit inside a partial struct, and the generator reports a compile error if it does not. The generator also recognises a few field shapes and gives them different surfaces: a plain value, a value with a consumed once flag, and a list that gets a container wrapper so a system can hand it an array, a buffer or a set.

set.short: The generated property. Its setter is the only way the value can change.
set.deep: The getter is the raw field; the setter is wired straight to the compare and notify helper. Because you never write the setter, you can never accidentally write the field and skip the notification, and there is no stored dirty bit anywhere for the two halves to disagree about.

gate.short: Compare old against new, and return doing nothing if they match.
gate.deep: This is the change detection, in full. It is not a system, not a pass, and not a schedule. The cost of a value that did not change is one equality test on a struct, which the compiler will usually reduce to a couple of instructions. The cost of a value that did change is everything to the right of this node.

ptr.short: The unmanaged data is pinned, and its address is the key back to the object.
ptr.deep: The struct sits on a tiny managed box purely so it can be pinned, because you cannot pin a field of an arbitrary object graph. The pinned address then keys a dictionary of view models. Unpinning on teardown is done in nested try and finally blocks, so a throw mid teardown still releases the handle.

tramp.short: A function pointer out of compiled fast code, installed once at code load.
tramp.deep: Fast compiled code cannot call a delegate, so the bridge packs any argument struct into a pointer and a length and calls one fixed callback signature. Three of these cover the whole surface: set a value, set a list, and notify without writing. The navigation half of the package uses the identical trick for commands.

vm.short: The managed view model, found by looking its address up in a table.
vm.deep: It raises change notification before and after the copy, so anything listening sees a proper transition rather than a torn read. Its base class implements the three notification interfaces at once, which is what lets both hand written properties and generated ones funnel through one place.

ui.short: An ordinary element, reading an ordinary property, redrawing.
ui.deep: Nothing here knows about entities. The markup names a data source type and a path, and the binding resolves it at import time, which is the origin of a famous trap: if the assembly holding that type has not been compiled yet, the reference is dropped silently and never retried.
ui.gotoLabel: The trampoline mechanism comes from here

lessons.title: The Floor Everything Stands On
lessons.blurb: Seen from inside a job: where a tuned number comes from, where a map is allowed to live, and how a line of text gets out.

chapters.title: The layer nobody demos
chapters.text: Every package above this one is built on the same handful of primitives, and none of them are exciting to look at. A way to get a tuned number into a job. A way to get a line of text out. Containers you are allowed to use where the ordinary ones are illegal. It is the standard library of this stack, and reading it is the fastest way to understand why the code above it looks the way it does.

chapters.title: Settings are routed before the game runs
chapters.text: This one caught me out. There is no runtime system that reads an attribute and decides which world a settings asset belongs in. The attribute is read in the editor, when the asset is created, and the editor writes that asset into the array on a particular prefab. By the time you press play the decision is already baked into a scene. So if a settings entity is in the wrong world, the bug is not in a system anywhere; it is in which prefab that asset was written onto, months ago.

chapters.title: Why the logging API looks so strange
chapters.text: Every call takes a fixed capacity string, and the capacity is spelled out in the method name. That looks like bad taste until you remember the constraint: compiled fast code cannot build a managed string at all, because building one means allocating. A fixed capacity string is a value type with its bytes inline, so it can be assembled on the stack. The capacity has to be in the name because it is part of the type. And the verbose and debug levels are compiled out entirely rather than filtered at runtime, so an unused log line costs literally nothing in a shipped build.

chapters.title: Config vars, and one ordering trick
chapters.text: A config var is an attribute on a static shared field, which is the one storage class that both managed code and compiled fast code can read. The scan is opt in at the type level, so it is an index rather than a sweep of every assembly. And there is a small detail worth stealing: the manager deliberately initialises the logging level variable first, before all the others, so that if anything goes wrong initialising the rest it has somewhere to report it to.

chapters.title: Two containers worth stealing
chapters.text: The first is a hash map whose entire storage is a dynamic buffer on an entity. Buckets, keys and values all live in that one allocation, addressed by offsets. Which means the map serialises, copies on instantiate, and dies with its entity, all for free. The second is a stream bucketed by worker thread rather than by element index. The engine's own version needs to know how many buckets to make before you schedule; this one asks the job system how many threads there are and stops caring. No count up front, and it works from any job shape at all.

asset.short: An ordinary settings object, marked with a world attribute.
asset.deep: The marker interface is what makes it discoverable by the settings window and the creation path; the world attribute is what makes it land somewhere specific. A separate base class exists for the kind that bakes components onto an entity, which is how a settings asset can push arbitrary data into a world without owning a behaviour of its own.

router.short: The editor reads the attribute and writes the asset onto a prefab.
router.deep: There is a small routing table mapping world names to authoring objects, with a default for anything unmatched. All of this happens at asset creation time. Nothing at runtime ever looks at the attribute again, which is why the failure mode is a missing entity rather than an error message.

entity.short: One baked entity per world, carrying whatever the assets asked for.
entity.deep: The baker tags it and then delegates to each asset in turn, taking a dependency on the asset so that editing it re-bakes the scene. Forget that dependency in your own settings type and you will edit values, see nothing change, and lose an afternoon.

cfg.short: A static shared field with an attribute, readable from compiled fast code.
cfg.deep: Shared statics are the vehicle because they are the only storage both worlds can see. Registration happens on code load, and command line arguments of the matching name override the stored value, which is what makes a headless server tunable without a build.

job.short: Your compiled code: no managed types, no allocator, no exceptions.
job.deep: Everything on this map exists because of that constraint. Each arrow into this node is a way of getting information in past the boundary, and each arrow out is a way of getting something back past it. Once you see the layer that way, the odd looking parts stop looking odd.
job.gotoLabel: A whole virtual machine built on this floor

log.short: Fixed capacity strings only, because that is all that can be built in place.
log.deep: Inside a system you fetch the logger as a singleton, so every line is stamped with which world and which frame produced it. Outside a system there is a global with the same shape. The level is checked before the string is assembled, and the verbose and debug variants are compiled away entirely in a shipped build.

dyn.short: A hash map whose entire storage is one dynamic buffer on an entity.
dyn.deep: Header, buckets, keys and values in one allocation, addressed as offsets so the structure survives being moved. Because it is entity data it serialises, copies on instantiate, participates in change filtering, and dies with its entity. There are set, multi map and perfect hash variants of the same idea.
dyn.gotoLabel: The most interesting user of this container

stream.short: One bucket per worker thread rather than one per element index.
stream.deep: The engine's own stream makes you supply the bucket count when you schedule, which means you need a length before you have one. This one asks the job system how many threads exist and lets each writer pick its own bucket. So it works from any job shape, and its size is bounded by cores rather than by entities.
stream.gotoLabel: The memory model all of this is shaped around

lessons.title: Three Assemblies, One AND Gate
lessons.blurb: Our own three assembly definitions, and the seven-input AND that deletes one without printing anything.

chapters.title: The build system is a circuit
chapters.text: This map is the smallest one in the book and it describes the failure that cost the most hours. Unity compiles one library per assembly definition file, and that file is a linker script with a gate in it. The gate is an AND across every symbol in a list. All inputs high, the assembly compiles. One input low, the assembly does not compile. Not partially. At all. And the gate has no output pin you can probe, because nothing is logged when it evaluates false.

chapters.title: Packages become symbols
chapters.text: First, where the inputs come from. A version define says: if this package is installed, define this symbol. Ours declare seven of them, one per package we care about. The scope is the thing to notice. A version define applies to the assembly that declares it, and nowhere else. Symbols do not inherit through references. That is why the same block of seven entries is copy pasted into every assembly definition in this project and in every one in the BovineLabs stack. It is not laziness. There is no other way to do it.

chapters.title: The seven-input AND
chapters.text: Then the constraint list. Seven symbols in ours: two for the graph packages, one for netcode, three for the Unity services, one for the platform toolkit. Every one of them must be defined or the assembly is skipped. There is no OR. There is no partial compilation. We hit this by stripping the package manifest to a minimum and discovering that an entire BovineLabs assembly containing sessions, ownership and approval had quietly stopped existing. Five of its six required symbols were unsatisfied.

chapters.title: The symptom points at the wrong file
chapters.text: Here is why it costs hours rather than minutes. The assembly that did not compile produces no error. The error you get is a type not found, in your own file, on your own line. Which looks exactly like a missing import. So you check your imports, then the spelling, then the namespace, then you start doubting the package version. The one thing you do not check is whether a completely different assembly, that you did not edit, silently ceased to exist. The probe is one shell command: list the compiled assemblies folder and look for the name.

chapters.title: Why three and not one
chapters.text: The second trap is what forced the three way split. Our runtime assembly once referenced an editor only assembly. In the editor everything compiled and everything worked. In a player build the editor symbol is undefined, that assembly does not exist, and the reference silently drops, taking every type we used with it. So it cannot fail until the day you make your first build, at which point it looks like a catastrophic regression rather than a boundary violation you introduced weeks earlier.

chapters.title: The rule, stated as three boxes
chapters.text: Components, systems and contexts go in the runtime assembly, which builds for all platforms and takes only the package constraints. Settings assets and bakers that touch authoring types go in the authoring assembly, which adds the editor symbol on top. Menu items and graph construction go in the editor assembly, which is restricted to the editor platform outright. References point upward only: editor may reference authoring, authoring may reference runtime, and nothing runtime is ever allowed to reach down. That is the whole contract, and it turns a build day surprise into a compile error.

vdef.short: If this package is installed, define this symbol — for this one assembly only.
vdef.deep: Ours declare seven, one per package the project depends on, each with an empty version expression meaning any version will do. The scope is the trap: symbols do not inherit through assembly references, so every assembly definition must declare its own copy of the block, and forgetting one gives you an inactive conditional block that compiles cleanly.

constraint.short: Seven symbols, all required. It is an AND, not a preference.
constraint.deep: Unity evaluates the list before compiling. All present, the assembly is built. One absent, it is skipped in its entirety and no diagnostic is emitted. There is no OR operator and no partial mode. The negation prefix exists, which makes it possible to write mutually exclusive assemblies, and that is the only escape hatch there is.

missing.short: One symbol short and the assembly is not compiled. Nothing is logged.
missing.deep: No error, no warning, no library file. Every type inside it stops existing. What you see instead is a type not found error in your own source, which sends you hunting through your imports for an hour. The only reliable check is to list the compiled assemblies folder and look for the name.

runtime.short: Components, systems and contexts. All platforms, unsafe code allowed.
runtime.deep: It references the graph packages, netcode, transforms, collections and the input system, and it is the only one of the three that ships in a player build. Because it builds for every platform, anything it references must also build for every platform, which is exactly the constraint that forced the split.
runtime.gotoLabel: The worlds these systems land in

authoring.short: Settings assets and bakers. The same seven symbols plus the editor one.
authoring.deep: It is not restricted by platform list; it is restricted by the editor symbol in its constraints, which amounts to the same thing and is the idiom the sample uses. It references the runtime assembly, never the other way round. Anything here that leaks into runtime code is a build day failure waiting to happen.

editor.short: Menu items and graph construction, restricted to the editor platform outright.
editor.deep: This one uses the platform include list rather than a symbol, and it references both of the others plus every editor side package assembly. It is where the client state graph asset is actually constructed. Nothing in it can ever be reached from a running player, which is the point.

lessons.title: Two Editors, One EEPROM
lessons.blurb: Virtual players are separate processes sharing one preferences store. Roles are the strapping pins that free them.

chapters.title: Not a simulation of a second player
chapters.text: Multiplayer play mode gives you extra editor instances so you can test two clients without building. The temptation is to read them as a lightweight simulation of a second player. They are not. Each one is a genuinely separate editor process, with its own worlds, its own sockets, its own domain, and no shared memory of any kind. Two facts about them do all the damage, and both are about sharing: they share your library folder, and they share your editor preferences.

chapters.title: A folder of symlinks
chapters.text: Look at what is actually on disk. Inside the library folder there is a virtual project directory per player, and inside each one, the assets folder and the project settings folder are symbolic links pointing straight back at your real project. There is no copy, no sync step and no divergence, because there is only ever one file. What the virtual project does keep for itself is small: a private library holding window layout, build profiles and a shader cache. The compiled assemblies are not in there. So an edit appears instantly in every instance, and a reimport stalls all of them at once, for exactly the same reason.

chapters.title: The pref they all read
chapters.text: Now the second shared thing, and it is the one that crashes. The play mode type, which decides whether an instance builds a server world, a client world or both, is stored in editor preferences under a key scoped by the product name. Not by the instance. Not by the player index. By the product name. Every process reading that key gets the same answer, and its default is client and server. So the second editor happily concludes it should build a server world too.

chapters.title: The cascade, and why it misleads
chapters.text: Two server worlds means two attempts to bind the same port. The first succeeds, the second fails, and then the failure cascades. Subscene loaders find two server worlds where they expected one. Entity assertions fire. The console fills with errors that have nothing to do with sockets, and the port bind message is buried three screens up. The cascade is louder than the cause, which is exactly why this one is hard, and it is a good general lesson: the loudest error is rarely the first one.

chapters.title: The obvious fix does not work
chapters.text: The instinct is to open the play mode tools window in the second instance and set it to client. You cannot. An additional editor does not get that window. And the value you would be changing in the main editor is the shared one, which would change it for the host too. So you are being asked to configure two independent boards by editing one shared memory chip, and there is no version of that which works. The problem is not the setting. The problem is that there is only one of it.

chapters.title: Roles are the strapping pins
chapters.text: The fix is to give each instance its own storage. Install the dedicated server package, and netcode's assembly definition defines a symbol for multiplayer roles. That symbol switches the preference getter to ask the roles manager first, and only fall back to the shared key if roles are disabled. Each player now carries its own role, saved in the play mode system data file next to its name and its identifier. Set the main editor to client and server, set the second player to client, and the topology is finally what you drew.

chapters.title: How you know it took
chapters.text: Two confirmations, one visual and one factual. Visually, the play mode type control in the play mode tools window goes grey, because roles have taken over and the old control is disabled. If it is still editable, the symbol is not active and you are still on the shared key. Factually, loop over every world in every instance and count the server worlds. There must be exactly one, across all of them. Then count ghosts: four for two players, because each player is a controller entity plus a capsule entity.

main.short: The one full editor. It owns the scenario and launches everything else.
main.deep: It is also the only instance with the play mode tools window, which is why it looks like the place to fix everything and is not. It is a player in the scenario in its own right, with its own role entry, so it is not privileged at runtime, only in the user interface.
main.gotoLabel: What its client does on connect

vp.short: A directory per player, whose assets and settings are symlinks to yours.
vp.deep: The assets folder and the project settings folder are symbolic links straight back at your project, so there is exactly one copy of every file and no synchronisation step at all. What it keeps privately is only editor instance state: window layout, build profiles, a shader cache. No compiled assemblies, no separate asset database. That is why edits appear instantly and why a reimport stalls every instance at once.

player.short: A real second editor process, with its own worlds, sockets and domain.
player.deep: It shares no memory with the main editor. No static state crosses between them, no singleton is visible from one to the other, and a domain reload hits them independently. It has no play mode tools window, which is why verification here goes through scripting rather than the interface.

prefs.short: One key, scoped by product name, read identically by every instance.
prefs.deep: The key is a prefix built from the product name plus the setting name, so it is per project and not per instance. Its default is client and server. That single default is what makes a second editor try to bind a port that is already taken, and the cascade of loader and entity errors that follows is much louder than the bind failure itself.

roles.short: A per-player role, consulted before the shared key ever gets read.
roles.deep: Installing the dedicated server package defines the roles symbol through a version define on netcode's own assembly. With it, the preference getter asks the roles manager first and returns immediately, so the shared key becomes unreachable. Each player's role lives in the play mode system data file alongside its name and identifier.

boot.short: Reads the requested play type once, and builds worlds accordingly.
boot.deep: It runs independently inside every process. Whatever value it reads is the value that process acts on, and there is no coordination between instances. Additional thin clients are bootstrapped after the main worlds, and only in the editor, which is one more reason the instance count and the world count rarely match.
boot.gotoLabel: The flags it stamps on each world

worlds.short: Server, client, or both. The count across all instances is the real test.
worlds.deep: Exactly one server world across every editor instance means roles are applied. Two means they are not. From there, four ghosts for two players is the healthy reading, because each player owns a controller entity and a capsule entity. Three would be an ownership bug, not a spawn bug.
worlds.gotoLabel: Telling which world you are in

lessons.title: Predicted physics
lessons.blurb: A rigid body solver re-clocked onto the prediction tick, and the two things that correct it.

chapters.title: The same solver, a different clock
chapters.text: Nothing about the physics solver changes when you make it predicted. What changes is the clock feeding it. It used to be driven by a wall clock accumulator that ticked once per frame. It is now driven by the prediction tick, which can issue ten edges in a single frame after a correction arrives. Everything on this map is a consequence of that one substitution.

chapters.title: Physics is moved, not called
chapters.text: At the first world update, a configuration system walks the fixed step group, finds the physics group and every system ordered around it, and moves the whole set into the predicted fixed step group. Then it removes itself from the update list, because the move only needs to happen once. If you wrote a system that orders itself relative to physics inside the fixed step group, it is now in a different group from the thing it was ordering against, and it will silently run at the wrong time.

chapters.title: Two gates, and both must open
chapters.text: A rate manager decides whether the physics group runs at all. By default it demands an entity that is both a predicted ghost and has a physics velocity, unless lag compensation is switched on. Above that sits a second gate: on the client the prediction loop itself only runs when predicted ghosts exist. This pair is the mechanism behind the most common complaint in the forums, where a raycast against static level geometry returns nothing because the collision world was never built.

chapters.title: What a rollback actually puts back
chapters.text: There is nothing physics specific about the restore. When a snapshot arrives, the update system copies the server's fields into the components. When no snapshot arrives, the prediction backup restores the last full tick. Both paths copy back only the fields that are actually replicated. Mass, gravity factor, and collider blobs are not replicated, so they are never restored, and a mutation you make to one inside the prediction loop is applied once per replayed tick and never undone.

chapters.title: The price, stated plainly
chapters.text: Rollback cost is predicted entities multiplied by replayed ticks, and physics multiplies both terms. A solve is broadphase, narrowphase, and a constraint pass over every body in the predicted world, repeated for each replayed tick. Batching replayed ticks is the emergency valve, and it is a real accuracy loss, because a batched step pushes a larger delta through the solver and contacts resolve differently. Shrink the predicted set before you reach for batching.

clock.short: The prediction group, issuing one tick edge per simulated tick.
clock.deep: On the server it advances once per frame. On the client it can advance many times in one frame, replaying every tick since the last correction. Everything downstream inherits that behaviour, including the solver, which is why physics had to be moved into this group in the first place.

gate.short: The rate manager that decides whether physics runs this tick.
gate.deep: It has three modes. The default requires a predicted ghost carrying a physics velocity. A relaxed mode accepts any entity with a velocity or a collider. The third mode always runs. In every mode, when nothing matches and lag compensation is the only reason to run, physics runs only on the first time a tick is fully predicted.

solver.short: The physics group, relocated out of the fixed step group at startup.
solver.deep: Its timestep is one over the simulation tick rate, multiplied by a configurable ratio that defaults to one. It never runs on a partial tick, so a rigid body's transform advances at most once per simulation tick no matter how fast you render. Anything smoother than that has to come from graphical smoothing.

snapshot.short: The authoritative correction, copied out of the received snapshot.
snapshot.deep: It writes only the fields that carry a ghost field attribute. For a physics body that means the transform and the linear and angular velocity, the latter quantized to one thousandth of a unit per second. Correcting position without correcting velocity would leave the client re-diverging immediately from the same wrong momentum.

bodies.short: The predicted rigid bodies, which must all be ghosts.
bodies.deep: A dynamic body that is not a ghost cannot be rolled back, so it would be simulated forward several times per frame and never corrected. A validation system finds them and logs an error naming the offending entities, or moves them to another physics world index if you configured one.

smooth.short: The render pose between two simulation ticks.
smooth.deep: The package restricts the graphical smoothing component to predicted prefab variants, so that interpolated clients do not have physics smoothing fighting the snapshot interpolation that is already positioning the body. Smoothing writes a render pose and must never be read back into simulation, because that is a feedback loop that diverges.

backup.short: A memory copy of the predicted state after the last full tick.
backup.deep: It exists so prediction can continue when no new server data has arrived, and it doubles as the reference for prediction error reporting and for smoothing the correction. The copy is of the whole component, but the restore touches only the replicated portion, which preserves any local state you keep beside it.

lessons.title: Predicted spawning
lessons.blurb: Two independent streams, one matcher, and an entity that is adopted rather than replaced.

chapters.title: The hole in the feedback loop
chapters.text: A player capsule can be predicted because it already exists. A projectile cannot, because at the moment of the trigger pull there is nothing to predict. Wait for the server and the rocket appears one full round trip after the input, exactly where the player is paying the most attention. Predicted spawning closes that hole, and the whole map is the machinery for the handover it needs.

chapters.title: The client creates it immediately
chapters.text: The spawn request rides on the prefab as an enableable component that is baked disabled, so your spawn code is nothing more than an instantiate. A system consumes the request, writes a ghost identifier of zero to mark the entity as client authored, stamps a spawn tick, and serialises the entity's current state into the first snapshot slot. The entity is on screen in the same frame as the input.

chapters.title: Why the match is a window
chapters.text: The two halves stamp their spawn ticks from different clocks. Inside the prediction loop the client stamps the tick it is simulating. Outside it, the client can only stamp the last full server tick it knows about. The server stamps its own tick at the end of its frame. The package's own comment on that branch says the two will normally differ by about one tick, and by more when a rate of fire is involved. That is why classification is a window and not an equality test.

chapters.title: The matcher, and what it compares
chapters.text: One system turns unknown spawns into interpolated or predicted, digging the owner identifier out of the received snapshot bytes for owner predicted ghosts. A second system, ordered last, does the actual matching. It compares two things and only two things: the ghost type, and whether the spawn ticks fall within a window that defaults to plus or minus five. On a hit it records the client entity and removes the pending record.

chapters.title: Adopt, or reap
chapters.text: On a match, the spawn system does something quietly remarkable: it returns the client's existing entity instead of instantiating anything. The entity keeps its transform, its trail, and every local component you added, and simply gains the server's ghost identifier. On a miss, the client copy stays in the pending list until the interpolation tick passes its spawn tick, and is then destroyed. The player sees a brief double image and one of them vanishes.

request.short: An enableable marker baked onto every prefab that supports prediction.
request.deep: It carries no fields at all. It is baked disabled, so ordinary queries do not find it, and it is enabled briefly during initialisation before removal is scheduled for the next frame. That brief enabled window exists to stop the initialisation running twice when the spawn system is invoked again inside the prediction loop.

initsys.short: Initialises the client spawn and stamps the tick everything depends on.
initsys.deep: It sets the ghost identifier to zero, the real ghost type, and a spawn tick. It sizes the snapshot ring, writes the entity's current state into slot zero with the same generated serializers the server uses, and applies the prediction start tick so rollback has a valid origin from the very first tick.

list.short: The pending list of client spawns waiting to be claimed.
list.deep: It is not indexed. Entries are searched by a key pair, the ghost type and the spawn tick, and a hit removes the entry with a swap back. It behaves like a small store buffer holding writes that retire when a matching authoritative write arrives.

queue.short: New ghosts arriving from the server, still unclassified.
queue.deep: The receive system never creates ghosts itself. It appends entries describing a new ghost with its type, its identifier, and the tick the server spawned it, and leaves the decision to the classification group. The field to compare against is the server spawn tick, not the tick the snapshot arrived on.

match.short: Compares ghost type and spawn tick, within a window.
match.deep: The window defaults to plus or minus five ticks. Widen it and misses turn into mismatches. Narrow it and mismatches turn back into misses. The moment two ghosts of one type can spawn within that window, the default matcher is no longer safe and you want your own, keyed on a replicated sequence number.

adopt.short: Returns the client's entity untouched instead of instantiating a new one.
adopt.deep: This is the entire payoff. The adopted entity is the same entity the player has been watching since the trigger pull. It keeps its position, its particle trail, and every purely local component, and from this point forward it receives the server's snapshots like any other ghost.

reaper.short: Destroys client spawns that were never claimed.
reaper.deep: The deadline is the interpolation tick, optionally pushed back by a configurable number of extra ticks that defaults to zero. Raising that number gives late-arriving server ghosts more chances to classify, but it also keeps mispredicted spawns visible for longer, so raise it in single digits.

lessons.title: Lag compensation
lessons.blurb: A tick indexed ring of collision worlds, and the delay measurement that selects a slot.

chapters.title: The player aims at a composite image
chapters.text: Three different nows are on screen at once. Your own body is drawn ahead of the server. Everyone else is drawn behind it. So when a player fires, the crosshair sits over a body that, by the server's clock, is already somewhere else. If the server tests that shot against its own present it will miss shots the player saw land, and the error grows with latency.

chapters.title: The client measures its own delay
chapters.text: The server does not estimate how far behind a client is rendering. The client measures it, as the number of ticks between the server tick and its own interpolation tick, adjusted by the sub tick fractions and floored at zero. That number is written into every command packet, stored per connection on the server, and copied onto the owned ghost when a command for that ghost arrives.

chapters.title: A ring that is really a cache
chapters.text: The history is thirty two collision world slots plus thirty two parallel tick fields. The slot is the tick modulo the size, which is why the size must be zero, one, or a power of two: the index is a mask, not a division, and it has to stay correct when the tick counter wraps. The tick stored beside the slot is the tag. A read hands you back the tag it found, so you can check that the line you got is the line you asked for.

chapters.title: The query that fails silently
chapters.text: The read has four behaviours. A tick newer than anything stored returns the live world. A tick in range returns its clone. A tick older than the ring is clamped to the oldest slot. And an uninitialised history returns the live world. The short overload of that call throws away the expected tick and the returned tick, so a high latency client is served the oldest world you have, forever, with no signal at all. Compare the two ticks and log the mismatch.

chapters.title: Somebody absorbs the latency
chapters.text: The server rewinds the target, not the shooter and not the level. So a player can be told they were hit while their own screen already showed them safely behind cover. That is not a bug in the implementation, it is the choice the design makes. Turn compensation off and the shooter absorbs the latency instead, by leading every moving target by their own ping. The interpolation window and the history size are the two bounds you actually control.

delay.short: Computes the interpolation delay and writes it into every command packet.
delay.deep: It is the tick distance from the server tick to the interpolation tick, nudged by one in either direction depending on the sub tick fractions, and never allowed below zero. It travels as a plain unsigned integer in the command header, so it costs four bytes on a packet the client was sending anyway.

ack.short: Stores the reported delay per connection on the server.
ack.deep: It lives alongside the acknowledgement bookkeeping for that connection, and it is only refreshed when a packet carrying a newer remote timestamp arrives. This is the single per connection value from which every per entity delay is copied.

cdid.short: The delay, copied onto the owned ghost when a command arrives for it.
cdid.deep: This component is not baked by default. You get it by enabling track interpolation delay on the ghost authoring component, and only when the ghost also has an owner. It is refreshed only when a command arrives for that entity, so if the player switches command target, the old entity keeps its last reported delay forever.

physhist.short: Clones the collision world once per fully predicted tick.
physhist.deep: It runs last inside the physics group, after the world has been built, so collider blob references are valid and copyable. It requires a lag compensation configuration singleton to exist at all, and it refuses to run on a re-simulated tick so replay can never overwrite history that was already recorded.

ring.short: Thirty two stored collision worlds, indexed by tick.
ring.deep: It is not an array of worlds. It is thirty two named fields read through a switch statement, because a collision world contains a broadphase tree that cannot simply be copied into an arbitrary slot. Holding thirty two live broadphase trees in memory, and cloning one per tick, is the real running cost of lag compensation.

rewind.short: Subtracts the delay from the current tick and hands back a world.
rewind.deep: It clamps in two directions. A request newer than the latest stored tick gets the live world. A request older than the ring gets the oldest slot. Both are reported through an expected tick and a returned tick, and comparing those two is the only way to learn that your history is too short for your player base.

hit.short: Your hit registration, running inside the prediction loop.
hit.deep: Three rules apply. Query inside the prediction group so the tick you pass matches the command. Gate the damage on the first time a tick is fully predicted, because damage is a one shot side effect. And filter on the simulate tag, exactly as every other predicted system must.

lessons.title: Ghost serializer codegen
lessons.blurb: Attributes and templates become compiled function pointers in a descriptor table.

chapters.title: It happens at compile time
chapters.text: Replication in this stack has no runtime reflection cost, and the reason is that none of it happens at runtime. A Roslyn generator runs during C sharp compilation, once per assembly, sweeping every syntax tree and sorting candidates into buckets. By the time a world exists, the serialization code is already compiled machine code with a Burst function pointer attached to it.

chapters.title: Attributes are the schema, templates are the shapes
chapters.text: Three attributes carry the declaration. One goes on fields and carries quantization, smoothing, composite change tracking, a sub type selector, and a send flag. One goes on the type and carries prefab type, send optimisation, owner send type, and whether children replicate. The third goes on the type and simply says: replicate the enabled flag as well as the fields. Alongside them sit the templates, one per supported field type, in quantized and unquantized variants.

chapters.title: What comes out
chapters.text: For each replicated component the generator produces a struct with a private snapshot layout and eight methods. Copy to snapshot applies quantization. Calculate change mask compares against a baseline. Predict delta derives a predicted baseline. Serialize writes only changed fields. Deserialize reads them back. Copy from snapshot dequantizes and interpolates. Restore from backup handles rollback. And a report method feeds the prediction error debugger.

chapters.title: A descriptor table, not a lookup
chapters.text: One registration system per assembly hands each serializer's descriptor to a collection, which ends up as a dynamic buffer on the ghost collection entity. Each entry carries sizes, mask bit counts, routing rules, and a small set of function pointers. Dispatch at runtime is an index into that buffer followed by an indirect call, exactly like a driver jump table. Nothing is looked up by name at any point after startup.

chapters.title: Predict, then encode the residual
chapters.text: Serialization does not delta against the previous value. It deltas against a prediction of the current value, derived from three baselines using fractions in sixteenths, falling back to the newest baseline whenever the extrapolation would be worse. The residual is then written through an entropy model, so a near zero delta costs a handful of bits. A body moving at constant velocity is almost free on the wire. It is the same structure as a lossless audio codec.

attrs.short: The three attributes that declare what replicates and how.
attrs.deep: Quantization defaults to negative one, meaning unset. Composite change tracking is off, so every inner field of a nested struct gets its own change bit. Smoothing defaults to clamp. Send data defaults to true, and the maximum smoothing distance defaults to zero, which disables the snap check entirely.

templates.short: One code template per supported field type, quantized or not.
templates.deep: They ship as additional files inside the package, and there are separate templates for the quantized and unquantized form of every floating point type, including the quaternion and every fixed string size. A custom sub type is how you point a field at a template of your own.

gen.short: A Roslyn generator running once per assembly during compilation.
gen.deep: It registers a syntax receiver that sorts candidates into seven buckets: components, remote procedure calls, commands, inputs, variants, ghost behaviours, and remotes. If an assembly does not reference the netcode package, the generator skips it entirely, and your attributes do nothing at all, with no error, because nothing ran.

ser.short: The emitted serializer struct for one component.
ser.deep: Its snapshot layout begins with a tick, then the change mask words, then the enabled bit mask words, then the component data, all aligned. Each replicated field contributes one change bit by default, and the composite option collapses a nested struct down to a single bit for the whole struct.

reg.short: One generated registration system per assembly.
reg.deep: It is ordered into the serializer collection group and created before the default variant group, so that variants can override which serializer a component actually uses. Its whole job is to call add serializer once for each descriptor the generator produced in that assembly.

state.short: The descriptor: sizes, masks, routing rules, and function pointers.
state.deep: It carries three hashes used for identity and protocol versioning, the component type, the in memory size and the on the wire size, the change mask bit count, whether the enabled bit is serialized, and the routing rules taken from the component attribute. Then it carries the pointers into the generated code.

wire.short: The send path, calling into the generated code by index.
wire.deep: It compares quantized integers rather than floats when building the change mask, which is the real reason quantization saves bandwidth: quantized values compare equal far more often, and an unchanged field costs only its mask bit. Set quantization too coarse, though, and prediction can never agree with the dequantized server value, so you roll back every single tick.

lessons.title: The Snapshot Budget
lessons.blurb: One packet per player per tick, and the arbiter that decides what fills it.

chapters.title: A fixed-width bus
chapters.text: The server does not send you the world. Once per network tick, per connection, it sends one packet, and that packet is about fourteen hundred bytes minus the pipeline header. Everything on this map exists to answer one question: given a budget that does not grow, which ghosts get to spend it this tick.

chapters.title: Priority times age
chapters.text: Each chunk of ghosts carries a base importance you set on the prefab. The server multiplies that by the number of ticks since the chunk was last sent. That second term is an age counter, and it is the reason a low importance object is never silent forever. This is a priority arbiter with aging, exactly as a bus arbiter avoids starving a low priority requester. Every grant resets that requester's age while everyone else keeps climbing.

chapters.title: Your own scoring function
chapters.text: Before the sort, the server hands the whole list of chunks to a function pointer you supply. The built in one is distance based: it takes the difference between the chunk's tile and the player's tile, squares the length, and divides priority by it. Anything within one tile in any direction is treated as here, because a player standing near a tile edge must not lose the tile they are looking at.

chapters.title: Where the player is looking
chapters.text: The scaling function needs a focal point per connection, and that lives in a component you put on the connection entity yourself. If you forget it, the scaling function is never called at all, no error appears, and every ghost simply falls back to plain aging. This is the single most common silent failure in interest management.

chapters.title: Relevancy is a different verb
chapters.text: Importance answers how often. Relevancy answers whether at all. A relevancy set is a map keyed by connection and ghost, and it runs in one of two modes: an allowlist where nothing is sent unless listed, or a denylist where listed things are excluded. For anything competitive you want the allowlist, because anything you forget to list in a denylist leaks.

chapters.title: Spending the packet
chapters.text: The serializer walks the sorted list and writes ghosts until the packet is full, delta compressed against whatever this particular client last acknowledged. A chunk that has not changed since an acknowledged zero change snapshot is skipped entirely. And when a ghost stops being relevant, it is not merely omitted; its history is cleared and a despawn is queued, so the entity is destroyed on the client.

chunks.short: Every ghost chunk on the server, with per connection state attached.
chunks.deep: The send system does not think in entities, it thinks in chunks. Each chunk carries, for each connection separately, the tick it was last sent and the snapshot history used for delta compression. That is why the cost of sending grows with player count even when the world does not change at all.

aging.short: Base importance multiplied by ticks since this chunk was last sent.
aging.deep: The product is compared against a minimum send importance floor, and dropped if it is below. Then it is multiplied by one thousand, purely to give your scaling function room to divide. If the whole chunk was irrelevant last time, the priority is divided down first, so barely relevant things do not churn.

focus.short: The per connection focal point your code puts on the connection entity.
focus.deep: Without this component the send system skips importance scaling entirely and logs nothing. The packet dump is the only place it tells you, printing that ghost importance is disabled. Add the component when the player takes control of a pawn, and update it as the pawn moves.

scale.short: Your batched scoring function, called once per connection with every chunk.
scale.deep: The batched form is preferred because it replaces thousands of function pointer calls with one. It may rewrite each chunk's priority, and it may also flip a whole chunk relevancy flag, which is a fast path that skips the relevancy hash map completely. After it returns, the list is sorted in descending priority order.

relset.short: A map from connection and ghost identifier to relevance for this tick.
relset.deep: It is consulted only when the faster archetype masks and the chunk level flag have not already settled the question. There is one asymmetry worth knowing: a ghost matching netcode's own internal relevancy rule can never be marked irrelevant by your code.

serialize.short: Writes ghosts into the packet, delta compressed against this client's acknowledgement.
serialize.deep: Three separate limits can stop it early: the number of chunks it is allowed to examine, the number it is allowed to send from, and the packet filling up. Set the examine limit too low and the packet goes out half empty, because that limit is applied before relevancy is even checked.

packet.short: One unreliable packet, sized to the maximum message size minus headers.
packet.deep: You can override the size globally, or per connection, which is how you hit a specific bandwidth target for a specific player. Ask for more than the message size and the snapshot quietly moves onto the fragmenting pipeline, which costs you reassembly and makes loss hurt more.

despawn.short: Ghosts that dropped out of relevance, plus ordinary destroyed entities.
despawn.deep: A third of the packet is reserved for despawn messages by default, before ghost data gets any of it, and the package suggests raising that toward three quarters at large scale. Because relevancy churn is spawn and despawn churn, a relevancy rule with no hysteresis will spend your packet on nothing but bookkeeping.

lessons.title: The Measurement Plane
lessons.blurb: Four bottlenecks that look identical from outside, and the counters that separate them.

chapters.title: Four problems, one symptom
chapters.text: Netcode has four bottlenecks: serialization work on the server, bandwidth on the wire, prediction replay on the client, and the quality of the link itself. From the outside they all look the same, because the game gets worse when there are more players. Reaching for a central processing unit profiler when you have a bandwidth problem is how weeks disappear.

chapters.title: None of this exists in a release build
chapters.text: Every metric component and every counter here is wrapped in a compile time condition. In a release player without the debug define, the types do not exist and nothing is emitted. The collector also gates itself on the profiler being enabled, and it creates its own singleton entity. If you had already made one to read metrics from your own code, it destroys yours and warns you.

chapters.title: The same numbers, two shapes
chapters.text: The collector publishes in two forms. One is ordinary entity components you can read from your own system: round trip time, jitter, command age, snapshot size in bits, per ghost type instance counts and sizes. The other is profiler counters in the network category, which is what the profiler window graphs. Read the components when you want a number. Read the counters when you want a shape over time.

chapters.title: The only two defined bad values
chapters.text: This chapter refuses to tell you what a bad millisecond looks like, because that was never measured here. But the package itself defines exactly two thresholds. Compression efficiency below seventy percent is flagged as poor. A snapshot approaching ninety percent of the maximum message size is flagged as reaching the ceiling. Those are the package's numbers, not invented ones.

chapters.title: Counting prediction ticks
chapters.text: Rollback cost is predicted entities multiplied by replayed ticks, and both terms are readable. Network time exposes how many predicted ticks have run this frame and how many the loop expects. It even prints them together in one string, which makes it the cheapest prediction probe you will ever write. Batching replayed ticks saves time and costs simulation accuracy, because one step with a larger delta is not the same as several small ones.

chapters.title: The dashboard that survives a build
chapters.text: The fastest netcode instrument is not a window. Query the network metrics, the snapshot metrics, and the network time in one client system, and log one line per second. Four numbers separate all four bottlenecks, and unlike a profiler window they keep working in a headless build on a real server.

server.short: Emits snapshot sizes, chunk counts, and per ghost serialization timings.
server.deep: This is also where the named profiler markers live. Prioritize chunks covers gathering and sorting per connection, relevancy covers per entity evaluation, and there is a marker for the static optimization check. There is an option to add a marker per component inside serialization, which costs performance and is meant to be turned on, read, and turned off.

client.short: Emits round trip time, jitter, snapshot age, and prediction error magnitudes.
client.deep: Prediction errors are reported as a buffer of magnitudes paired with a buffer of names, joined only by index. Read one without the other and you have numbers attached to nothing. The client is also where you count predicted ticks per frame, which is the client side cost term.

collector.short: One system per world that gathers stats and publishes them twice.
collector.deep: It only runs while the profiler is enabled, and it cleans up when the profiler is switched off. It creates a singleton entity named metrics monitor carrying six required component types. Server worlds get instance count and snapshot size counters; client worlds get those plus jitter and round trip time.

counters.short: Profiler counters in the network category: bytes, counts, and nanoseconds.
counters.deep: Snapshot size is published in bytes, converted from a bit total. Round trip time and jitter are stored in milliseconds on the component and multiplied by one million for the nanosecond unit the counter declares. If you want milliseconds, read the component rather than the counter.

singletons.short: Ordinary entity components holding every metric the collector gathered.
singletons.deep: Network metrics carries round trip time, jitter, command age, and the minimum and maximum snapshot age. Snapshot metrics carries total size in bits, total ghost count, and despawn counts. Ghost metrics is a buffer with one entry per ghost type, holding instance count, size in bits, and chunk count on the server.

modules.short: Two profiler modules, one for the client world and one for the server world.
modules.deep: The per tick view breaks a snapshot into rows with size, percentage of the snapshot, instance count, compression efficiency, and average size per instance. Two rows are not ghost types at all: snapshot overhead for spawns and prefab lists, and ghost prefab overhead for identifiers, spawn ticks, and baselines. Note that the older browser based network debugger is marked deprecated in this version.
