hud.short: Your own system reading the metric components and logging a line.
hud.deep: Four numbers are enough to separate the four bottlenecks: round trip time, jitter, snapshot bits, and predicted ticks per frame. Because these are plain components, this probe compiles into a development build and keeps reporting from a real server under real load, which no editor window can do.

lessons.title: The Transport Stack
lessons.blurb: From a call to Listen down to the bytes, and where a relay actually sits.

chapters.title: Four independent choices
chapters.text: People collapse four separate decisions into one word and then argue about it. Topology is who owns the authoritative simulation. The driver store is which driver instances exist. The interface is how bytes leave the process. Reachability is whether the client can address the host at all. A relay answers the fourth question and changes nothing about the first.

chapters.title: There is no client hosted mode
chapters.text: The play type has exactly three values. Client and server creates both worlds in one process, which is a listen server. Client creates one world that must connect to something. Server creates one world that can only listen. What people call client hosting is simply client and server running on a player's machine, with every consequence that implies for who you are trusting.

chapters.title: One property is the extension point
chapters.text: A single static property holds the driver constructor, and swapping it is how you inject relay parameters, transport layer security, or unusual queue sizes. You do not write driver creation by hand: the default builder gives you a register helper for every combination, and you mutate the settings object before handing it over.

chapters.title: The server holds two drivers
chapters.text: A server in the editor usually registers two drivers: one using inter process communication for the client living in the same process, and one socket driver for everyone else. The client picks the in process route only when a server world already exists and the network simulator is off. That last condition is why turning the simulator on forces sockets, since there would otherwise be nothing to emulate.

chapters.title: The pipeline stack
chapters.text: Each driver creates three pipelines. Unreliable sequenced carries snapshots and commands. Reliable sequenced carries remote procedure calls. A fragmenting pipeline carries snapshots too big for one message. In the editor, with the simulator on, a fourth stage is appended to all three on the client only. Each stage adds header bytes, and the send system subtracts them before deciding how big a snapshot may be.

chapters.title: What is not in the box
chapters.text: Search the whole transport package for hole punching or address translation traversal and you find nothing. There is a relay client that takes an endpoint, an allocation identifier, and a key. Everything that produces those values, along with matchmaking, lobbies, and hosted fleets, is a service running somewhere else. This book verified the struct and the driver parameter, and it verified nothing about the service.

api.short: The singleton your game calls to listen or to connect.
api.deep: It also exposes the driver store itself, so you can ask which address a given driver actually bound to. When a listen server's own player feels mysteriously laggy, that query tells you whether the local connection went over the in process driver or fell back to the loopback socket.

ctor.short: A static property you replace to control how drivers are built.
ctor.deep: It has two methods, one for the client world and one for the server world, and it lazily defaults to a constructor that registers in process and socket drivers. Assign your own before any world is created. Relay parameters, certificates, and queue sizes are all just settings you apply before calling the register helper.

store.short: An array of driver instances, each tagged in process or socket.
store.deep: The server usually holds two, the client holds one. The order matters more than people expect: the local client only gets the fast in process driver if the server world already exists, so you must start listening before you try to connect. Get that wrong and your host player quietly routes through the loopback socket.

relay.short: An allocation from a hosted service: an endpoint, a key, a join code.
relay.deep: Netcode applies it as driver settings on the socket driver only. On a server the in process driver is deliberately registered without relay parameters, so the host's own player keeps the fast path while remote clients take the longer route. A relay is a reachability fix, not a topology, and it costs an extra hop of latency.

ipc.short: An in process driver with no socket, no latency, and guaranteed delivery.
ipc.deep: It is what makes a listen server's own player feel instant, and it is also what makes editor testing dishonest, because a perfect link hides exactly the class of bug that ships. Develop with the simulator on, which forces even the local client onto a real socket.

socket.short: A datagram driver, or a web socket driver when targeting a browser.
socket.deep: A browser client cannot open a datagram socket, so it uses web sockets, and it cannot listen at all. The default server constructor throws for that target and tells you to build a custom constructor using relay settings instead. This is the one case where reachability dictates topology.

local.short: The host's own player, connected through the in process driver.
local.deep: It is a real connection with a real network identifier, running the whole netcode flow, just with a transport that never drops or delays anything. Whether the host's zero latency advantage is acceptable is a design decision. In a shooter it usually is not, and no configuration removes it.

wire.short: The three pipelines every driver creates, and the bytes they carry.
wire.deep: Defaults worth knowing: a maximum message size of fourteen hundred bytes, a reliable window of thirty two, a fragmentation payload capacity of sixteen kilobytes, and a thirty second disconnect timeout with a half second heartbeat. In the editor a maximum frame time is set so a breakpoint does not look like a dropped connection.

lessons.title: The Trust Boundary
lessons.blurb: What a modified client can assert, and exactly where each assertion is bounded.

chapters.title: Intent, never results
chapters.text: The security model is one sentence: the client sends intent and the server computes results. Everything inside the client box belongs to the attacker, including the parts netcode fills in automatically. Everything the server derives from those fields belongs to you. The strength of the whole model is how much the server derives and how little it accepts.

chapters.title: A mailbox, not a shared bus
chapters.text: Think of this as a privilege boundary with a mailbox. The client writes a message; the server reads it as a request and executes in its own address space. A design where the client sends a position is a design where the untrusted side has a write port into privileged memory. Every hole on this map is either an unvalidated field in the mailbox, or a read port that was opened too wide.

chapters.title: What is already bounded for you
chapters.text: A command packet carries at most thirty two commands. The buffer they land in is a ring of sixty four slots keyed by tick, and the prediction loop reads exactly one command per tick. Commands older than the current server tick are rewritten to it. So flooding does not multiply your actions; it wastes your own bandwidth and costs the server a little work.

chapters.title: What is not bounded at all
chapters.text: The receive path deserializes your input struct field by field with no range check, no clamp, and no normalisation. A movement vector arrives as whatever bit patterns were sent, and the server then multiplies it by speed and delta time with full authority. That is an authoritative teleport. Clamp on read, and do it in the shared predicted system, because a server only clamp the client does not apply is a permanent misprediction.

chapters.title: What lag compensation gives back
chapters.text: To rewind the world to what a client saw, the server has to know how far behind that view was, and the client is the one who says. Inflate that number and the server rewinds further than your view required. The structural bound is the history buffer, which holds at most thirty two collision worlds, so your history size is literally your maximum exploitable rewind.

chapters.title: The read port
chapters.text: A client can render anything it received, so quantization, obfuscation, and encryption do not stop a wall hack. The only defence is not sending the data. Relevancy in allowlist mode, and marking private state as owner only, are the structural answers. An aimbot that cannot see you cannot aim at you, and that is the netcode contribution to a problem netcode cannot otherwise solve.

client.short: A process the attacker fully controls: memory, code, timing, and clock.
client.deep: Nothing it reports is evidence of anything. It can put any value in any input field, send at any rate, claim any tick, and report any interpolation delay. What it cannot do is write a replicated field, because those flow only from server to client, and it cannot change what the server would have simulated.

packet.short: Input fields and a tick number, at most thirty two commands per packet.
packet.deep: The count is five bits, and the number actually sent is the target command slack plus the additional commands setting, which is redundancy against loss rather than a rate. Late arrivals and duplicate resends are both counted in a statistics block on the connection, which is where you detect a client behaving strangely.

delay.short: The interpolation delay, written into the command header by the sender.
delay.deep: The component that receives it is documented as the latest reported delay, which is exactly as trustworthy as it sounds. It is also never reset when the client switches which entity it is controlling, so a stale value from a previous vehicle silently applies to the next one. That is a correctness bug before it is a security one.

ring.short: Sixty four slots keyed by tick, read once per tick by the prediction loop.
ring.deep: This is what makes flooding pointless. Inserting into an occupied slot replaces its contents and counts as a redundant resend. Commands for future ticks simply wait until the server reaches them, which is normal because clients deliberately run ahead. The only way this becomes a hazard is if your own code reads the buffer directly instead of by tick.

rewind.short: The collision history, and the clamp that bounds how far back anyone can reach.
rewind.deep: The requested delay is clamped to one less than the history size, and the raw buffer holds at most thirty two worlds. At sixty simulation steps per second that is a little over half a second. The lookup returns both the tick you asked for and the tick you got, and the package documentation tells you to compare them to find players sitting on the clamp.

sim.short: The only writer of truth, running the same rules the client predicted.
sim.deep: This is where your input domains have to be enforced, in the shared predicted system so both sides agree. Directions get normalised, non finite values get zeroed, angles get wrapped. Outcomes that decide anything, such as damage, loot, or score, belong in a server only system that the client never runs at all.

relev.short: The gate deciding which ghosts each connection is allowed to receive.
relev.deep: Allowlist mode sends nothing unless listed, which is the correct posture for a competitive game. Denylist mode leaks anything you forget. Marking a component as owner only removes ammunition, cooldowns, and private state from every other client's snapshot entirely. Distance driven relevancy still leaks through walls at close range, which is exactly where it matters.

lessons.title: Two Clock Domains
lessons.blurb: Every ghost on a client lives in the server's past or the client's future. Ownership picks which.

chapters.title: There is no single now
chapters.text: Here is the thing the dropdown never tells you. A client does not have one clock. It has two, running at different offsets from the server, and every replicated entity is assigned to one of them. One domain plays back the server's past out of a buffer. The other guesses at the client's future and gets corrected. They are not two settings on a spectrum. They are two different machines, and this map puts them side by side so you can see that.

chapters.title: The past is a delay line
chapters.text: Take the interpolated side first, because it is the one you already know from hardware. Snapshots arrive and go into a ring. A read pointer trails the write pointer by a fixed number of ticks. You read out whatever the buffer held that many ticks ago, and you interpolate between the two entries that bracket it. The client never simulates this entity. Not once. It is a delay line with a lerp on the output, and like every elastic buffer it can be late, but it cannot be wrong.

chapters.title: The future is speculative execution
chapters.text: Now the other side, and this one you have definitely built before, in silicon. A predicted entity is simulated ahead of the server, on the client's own timeline. Every frame it restores that entity to the last tick the server confirmed, then resimulates every tick from there up to the present. Each arriving snapshot is a checkpoint. It either agrees, in which case the restore changes nothing, or it disagrees, and the replay lands somewhere different. That is speculative execution with a pipeline flush, right down to the cost model.

chapters.title: Ownership is the selector
chapters.text: So which domain does an entity get? For the two simple modes it is fixed at bake time and it is the same everywhere. Owner predicted is the interesting one. It selects per machine, at runtime, by ownership. The client that owns the entity predicts it. Every other client interpolates it. Which means the very same prefab, spawned once on the server, is sitting in different time domains on different machines at the same instant. That is not a bug in your mental model. That is the design.

chapters.title: The rule that wrecks projects
chapters.text: And now the edge in the middle of the map, the one drawn in red. A predicted entity cannot correctly interact with an interpolated one. They are not simulating the same instant. One of them is roughly half a round trip ahead and the other is roughly two snapshots behind, so a collision between them is a collision between two different moments. The consequence is that anything a predicted entity touches must itself become predicted. Prediction is contagious. You set out to predict one capsule and you discover you have signed up to predict the crate it pushes, the platform it stands on, and the door it opens.

chapters.title: What it costs, plainly
chapters.text: The asymmetry is brutal and worth stating in numbers. An interpolated ghost costs two buffer reads and a lerp. No gameplay system runs for it on the client at all. A predicted ghost costs ticks behind, times entities, times your predicted systems, every single frame. And the ticks behind term is the same for all of them, because there is one loop covering the whole predicted set. So the only lever you really have is the size of that set. Owner predicted exists to make that set exactly one.

authoring.short: The prefab component where the whole decision is made, at bake time.
authoring.deep: Two fields matter. The default mode says which domain a ghost lands in when it spawns. The supported modes mask says which domains it is allowed to occupy at all, and narrowing it lets the baker strip out the machinery for the other one. The mask defaults to allowing both, which is the safe choice and also the one that leaves optimization on the table.
authoring.gotoLabel: What the generator does with this

server.short: The only machine with a real present, and it never renders it.
server.deep: There is exactly one authoritative timeline and it lives here. Everything on the right half of this map is a client's attempt to be somewhere useful relative to this tick. One side lags it deliberately, the other side runs ahead of it deliberately, and neither is ever equal to it.

owner.short: The per-machine selector: is this entity's owner me?
owner.deep: The server stamps an owning network identifier onto the ghost. On each client that identifier is compared with its own, and under owner predicted the answer picks the time domain. It is the only setting in the system whose effect differs from machine to machine, which is exactly why it confuses people looking at one Inspector.

buffer.short: A ring of received snapshots, written at the rate the wire delivers them.
buffer.deep: The write pointer moves whenever a packet lands, which is irregular. The read pointer moves smoothly with the client's clock, a fixed number of ticks behind. That gap is the entire jitter budget. Too small and you underrun and see a freeze. Too large and you have added latency for nothing. Same knob, same trade, same tuning instinct as any elastic buffer between two clock domains.

interp.short: An entity the client plays back and never simulates.
interp.deep: No gameplay system touches it. Its transform is written by the update system from two buffered snapshots, and that is all that happens to it on this machine. It can be extrapolated forward for a short while if data is missing, but it is never predicted, because prediction means running your simulation and this entity's simulation is somebody else's job.

replay.short: Rewind to the last confirmed tick, then resimulate forward to now.
replay.deep: Every frame, not just on a mismatch. When a snapshot arrives, the restore point is the tick that snapshot describes. When nothing arrives, the restore point is the client's own backup of its last full tick, so the loop keeps running on its own history. One loop covers every predicted ghost, and it rewinds as far as the oldest of them requires.

predict.short: An entity the client simulates ahead of the server, and pays for.
predict.deep: Its cost is ticks behind, times entities, times the systems inside the prediction group. The first term comes from the round trip and you do not control it. The third you can optimise. The second is the one you actually decide, and the contagion rule is what makes that decision leak. Every predicted thing must also be deterministic enough that replaying it lands in the same place twice.

lessons.title: Which world am I in?
lessons.blurb: Six address spaces, one authored prefab, and an integer that correlates two entities which never touch.

chapters.title: World zero is a physics index
chapters.text: The phrase world zero is real, and it does not mean what it sounds like. It names the default collider partition inside one entity world, the one a body belongs to unless you say otherwise. An entity world is an address space. A physics world index is a bucket of bodies inside one of those address spaces. One entity world can hold several physics indices, and every index exists separately on the client and on the server. Saying physics runs in world zero is like saying a process runs in heap arena zero. True of the allocator, silent about the process.

chapters.title: What creates each world
chapters.text: The bootstrap is a single method that says: I will take over world creation. Return true from it and the engine builds nothing of its own. Netcode's implementation branches on one setting, the requested play type. Server or client and server gets a server world. Client or client and server gets a client world. Thin clients follow in the editor. Each world is then populated by asking the type manager for every system carrying a particular filter flag, which is why the two columns on this map are different things. The world flags say what the world is. The filter flags say what got put in it.

chapters.title: What default really expands to
chapters.text: This is the question that trips everyone. The default filter flag has two different expansions, and which one applies depends on who is asking. When a world is being populated, default expands to local simulation plus presentation. When a system is being classified, default expands to whatever its parent group declares as its child default, walking up the ordering chain. If that walk reaches a group with no parent, the fallback is local, server and client simulation. That fallback is the one you meet in practice, because the root simulation group carries no filter attribute at all. It is why an unfiltered gameplay system runs in every game world, including the server.

chapters.title: Simulation is not presentation
chapters.text: The server spawns a fireball. The server has no mesh, no material, no camera. It is tempting to conclude the server does not know where the fireball is. It does. The server computes that position every single tick, including the full rigid body trajectory, because the physics systems resolve into server simulation. What the server lacks is rendering, and rendering is a separate flag on a separate bit. The server world was populated without it, so the systems that turn a transform into pixels were never added. The transform is computed. Nobody draws it. A headless server is not a partial simulation. It is a complete simulation with the display driver unloaded.

chapters.title: One prefab, several baked entities
chapters.text: So how does the client's visual attach to the server's fireball? It does not. There is no attachment. They are two entities in two address spaces and nothing points from one to the other. What crosses the wire is an integer: a ghost identifier and a prefab index. The client looks that index up in its own prefab collection and instantiates its own local copy. Both worlds baked the same authored asset, so both already agree what index seven means. And the two copies are not identical, because baking emits one prefab plus a set of per world removal lists. At startup each world picks the list for itself and strips its own copy before the first instance exists. Renderers and effects are removed on the server. Authority logic is removed on the client. Same asset, different entities.

chapters.title: Singletons are per world
chapters.text: A singleton is an entity in one world's entity manager. There is no process wide registry. Ask for one in the client world and you cannot see the copy in the server world. This is the single most common source of works in the editor, fails in the build, and the reason is mechanical. In the editor both worlds live in one process, so a system reaching for a singleton it does not own often finds a copy anyway. The wrong one, but a plausible one. Ship a dedicated server and the client world is simply not there. The lookup that was quietly wrong becomes loudly absent.

bakeworld.short: A transient world that exists only long enough to turn authored objects into entities.
bakeworld.deep: It is created, used and disposed inside a single call, and it carries the baking filter flag so only baking systems land in it. Anything decided here was decided before either runtime world existed, which is why a wrong baked value can never be fixed by a runtime system.

prefab.short: The baked ghost prefab, plus four lists describing what to remove from it per world.
prefab.deep: Baking does not emit one prefab per world type. It emits one entity graph and four blob arrays: remove on server, remove on client, disable on predicted, disable on interpolated. A component marked as belonging to every variant short circuits the classification and appears in all of them.

strip.short: Picks the removal list for this world and edits the prefab before anything is instantiated.
strip.deep: It tests whether the world is a server, selects the matching list, and removes each named component from the prefab entity and its children. Then it drops the marker saying stripping is pending. Where a ghost can switch between predicted and interpolated at runtime the difference becomes a disable rather than a removal, because the same entity may change mode later.

bootstrap.short: The one hook that decides which worlds exist at all.
bootstrap.deep: Returning true from its initialize method means the engine creates nothing on its own. Netcode's implementation branches on the requested play type. The Nerve bootstrap layers a lifecycle on top: a persistent service world that outlives everything, a menu world, and client and server worlds created and destroyed on demand. Netcode decides whether they exist. Nerve decides when.

serverworld.short: Authority. Populated with server simulation only, and deliberately without presentation.
serverworld.deep: It runs the full simulation including the physics solver, because the physics systems resolve to local, server and client simulation. It has no renderer because presentation is a different flag bit and was never requested. When two players disagree about a position, this is the world that is right.

wire.short: A ghost identifier and a prefab index. No entity reference ever crosses.
wire.deep: Entity references are meaningless across worlds, so replication carries numbers. The identifier is recycled when a ghost dies, so on its own it is not unique. Paired with the tick it spawned on, it is guaranteed unique, because at any moment only one ghost can hold that identifier having spawned on that tick.

clientworld.short: Prediction plus rendering. The only world that asks for the presentation flag.
clientworld.deep: It is the world to reason about when the local capsule feels laggy, when a remote capsule stutters, or when nothing appears on screen. Its physics is a guess corrected by snapshots. A raycast here queries a predicted collision world, not authority, and that difference is invisible until it matters.

thinclient.short: A keyboard with a socket. Connects, sends input, simulates almost nothing.
thinclient.deep: It is populated with the thin client flag alone, which the physics systems do not carry, so a thin client has no physics at all. That is the point: it is the cheapest way to put load on a server, and it is why a bug that only reproduces with thin clients is usually a missing filter rather than a missing feature.

lessons.title: Physics on the server
lessons.blurb: Where the solver actually lives, what the tick does to it, and the budget you sign up for when everything is a rigid body.

chapters.title: The solver has no world filter
chapters.text: Open the physics package and search it for world filter attributes. The runtime has none. The only ones in the whole package are on baking systems and debug display systems. The physics group carries exactly one attribute, saying which group it updates in, and nothing about where it is allowed to exist. That silence is the answer to the question. An unfiltered system resolves to the default flag, the default flag is replaced by the parent group's child default, and a chain that ends at the root simulation group falls through to a hard coded fallback: local, server and client simulation. So the solver runs in the single player world, the client world and the server world. It does not run in a thin client.

chapters.title: Netcode re-clocks the whole group
chapters.text: Physics normally runs in the fixed step group, driven by an accumulator against wall clock time. That is the wrong clock for prediction, because prediction needs to run the same tick several times. So netcode moves it, on the client and on the server both. The move is a transitive closure, not a list: it seeds a set with the physics group, then repeatedly scans the fixed step group adding any system whose ordering attributes name something already in the set, looping until a full pass adds nothing. Think of it as a clock domain crossing. The logic is untouched. Only the clock feeding it is swapped, from a wall clock at one edge per frame to a prediction tick that can issue many edges in a single frame.

chapters.title: Static bodies are free
chapters.text: The physics world is built from two queries. Dynamic bodies are entities that have a velocity. Static bodies are entities that have a collider and no velocity. The export system writes back exactly two component types, a transform and a velocity, so a static body never has anything written to it and never changes. And the validation system that complains about non ghost dynamic bodies only matches entities that have a velocity, so a static collider never trips it. The rule that falls out is where the bandwidth is won in a physics game: a body baked into a subscene that never moves needs no ghost, no snapshot and no prediction. Both worlds baked it from the same data, so both already agree.

chapters.title: The contagion rule, and the arithmetic
chapters.text: A predicted body and an interpolated body are in different time domains. One is ahead of the server, one is behind it. They are never simultaneously correct, so a contact between them is a contact between two different moments, and it resolves differently on every machine. In a game where everything is physical that rule propagates. If the player can push a crate, the crate is predicted. If the crate can knock a barrel, the barrel is predicted. The predicted set is the transitive closure of what can be touched by something predicted. Now the arithmetic. The server steps once per tick, sixty times a second by default. The client steps once per tick it is replaying, and the replay depth is roughly round trip time converted to ticks. On an ordinary connection that is around eight solves per rendered frame where the server does one. The server's cost scales with body count. The client's scales with body count times replay depth.

chapters.title: What actually replicates
chapters.text: The package ships two default variants for physics and they are the entire contract. Velocity is replicated, linear and angular, quantized to a thousandth of a unit, and only sent to clients that are predicting the ghost. Graphical smoothing is restricted to server and predicted client versions, which is a deletion rather than an addition, so that an interpolated client does not have physics smoothing fighting the snapshot interpolation already positioning the body. That table is complete, and the completeness is the point. Mass, gravity factor, damping and colliders appear nowhere in the netcode runtime. They are not replicated, and therefore they are never rolled back. Mutate one inside the prediction loop and the mutation applies once per replayed tick and is never undone.

chapters.title: The second physics world
chapters.text: The predicted physics world can only contain things that roll back, so a dynamic body that is not a ghost is an error. If you want ragdolls, debris or cosmetic impacts, and in a physics heavy game you will, they have to leave the default index. Set the non ghost world index in the netcode physics config, give the prefabs a matching index, and the validation system stops complaining while the predicted world stays small. The config is baked from a component in a subscene, and when it is absent the rate manager falls through to a default initialised struct, which is enum value zero, which is the narrowest of the three run modes. No config is not everything on. It is the most restrictive gate.

authored.short: A shape plus a motion type, authored before any world exists.
authored.deep: Two authoring stacks bake to the same runtime components. The hybrid path bakes Unity's own rigid body and collider components. The custom path adds its own body and shape behaviours plus joints, motors and material tags. Never mix them on one body hierarchy: mixing double bakes, drops colliders, or produces conflicting motion types.

moves.short: The only question that matters first: does this body have a velocity?
moves.deep: This is not a design preference, it is the query the physics world build actually runs. Bodies with a velocity go into the dynamic set. Bodies with a collider and no velocity go into the static set. Everything downstream on this map follows from which side of that query a body lands on.

staticbake.short: Baked level geometry. No ghost, no snapshot, no prediction, no cost beyond broadphase.
staticbake.deep: Start here and justify every promotion out of it. The export step writes back only transforms and velocities, so a static body is never written to at runtime and cannot drift. Both worlds baked it from the same subscene, so they already agree without a single byte on the wire.

touch.short: Can a player reach this body, directly or through a chain of contacts?
touch.deep: The answer is transitive, and that is the expensive part. A body the player can push must be predicted. Anything that body can hit must also be predicted, or the contact happens between two different moments. Draw the closure honestly before you count the budget, because the closure is usually larger than the intuition.

interp.short: The server solves, the client interpolates, the client's solver is never involved.
interp.deep: This is the cheapest replicated option and it is under used. Anything dynamic the local player cannot touch belongs here: distant props, vehicles you only watch, machinery. Netcode strips physics graphical smoothing from the interpolated variant precisely so smoothing does not fight the snapshot interpolation.

predict.short: The same rule executed in both worlds, and re-executed on every replayed tick.
predict.deep: Each predicted body costs a full broadphase, narrowphase and constraint solve per replayed tick, not a transform integration. Raising substeps or solver iterations multiplies against replay depth, which is why both are the wrong first knob under prediction. Fix the predicted body count first.

otherworld.short: A second physics index for dynamic bodies that are not ghosts.
otherworld.deep: The predicted world can only hold things that roll back, so a dynamic non ghost left in the default index is flagged as an error naming the offending entities. Configure the alternate index and the same bodies become legal client only debris. This is the only way to have ragdolls in a predicted physics game without failing validation.

lessons.title: One Asset, Two Clocks
lessons.blurb: A timeline is a pure function of two numbers. Rollback decides which two.

chapters.title: Six bytes for a two second action
chapters.text: A timeline is the cheapest thing you will ever replicate. The authored asset is baked into the build, so it is identical on every machine, and everything visible about a playing timeline follows from two numbers: which timeline, and how far into it. That is a short identifier and a start tick. Six bytes, written once when the action begins and never changed again. Compare that to streaming a character's transform, which costs bytes on every single tick. Replicating the cause instead of the result is the whole argument, and it is a good one.

chapters.title: Accumulate versus derive
chapters.text: Here is the entire chapter in two lines. Elapsed plus equals delta time. Or, elapsed equals current tick minus start tick. The first is a register with feedback: its value now depends on its value last tick, all the way back to the beginning. Rewind the machine and it is wrong unless somebody saved and restored it. The second is combinational logic hanging off a counter. It has no memory, so there is nothing to restore, and netcode already restores the counter for free. The shipped package accumulates. That single addition is the only sequential element in the whole chain.

chapters.title: Where the shipped group actually sits
chapters.text: The timeline root group lands inside the before transform group, which lands directly inside the simulation system group. The predicted simulation system group is a sibling of that, ordered first. So the timeline runs strictly after the entire prediction loop has already finished. It is outside prediction, and no amount of squinting at the group chain changes that. The good news is the world filter: the monorepo package is genuinely present in the server world. Present on the server and correct under prediction are two different properties, and the package has the first one only.

chapters.title: Two rate managers, two shapes of delta
chapters.text: On a dedicated server, the rate manager re-enters the whole simulation system group once per pending tick, pushing a tick sized delta each time. The timeline is evaluated once per tick, at integer tick boundaries. On the client, the rate manager lets the group run exactly once per rendered frame, and the delta it pushes is how far the predicted target tick moved that frame, fractional part included. So the two sides advance the same sum with differently shaped steps, and land up to a tick of phase apart. Nothing ever brings them back together.

chapters.title: The rollback boundary
chapters.text: Say this one out loud, because everything else follows from it. Rollback restores component values. It does not restore entity existence. The prediction history backup is a memory copy of ghost components into a side buffer, and on restore it writes back only the fields that were serialised. There is no create and no destroy in it. An entity your clip spawned during a replayed tick is still there when that tick replays, and your clip will cheerfully spawn a second one. Netcode's answer is not to undo the spawn. It is to make the duplicate reconcilable.

chapters.title: Four kinds, four homes
chapters.text: Clips sort into exactly four kinds. Value clips are sampled and pure, and run predicted in both worlds. Cosmetic clips run on the client only, gated so they fire on the first full prediction of a tick and not on every replay. Spawn clips route through a predicted spawn request and get matched against the authoritative spawn instead of doubling. Authority clips are stripped from the client prefab entirely. The temptation is to put that table on a wiki and ask designers to respect it. Make it a type, so the wrong thing is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

chapters.title: Kinematic is a compression scheme
chapters.text: A root motion move driven entirely by a timeline really is a function of the identifier and the elapsed time. The character goes where the clip says regardless of what it brushes past, so both machines compute the same path from the same six bytes, and the transform does not need to replicate at all during the move. The moment a clip emits force into a dynamic body, that stops being true. The outcome now depends on contact, which is not derivable from the asset, so it has to go on the wire. Kinematic is compression. Force is a bandwidth commitment.

asset.short: One baked blob of clips, curves and timestamps, identical on every machine.
asset.deep: Because it ships in the build rather than over the wire, both sides already agree on everything except the position of the play head. That is why only a short timeline identifier and a start tick ever need to travel, and why a field that never changes costs almost nothing after the first snapshot.

kind.short: The routing decision: which of the four clip kinds this is.
kind.deep: This should be carried by the interface a clip implements, not by designer discipline, because the interface can decide which system group evaluates it. A cosmetic clip that physically cannot run outside the gated client system is a clip nobody can misuse. Close the remaining gap at bake time, the way the graph packages in this stack already reject an invalid graph before the game ever runs.

presclock.short: Frame rate evaluation, client only, for anything a human eye is the sole consumer of.
presclock.deep: This is the shipped package doing exactly what it was designed for. Leave it there. Moving visual effects into the prediction loop would re-emit particles on every replay and cap effects at the tick rate. The one change worth making is to have it read its position from the gameplay clock instead of keeping its own sum, so it becomes a display rather than a second source of truth.
presclock.gotoLabel: The two time domains a client lives in

gameclock.short: Tick minus start tick, evaluated inside prediction, on both client and server.
gameclock.deep: Stateless by construction. Replay the same tick nine times and it returns the same number nine times, because its only input is the tick, and the tick is restored for you every frame. This is the whole reason to derive rather than accumulate: you are not asking rollback to save and restore anything, you are asking it to leave you alone.

cosmetic.short: Visual effects, audio and interface, fired once and never un-fired.
cosmetic.deep: A particle burst is not a component value, so replay cannot take it back. The gate is a single flag on the network time singleton that is set only when a tick is being fully predicted for the first time, and cleared on partial ticks. Four lines, and it is the only netcode aware code most clip authors will ever have to write.

value.short: Continuous sampled output: curves, offsets, root motion, stat modifiers.
value.deep: The easiest kind to migrate, because everything downstream of local time in the package is already pure. Clip local time, the active bit and the weight curve are all functions of the timer position. Change what feeds the timer and the rest becomes rollback safe without being touched. A kinematic move authored this way needs no transform replication at all.
value.gotoLabel: What a force emitting clip commits you to

spawn.short: Creates an entity, and therefore cannot rely on rollback to clean up after it.
spawn.deep: The client marks its speculative spawn with a predicted spawn request. When the authoritative version arrives, a classification system matches the two instead of creating a second, and any predicted spawn that never gets matched is destroyed once it ages out. So duplicates are reconciled rather than prevented, which is the only thing that works when existence itself is never rewound.

authority.short: Server only decisions: score, loot, damage application, state authority.
authority.deep: The cleanest gate in the set, because it is enforced at bake time rather than at runtime. Marking the component as server only means the client prefab never receives it, so there is no branch to forget and no flag to check. If a client could not run it even in principle, a client cannot get it wrong.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: You already know how a machine works. You know that a cache line is 64 bytes, that a branch mispredict costs you ~15 cycles, that D M A exists so the CPU can stop babysitting the bus. That knowledge is not a handicap here. It is the whole advantage.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Because Unity DOTS is not a game engine feature. It is a memory-layout argument that won, wearing a game engine as a coat.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: And Unity Net Code is not "multiplayer". It is a distributed system with a fixed clock, a command ring buffer, and speculative execution with rollback, which is to say, it is a CPU pipeline. You have debugged this shape before. You just called the parts different names.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Trace one keystroke from the USB interrupt to two capsules moving on two screens, naming every system it passes through and every buffer it lands in. Open any package in this stack, find the system responsible for a symptom, and say why it is responsible before you read its body. Author a Grove graph in code, know what bytes it becomes, and know which function pointer executes them. Diagnose a bug class none of us have hit yet, because you understand the mechanism rather than the symptom.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: That last one is the actual goal. Symptoms are infinite. Mechanisms are about forty.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Chapters are short on purpose. Each one is a single idea you can hold in your head while walking to the kitchen. Read them in order the first time, Part III leans on Part I hard.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Every claim is checkable. Where a chapter says "system X does Y", there is a file path. Go look. If I got it wrong, the file wins. No hand-waving at the interesting part. When something is genuinely a hack, it is labelled a hack, with the reason it exists and the cost of removing it. Failure stories are first-class. Every trap in Part V is one we actually hit and actually fixed. The war stories are where the mechanism becomes memorable.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: This book documents a stack that includes commercial packages (Bovine Labs Core, Grove, Canopy, Nerve, Anchor). It describes behaviour, cites file paths, and quotes small API signatures, the way a book about an SDK should. It does not reproduce those packages. If you want to read the implementations, buy them; they are worth it, and this book is much better with the sources open beside it.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Prose and diagrams here: MIT. The packages remain their authors'.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a bridge from something you already own.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Trap, something that fails silently. These are the expensive ones.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Probe, a command you can run right now to see the thing with your own eyes.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Let's start where everything starts: a clock edge.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Power rail comes up. The reset line releases. The core fetches its first instruction from the reset vector. Some tens of millions of instructions later, firmware, bootloader, kernel, init, display server, a process called Unity gets a PID and a main thread.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Everything in this book happens inside that one process. Let's zoom until it hurts.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: A frame is a scheduling quantum, not a unit of time

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Here is the first thing that trips up people from embedded: a frame is not a timer interrupt. Nothing fires it. It is a while (true) loop that runs as fast as the machine and the presentation engine allow.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: The only thing that makes it periodic is present blocking on the display. That is your clock, and it is a lousy one: it jitters, it drops, it changes when the user drags the window to a 60 hertz monitor from a 144 hertz one.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, the frame loop is a free-running superloop, not an ISR. Everything that needs real periodicity has to build its own timebase on top. That is exactly what Net Code's tick system does, and why Part III spends a whole chapter on it.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Unity's Player Loop is a tree of function pointers grouped into phases: Initialization, Early Update, Fixed Update, Pre Update, Update, Pre Late Update, Post Late Update. You can read it, modify it, and write it back at runtime.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: DOTS uses this. When a World is created, Entities inserts callbacks into that table so its three root system groups get ticked:

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, the Player Loop is a vector table you can patch. DOTS installs three entries. Everything DOTS ever does is downstream of those three function pointers being called once per frame per world.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: That is the whole bootstrap secret. There is no daemon, no scheduler, no magic. Three function pointers.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Our project has, at peak, six live worlds in one process (Part I chapter 3 explains why). Each one registers into that same table. So a single frame looks like:

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Single-threaded at this level. The worlds do not run concurrently with each other. They run in sequence, in one frame, which is why "the client and the server are in the same process" is a statement about determinism and not about parallelism.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Trap, because it is one process, a stall in the server world is a stall in the client world. When you see Net Code's "Server Tick Batching has occurred" warning in the editor, it usually means the editor itself hitched, not that your server logic is slow.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Inside a system, System API.Time.Delta Time gives you the world's delta. Which delta depends on where the system is standing:

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: In Simulation System Group at the top level then frame delta (variable, jittery). Inside Fixed Step Simulation System Group then fixed delta, catch-up loop. Inside Predicted Simulation System Group then the network tick delta, and the group may run the same system many times in one frame during a rollback.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: That last one is why Player Move System in our project reads System API.Time.Delta Time without further thought and is still correct. It is standing in the prediction group, so the delta it gets is one network tick, every time, including during replay.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Probe, in play mode, dump the live loop: You will see the DOTS entries sitting in the table next to Unity's built-ins.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Next: why any of this needs a new memory model at all.

lessons.title: 02 · Cache lines all the way down

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: You know this graph in your bones: DRAM latency has been roughly flat for twenty years while core throughput went up two orders of magnitude. A cache miss costs you a few hundred cycles. A modern core can retire a dozen instructions in that time, times however many lanes your simmed unit has.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: So the fastest code is not the code with the fewest instructions. It is the code that streams.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Classic Unity Game Objects do the opposite of streaming. Every Mono Behaviour is a managed heap object with a vtable and a pointer back to a native Transform, which lives in a different allocation, which points at a parent, which is somewhere else entirely. Iterating a thousand of them is a thousand pointer chases into cold memory. It is a linked list wearing an OOP costume.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: E C S is the fix, and the fix is just struct-of-arrays with a scheduler bolted on.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: The chunk is the whole idea. Inside one chunk, memory is laid out as parallel arrays:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Walking Local Transform for every entity in that chunk is a linear scan of contiguous memory. The prefetcher sees it coming from the second element onward. There is no indirection, no vtable, no null check.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a chunk is a D M A-friendly buffer. You picked 16 kibibytes for the same reason an embedded engineer picks a buffer size: it fits comfortably in L1/L2, and it amortises the per-block bookkeeping over hundreds of elements.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: An archetype is the set of component types. {Local Transform, Player Move Input, Ghost Owner, Simulate} is an archetype. Every chunk belongs to exactly one archetype, and every entity in a chunk has exactly that component set, no more, no less.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: This is what makes queries fast. System API.Query<Ref RW<Local Transform>, Ref RO<Player Move Input>>() does not scan entities. It:

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Matches the query mask against the (small) list of archetypes, a handful of bitwise ops. For each matching archetype, walks its chunk list. For each chunk, takes a raw pointer to each component array. Loops 0.count.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: The per-entity cost is a struct read and a struct write. The per-query cost is the archetype matching, done once.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Trap, adding or removing a component moves the entity to a different chunk. That is a memcpy of every component plus bookkeeping, and it invalidates any raw pointer you were holding. This is why DOTS code obsessively defers structural changes into an Entity Command Buffer and plays it back at a known safe point. It is the same discipline as "don't free() inside the interrupt handler".

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Moving chunks for a boolean is absurd, so Entities added enableable components. The chunk header carries a 128-bit mask per enableable type. Disabling one flips a bit; the entity stays put. Queries respect the mask via Chunk Entity Enumerator.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Remember this word: Simulate. It is an enableable tag component, and in Part III it becomes the single most important bit in the whole prediction system. Net Code flips it to say "this entity should tick on this tick". Forget to respect it and your capsule integrates its velocity five times per frame instead of once.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Every chunk stores a uint version per component type, bumped whenever a system takes write access. With Change Filter<T>() compares versions and skips whole chunks.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a dirty bit per cache line, except the granularity is a chunk and the write-back is a system deciding whether to bother.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Nothing is free. The bill for all that throughput:

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: No references. A component cannot hold a class. It holds an Entity handle and you look it up, which is a random access, i.e. the exact thing you were avoiding. Structural changes are expensive. Design so they are rare and batched. Debugging is different. There is no object to inspect. You inspect chunks. Get comfortable with the Entities Hierarchy and Entity Query in the debugger.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Next: how many independent machines are we actually running?

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: then 03 · Worlds: six machines in one process

lessons.title: 03 · Worlds: six machines in one process

chapters.title: b1
chapters.text: 03 · Worlds: six machines in one process

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: A World is an Entity Manager (its own chunk allocator, its own entity IDs) plus a list of systems. Two worlds share nothing. Entity #42 in Client World and entity #42 in Server World are unrelated, the way PID 42 on two machines is unrelated.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a world is a separate address space. Same silicon, same frame, zero shared state. The only way data crosses is a message on the wire.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Service World is the one that outlives everything, it owns the state graph that says "we are in Menu" or "we are in Game", and it is what creates and destroys the others.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Chapter 42 is the definitive account: every world netcode can build, what World System Filter Flags.Default really expands to, and which world to reason about when debugging what.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Each world carries World Flags. Systems declare where they are allowed to exist:

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Bovine Labs adds its own world kinds on top of Unity's, in Bovine Labs.Core/Worlds.cs:

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Worlds.Server Local is doing real work: it means "authority", whether that authority is a netcode server or an offline single-player world. Write your authoritative rules against that and single-player comes free.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Trap, a system with no [World System Filter] defaults to Local Simulation | Server Simulation | Client Simulation, so it lands in every game world including the server. Half of all "why did that run twice?" bugs are a missing filter.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Groups: the ordering is a graph, not a list

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Systems do not run in declaration order, alphabetical order, or file order. They run in the order of a topologically-sorted dependency graph built from attributes.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Trap, [Update Before] only works between systems in the same group. Point it at a system in another group and Unity logs a warning and ignores it. You will see exactly this warning in our project's console, coming from Unity's own Companion Game Object Update Transform System. Harmless there; not harmless in your code.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Our project uses ISystem everywhere except where it genuinely cannot, the same rule the packages follow. Connection Approval Server System is a System Base precisely because it awaits an HTTP call to Unity Authentication.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: ICustom Bootstrap lets you take over world creation. Nerve does, via Bovine Labs Bootstrap: Client Server Bootstrap. It is why our worlds are named and shaped the way they are, and why Create Client Server Worlds() is the thing the service graph calls when you press Start Game.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Next: the part where all those chunks get chewed in parallel.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Two separate technologies that people blur together. Keep them apart in your head:

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Burst is a compiler. It turns a subset of C# into machine code via LLVM. Jobs is a scheduler. It runs work on worker threads with enforced data safety.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: You can use either without the other. Together they are why DOTS is fast.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, Burst is a cross-compiler with -O3 -ffast-math -march=native aimed at a language that normally forbids all three. [Burst Compile] is you signing the waiver.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Trap, [Burst Compile] on the methods but not on the struct silently does nothing. There is an analyzer for this, EA0010, "Containing Type is missing Burst Compile attribute" (Source Generators/./Diagnostics.cs:72), but it returns without warning for ISystem types (Burst Compiler Analyzer.cs:65), which is exactly the case here. So the warning exists everywhere except where you need it. Your system just runs at Mono speed forever. This is the single most common invisible perf bug in DOTS.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Inside a bursted method you may not touch: class, string, object, try/catch (in release), Unity Engine.Debug.Log, LINQ, delegates that aren't Function Pointer. Our Player Gather Input System deliberately has no [Burst Compile] on On Update, because Keyboard.current is a managed object. That is the correct call, not a compromise.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Burst compiles a separate copy of static fields. A static int written from managed code is invisible to bursted code. The supported bridge is Shared Static<T>:

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: That is exactly how the sample's Start Game button reaches E C S, and how Nerve's Client Disconnection Outcome escapes the graph. When you see Shared Static, read it as "a global that Burst and Mono agree on".

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Jobs: a dependency graph the compiler checks

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: state.Dependency is a Job Handle, a token in that graph. Schedule a job, get a handle, pass it on. The safety system tracks which Native Arrays each job reads and writes and refuses to compile or run an unsafe combination.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, the job system is a scoreboard. Every Native Container is a register with readers and writers tracked; the scheduler stalls dependents until hazards clear. Unity's version just yells at you at compile time instead of stalling silently.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: The escape hatches, and when they are legitimate

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: All three appear in this stack. Client App Context uses the third to hold a System State*, because a Grove context must reach the system it is running inside. That is not sloppiness, it is the same reason you cast away volatile exactly once in a driver, in a place with a comment.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Why our capsule code runs single-threaded

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Player Move System uses System API.Query with foreach, on the main thread, bursted. Two capsules. Scheduling a parallel job for two entities would cost more in scheduling overhead than it saves.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: The lesson generalises: parallelism is a throughput tool with a fixed setup cost. Below a few thousand entities, foreach on the main thread wins. Measure before you schedule.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Probe, Jobs then Burst then Open Inspector in the editor shows the actual assembly Burst generated for any bursted method. Read it. If you were expecting vmulps and you see a call into a math library, something broke your vectorization.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Part I done. You now know the machine. Next: what is actually installed on it.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: 21 direct dependencies. Every one earns its slot, we got the manifest down from 49 and then had to add several back, because of a mechanism you will meet in the next chapter.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: The dependency direction matters: Grove knows nothing about games. It is a generic graph executor. Canopy adds "states". Nerve adds "multiplayer app". Read them in that order and each one is small.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Entities and Net Code are pinned to a fork in vex-studio/tertle-monorepo, at one exact commit. Bovine Labs needs behaviour the shipping packages do not expose yet. The pin is a commit SHA, not a branch, which is the only sane way to depend on a fork.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Trap, mixing a forked com.unity.entities with a registry com.unity.netcode gives you version-solver errors that read like nonsense. Both come from the fork or neither does.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: That table is the chapter's whole point. Four of our packages exist purely to satisfy compile-time constraints. Chapter 06 explains the mechanism, and it is the nastiest silent failure in the entire Unity toolchain.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Three assemblies for ~400 lines of code looks like over-engineering. It is not; chapter 06 shows what happens when you collapse them.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Probe, the real resolved graph, including transitives:

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: then 06 · Assemblies, and the silent-death trap

chapters.title: b1
chapters.text: 06 · Assemblies, and the silent-death trap

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: This chapter is worth more than its length. It describes a failure mode that produces no error, no warning, and no output, the code simply is not there. We lost hours to it twice.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: An assembly definition is a compilation unit

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Unity compiles one DLL per.assembly definition. The file is the linker script:

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: version Defines, "if that package exists, define this symbol"

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Note the scope: per assembly. Every assembly definition that wants UNITY_NETCODE must declare its own version Defines entry. Symbols do not inherit from referenced assemblies. This is why the same 8-entry block is copy-pasted into every assembly definition in the Bovine Labs stack, and now into ours.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: define Constraints, "compile me only if ALL of these are defined"

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: THE TRAP, define Constraints is all-or-nothing at the assembly level. If one symbol is missing, Unity does not compile the assembly. Not partially. At all. It produces no DLL, logs nothing, and every type in it silently ceases to exist.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: We had stripped the manifest to a minimum. Five of those six were unsatisfied. So Bovine Labs.Nerve.State, the assembly containing sessions, ownership, approval, and every client node, was not built. The symptom was "these types don't exist", which reads like a bad using, which sends you hunting in exactly the wrong place.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: The fix was installing four packages we thought we did not need. That is chapter 05's table.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Probe, the only reliable check. If your assembly is missing from this list, its constraints failed:

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: The second trap: referencing an editor-only assembly from runtime code

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Bovine Labs.Nerve.State.Authoring has "UNITY_EDITOR" in its define Constraints. It is an editor-only assembly.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Our Daggertooth assembly definition referenced it. In the editor: fine, everything compiles, everything works, ship it. In a player build, UNITY_EDITOR is undefined, that assembly is not built, and the reference silently drops, taking every type we used from it.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: This is a bug that cannot reproduce until the day you make your first build, at which point it looks like a catastrophic regression.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Rule of thumb, and it is the same rule the sample follows:

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Most Bovine Labs assemblies set auto Referenced: false. That means they are not automatically visible to Assembly-CSharp, you must reference them explicitly. It is deliberate: it prevents accidental coupling and it keeps compile times down. It also means "I can't see the type" often just means "add the reference".

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: Is the DLL in Library/Script Assemblies/? Does your assembly definition reference the assembly? Does your assembly definition declare the version Defines for symbols you use in #if? Do your define Constraints match the constraints of everything you reference? Is anything you reference UNITY_EDITOR-only while you are not?

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Five questions. They would have saved us both incidents.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: then 07 · Core: settings, logging, and the registry

lessons.title: 07 · Core: settings, logging, and the registry

chapters.title: b1
chapters.text: 07 · Core: settings, logging, and the registry

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Bovine Labs.Core is the base plate. Four subsystems matter to us.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: 1. Settings, a Scriptable Object that becomes an entity

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: The problem: designers want to tune numbers in the Inspector. E C S wants blittable data in chunks. Settings is the bridge.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Each Settings Base implements Bake(Baker<Settings Authoring>) and adds whatever components it wants onto one entity.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Which world does a settings asset land in? [Settings World("client")] says. The lookup lives in Editor Settings:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Editor Settings Utility.Get Settings<T>() does the whole dance in one call: finds or creates the asset in Assets/Settings/Settings/, reads [Settings World], and inserts it into the right prefab's array (sorted, deduped, null-pruned).

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: That one call is how our Client State Settings got wired. Read it as the supported API and never hand-edit those prefab arrays.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Probe, after creating a settings asset, confirm the link:

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: 2. K, typed constants without magic strings

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: K is a code-generated set of named byte/int constants sourced from settings assets, so layer masks and enum-ish IDs stop being magic numbers scattered through code. You will see Assets/Settings/K/ in this project. It is small; it is not on our critical path; know it exists so you do not reinvent it.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Unity Engine.Debug.Log is a managed call. Bursted code cannot make it. BLLogger is a singleton component holding a native ring buffer:

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: A managed system drains the buffer each frame and forwards to Unity's console. Grove's Graph Impl grabs it into Grove Context.Logger so any node, anywhere, can log without breaking Burst.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, this is a UART with a D M A ring buffer. The fast path writes into a circular buffer with no formatting; a slow consumer drains and formats. Same pattern, same reason.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: 4. Object Definition, a handle registry for prefabs

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: The problem: an E C S component cannot hold a prefab reference. It can hold an int.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Each prefab gets an Object Definition asset carrying a stable numeric ID. A settings asset registers them all. At bake time that becomes a lookup table; at runtime you spawn by ID.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Our two definitions: Player Capsule = 2, Player Controller = 3. Server Settings points player Controller and player Character at them, which is how Nerve's spawn code knows what to instantiate for a joining player.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: IDs are assigned by an editor post-processor, Auto Ref Processor. It batches work through Editor Application.delay Call and keeps an Already Processed Assets set marked [No Auto Statics Cleanup], so the set survives domain reload.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Trap, if an asset lands in that set before it is fully importable, it is skipped and never revisited. Symptom: every Object Definition.ID is 0 and the registry is empty, with no error. We hit this exactly once and unstuck it by reflecting into the processor to clear the set and re-run. That is unsupported and still sits in our debt list; the supported unstick is to delete Library/ and let the import order be natural.

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Four patterns, all of which you will now recognise in Nerve because Nerve is built from them:

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Inspector data then entity via a baker on a prefab in a world-targeted scene. Managed identity then runtime identity via a numeric handle and a table. Slow, managed work then ring buffer drained by a managed consumer. Editor-time wiring then a utility that owns the whole dance, not hand-edited assets.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: then 08 · Grove: a virtual machine for gameplay logic

lessons.title: 08 · Grove: a virtual machine for gameplay logic

chapters.title: b1
chapters.text: 08 · Grove: a virtual machine for gameplay logic

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: This is the chapter where your background pays the biggest dividend, because Grove is not a "visual scripting tool". Grove is a bytecode VM with an ahead-of-time linker, a flat instruction image, and a switch-dispatch interpreter generated at compile time.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: You have written one of these. Possibly for a bootloader.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: One node exists in four forms, and confusing them is the main source of Grove pain:

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, Node then Auth then Data is compile then link then flash. Execute is the instruction decoder. [Execute Node((int)Nerve Execution Types.Client Go In Game, …)] is an opcode assignment.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Literally an opcode table. The negative offset namespaces Nerve's opcodes away from Grove's built-ins so two packages can extend the same VM without colliding.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: At bake time the whole graph is flattened into one Blob Asset Reference<Graph Data>, a single contiguous allocation, relocatable, with internal offsets instead of pointers.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Nodes is a hash map, not an array, and that detail earns its keep: a runtime lookup by name is a scan, not an index. It is why Canopy resolves a named jump the way it does.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Blob Ptr<T> is a relative offset, not an address. That is what makes the whole image memcpy-able, cache-friendly, and shareable read-only across every entity running the graph.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, position-independent code with PC-relative addressing. Same trick, same reason: you do not know where it will be loaded.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Dispatch: source generation, not virtual calls

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: A blob cannot hold a delegate. So Grove's source generator scans for [Execute Node], collects every opcode, and generates a switch:

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Burst compiles that switch into a jump table. No virtual dispatch, no function pointer indirection, fully inlinable. This is why Grove is fast enough to run per-entity.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: The generic <T> on every Execute is the context type. The generator instantiates the switch once per context type, so Client App Context gets its own specialised copy with everything monomorphised.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Every node receives ref T context. Nodes are pure functions over (their data, the context). The context is how a node reaches the world.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: partial matters: the generator adds Create Generated / Update Generated / Set Chunk Generated and the IContext Generator<T> implementation by scanning your Buffer Container<> / Component Container<> fields.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: The blob is read-only and shared. Anything a node needs to remember goes in Dynamic Buffer<Grove State> on the entity, a hash map keyed by Graph State Util.Get Key, which has three overloads, (context, key), (context, scope Id, key) and (context, Hash128) (Grove/Core/Graph State Util.cs:20:31:41). The middle parameter is a scope, not a node id, a node id is merely the most common scope. The key itself is Grove State Key { graph Id, scope Id, key0, key1 }, so two graphs and two scopes never collide.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: That is exactly how Client Go In Game remembers "I already sent the remote procedure call for this connection" across ticks, and how Client Connection Tracker publishes the snapshot the gate reads.

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, blob = ROM, Grove State = RAM, Grove Context = the register file plus MMIO window. The VM is Harvard architecture.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Note the ordering that makes our client system work: Get Execution copies the context by value, so writing execution.Context.Connection afterwards is what the run actually sees.

chapters.title: b28
chapters.text: Now: what happens when you build a state machine on top of it.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Canopy is one idea: a state is a node that can contain other states. Everything else follows.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Rules the validator enforces (Canopy Graph Validation):

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: That third one is delightful and worth pausing on. Canopy State Id is a single 32-bit int (Canopy.Data/Canopy State Id.cs:12) hashed from the lowercased string (:26). Two consequences the name does not advertise: state ids are case-insensitive, Gameplay and gameplay are the same state, and 32 bits is a small enough space that collisions are worth brute-forcing for. The validator brute-forces the check at author time rather than letting you ship a 1-in-2^n heisenbug.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a CAM with collision detection at programming time. Same reason you validate a hash table's key set offline when lookups must be O(1) and correct.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: At any moment the machine has an active path from root to a leaf, not a single state. In our client graph the active path is root then gameplay. Both are active. root's blocks run every tick, which is exactly why the connection tracker lives there and keeps working no matter which child is current.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Trap, put the connection tracker on connecting instead of root and you stop detecting disconnects the moment you enter gameplay. The bug appears only after a successful connection, which is the worst possible time to find it.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: A state is a container. The work is in blocks attached to it.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Blocks receive a Canopy Update State, which is an enum-ish signal:

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Every block must check for Exit and bail. Look at any Nerve node and the first three lines are the same:

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Trap, forget that check and your block does its work while the state is being torn down, typically after the data it depends on is gone.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: There are no transition edges in the graph. A node just calls:

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: where On Disconnection is a Canopy State Id authored as a string. The machine resolves it, exits the old path bottom-up, enters the new path top-down.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: This is deliberate. Edges in a visual graph get unreadable fast; a named jump is a goto and is honest about it. The validator still checks that every Canopy Go To target exists.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Re-entrancy. Every transition bumps a version counter in grove state, and the enter and update loops recheck it to abandon a stale walk. A jump fired from inside Exit throws (Canopy State Machine.cs:461). So "check for Exit and bail" is necessary but not sufficient, you must not start a transition from a teardown path at all.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Remember History on a composite state makes re-entry resume the child you left, instead of the default child. Classic UML shallow history. Free, and occasionally exactly what a pause menu wants.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Three calls, and that is the whole driver system:

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: Plus Exit on destroy, which walks the active path calling every block with Canopy Update State.Exit so nothing leaks. Our Client App State System.On Destroy does this, skip it and the last state never cleans up.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Because "app flow" is a hierarchical state machine, and once it is data:

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: a designer can see it the validator can prove it well-formed the tests can build one in six lines (Client Connection Tracker Execution Tests does) and you can ship a different one per world without recompiling

chapters.title: b28
chapters.text: That last point is the one we exploited today: the sample shipped a service graph and a menu graph, and we added a client graph without touching a single package file.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Nerve is the layer that answers: who creates the worlds, what loads into them, who is allowed to connect, and what do they get to control?

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Bovine Labs Bootstrap implements ICustom Bootstrap. It creates Service World at startup and exposes Create Client Server Worlds(), which the service graph's Create World node calls when you press Start Game.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Trap, Requested Play Type defaults to Client And Server. In a Multiplayer Play Mode virtual player that means it builds a second Server World, which tries to bind 127.0.0.1:7979, which is already taken. Chapter 23 is entirely about this.

chapters.title: b8
